I've started reading this book on at least three separate occasions, and I've never been able to get farther than around 20% through - the front-loaded ableism is too relentless, too excruciating. The author goes out of her way to undermine it in the narrative, but as much as she portrays Morgan without infantilizing him, as much as I love his sense of humor, as delighted as I was that his nearly-first line was 'thanks for the cock block, asshole', it wasn't enough to counterbalance having to deal with Grant's perspective. The main obstacle to this novel's romance is the protagonist's stubbon prejudices and preconceptions about autism, and as an autistic reader, that killed this for me. Morgan's portrayal isn't without flaws, but he's written better than many autistic characters by non-autistic authors. If this book had just been from his point of view, I might have enjoyed it, even loved it. At the very least, I would likely have enjoyed Morgan, even if I was inwardly screaming that he deserves better than this guy he's falling for. Instead, I get battered and bruised by the narration over and over again. Yes, the entire point is for Grant to learn a lesson and stop being such a scumbag, but the lesson doesn't come anywhere soon enough for the pending romance to be worth how the setup makes me feel. This might be a perfectly fine, even great, even horizon-broadening book for non-autistic readers, but I would advise my fellow autistics to steer clear of this one.

When I'm cleaning up the house at night, I like to listen to something that doesn't require too much brain power. Since I enjoy mysteries, I thought this book might be a good fit. It wasn't. There's a big difference between "doesn't require too much brain power" and "kills brain cells due to the sheer stupidity of the writing." It should be enough just to say that a huge turning point toward the end of the book occurs when the chief medical examiner (and one of the main characters) reveals that she ASSUMED that some physical evidence found at the scene belonged to the victim and not the killer. Therefore she never had it tested. HUH?! I'm supposed to believe that this woman, who is said to be one of the best in the state of California, never tested physical evidence found at the scene of a murder? And it's mentioned so offhandedly, as though that's a normal thing to happen. Oh brother. The characters were flat, the mystery was thin, the friendships between the women were cliched, boring, and not believable, and the romance was plain awful. And what's worse, there was too much sexual deviance to the mystery, which is ironic since I chose the book thinking that I'd avoid that sort of thing with Patterson. Bleh.
It was all very well and good, until the rushed ending, which left part of the plot hanging in the air.
Just One of the Guys is a feel good novel with a great HEA. Who can resist? I've read this several times and I've loved it each time.

When I started this book, I had a very clear image in my mind of what the lawyer, Jake, was going to be like: noble, dignified, patient, wise, he would be a heroic warrior for the oppressed and victimized. In short, I opened the book and hoped to find the second coming of Atticus Finch. I was disappointed. Jake wasn't a bad character, he was more realistic than Atticus in a lot of ways, but I just couldn't help but compare the two and find Jake somewhat less than amazing. There was also a comment about how he sought a wife who would be happy to make babies and not try to wear the pants that, to be honest, kind of pissed me off, but that's an issue for another day. The story was interesting and offered an extensive look on the debate over taking the law into ones own hands and seeking retribution. For a first novel, it was pretty good, but I feel like it could have done with being a bit shorter. I plan to read more of Grishams books in the future when I'm looking for a quick read.

where this had power originally, it retains its impact. watching the joker beat robin with a crowbar is as horrendous now as it was then ~ so this book will always have an important place in not only batman lore, but all of comic book lore. if you can read it just to appreciate the genuine shock of robin's death, it's well worth it. unfortunately the rest of the story from there goes south in a bad way, which makes it harder to take seriously. maybe 10-15 years ago i could have given this four stars, but it hasn't aged well at all. the art and coloring (gad, the coloring) is uniformly dated. the writing, with a few moments of exception, is mostly pretty weak, and likewise trapped in another era entirely. a must-read for batman fans, people catching up to what's "canon" in the current dc universe, and serious students of comic book history. not recommended for the casual reader since without serious context, it could all be laughably silly.

An interesting premise for a book, but it's so devoid of any redeemable qualities that I really can't recommend it at all. My problems with the book: A Flat Main Character- As a character Amy, or as I mentally referred to her throughout- 'Sad Sack' - is just too sad. Everything is terrible, no one likes her, everyone is mean to her, her mother is a drug addict who doesn't love her, she lives in a sad trailer park, her mother steals her money, she is bullied and manipulated by other people, etc... it just went on, and on, and on... we get it already Sad Sack is the sympathetic character. The author attempts to flesh out Sad Sack by making her appear to struggle with a variety of 'moral' choices but these feel so contrived and one sided that they merely emphasize her flatness. A Cartoonishly Terrible World-The world of Oz is so over the top terrible as to be ridiculous. I've read some reviews that describe it as being like 'The Nightmare before Christmas' and I feel like that's a fair characterization. But sometimes less is more- especially with books, and describing weird henchmen- one of whom shoots deadly bubbles from a tube in their mouth, and another who has a bicycle for a body- isn't creepy-- it's stupid, and it emphasizes how unrefined every other aspect of this book is. A Poorly Plotted out Plot- throughout the book we build to what is initially portrayed as a complex assassination plan but eventually boils down to attempting to stab Dorothy at a dinner party-- and it doesn't even manage to deliver in that respect leaving us with a cliff-hanger ending, and the unappetizing prospect of a sequel or 2. Teenage Nonsense- Sad sack manages to fall in love with every one with a Y chromosome in the book for no discernible reason other than superficial attractiveness. We are also treated to a wide range of unnecessary commentary regarding everyone's clothes, footwear, makeup, and hairstyles while artfully skirting anything approaching meaningful character development. This book will likely only appeal to teenage goths, or fans of similarly terrible books like Twilight, or A Discovery of Witches.

Originally posted at Vampire Book Club In every generation a set of triplets is born. Each blessed by the Goddess with powers. In this time it's Mirabella, an elemental who can conjure the fiercest storms, Katharine, a poisoner who is able to ingest the deadliest of poisons without a bat of the eye, and Arsinoe, a naturalist who can control the most lethal animals in the kingdom. In the end there can be only one. Sorry I couldn't help myself! So, in all seriousness, only one Queen can sit atop the throne. When the girls turn sixteen, all bets are off as Beltane approaches, which means it's open season for the Queens to fight each other to the death. The poisoners have held the position for many years running. But this time around it seems as though Mirabella, the elemental, could usurp their closely guarded power. Of course each Queen has their own set of backers and they will each do everything they can to assure their Queen wins. From the beginning, it's clear that the girls are pretty much pawns in a bid for power between the varying factions on Fennbirn island. As we quickly learn, they're each not above devious plots in order to assure their Queen wins. Right off the bat I felt sadness for these girls. The pressure to be able to perform their magics to perfection and convince people to support them coupled with the fact that at the end of it all they have to kill two of their sisters in order to be crowned is quite terrible. Added to this is the fact that, despite some affection, the families that foster the Queens through their lives are more in a bid for power rather than looking out for the best interests of the girls. Through all this, however, I loved each of the Queens for who they are and the lives they have separate from their destiny. Each chapter switches point of view from one Queen to another (or from a member of their retinue). They are each so unique and their personalities so different, Kendare Blake makes it really easy to understand what each Queen is going through, and makes it easy for readers to want all of them to somehow, at the end of all of this, succeed and be happy. Because one other thing that has been clear, with the dread of what is to come upon their sixteenth birthdays, it's difficult for any of the girls to be truly happy. As is common in many courtly-type books, there is a lot of intrigue. This type of common plot thread always makes it hard for me to really connect with some of the characters because I'm always paranoid of ulterior motives. Besides the Queens, it was difficult for me to really like any of the secondary characters due to this fact. And with all the switching points of view it was easy to confuse which character is supposed to support which Queen. I really loved the world and mythology Kendare Blake sets up with Three Dark Crowns. So many actions hinge on events and traditions of the past. Every time we would get background information on the Queens that came before I would sit up and listen with rapt attention. The pacing is at times slow, but it's always steady. There were enough twists and turns throughout that it easily kept me reading "just one more chapter." Three Dark Crowns is definitely a set-up for what is to come next, and I can't wait to see what that will be.

meh, I didn't hate it. I like Stephanie, she's smart, funny and tough when she needs to be but I found it lacking in some parts. It's a good read, a good mystery and crime just not something to write home about. But alas, I am still going to read the next one.

Then at the end of the book Noah suddenly wants Dave and BAM they have sex! Where's the build-up? There was not even a hint that they would get together. This was disappointing and ruined the story.

So, my second time reading this book, it became apparent to me why I had to read the next one to get officially hooked on this series: while she's an obviously gifted storyteller, Gabaldon hadn't yet hit her "writing stride" with her first book. A few scenes were started or ended much too abruptly and were a bit confusing as a result, and there were some editing errors that I hate to hold against the book but kind of do anyway. For instance, Geillis Duncan was described as having gray eyes a few times, when they are clearly supposed to be green (as noted in the later books). But nevertheless, it was a wonderful story as I remembered, and I constantly marvel at the fact that this was not written by a Scottish or English woman but an American from freaking Arizona! Which just blows my mind since I don't understand how she so precisely conjured the Scottish Highlands when she lives in the desert. And I'm again struggling not to start the second one (I have a new bestseller on hold at the library and have to finish that one first). P.S. Weirdly, I was having trouble thinking of Jamie as a young man again. He makes more sense to me as a middle-aged guy, what with his learned-ness and wisdom and such.

Thanks to HarperCollins for providing my with an ARC of this book in exchange for an honest review. This in no way impacted my views and opinions below. This was hands down the most epic conclusion to a fantasy series ever. Take notes, authors! Complex, electrifying, and gorgeous, this book managed to wrap everything up perfectly - but not in that cliche perfect way. There were still stuff that everyone had to deal with obviously, but overall this was a very satisfying conclusion to a duology. I admit, at first, it took me a few days to actually get into the book, which was mostly due to the fact that I didn't reread The Orphan Queen and I forgot a few stuff, but I still managed. So I'd definitely recommend a reread before going into this book. Okay, can we just talk about how much I admire Wil?! She has to deal with reclaiming her kingdom, which is in pieces, in a time fraught with disaster and chaos. I love how she dealt with the pressure of everything and I think her character growth is off the charts! As for Tobiah, I admit I was iffy about him at the beginning. However, I've really grown to like him and become emotionally attached to him. The secondary characters like James and Melanie were reallyy dimensional. I didn't like Melanie in the first book, though. This is because I felt like her relationship with Wil wasn't portrayed very well. For the first half of TMK, Wil goes on and on about the strong friendship bond between them but I really couldn't bring myself to care about Melanie until halfway through. The Ospreys, on the other hand, were extremely memorable characters. The dynamic and bonds they had with each other were realistic and I just loved their interactions! I felt a little twinge in my heart when I thought they died. The characters in this duology are spot on, to be honest. The plot of The Mirror King is even more complex than that of The Orphan Queen's. Literally, there was never a dull moment. The book opens up immediately after The Orphan Queen's drama - smack-dab in the middle of it, in fact. It really sucks you in from beginning to finish; such a page turner! I was worried about how everything is going to happen in one book because there are a ton of things to be done, but Jodi managed that excellently. The important loose ends were tied, not hastily (thank god), and the character's troubles were far from over but it was still an excellent conclusion. I can't even find the words to describe how satisfying it was to finish this book. In short, The Mirror King features a memorable cast of characters, excellent character development, a hell of an intricate plot, and it was a perfect wrap-up to the series. Props to Jodi Meadows for this exceptional duology! Follow me on my blog, Book Whizz | Bloglovin' | Twitter

I am so fucking confused. I don't know how to rate this book, I don't know what I thought of it. I don't know how to explain it. I just don't fucking understand it. No rating. I can't, I just can't. What is this book? I don't even know what to classify it as. Is it purely contemporary or was there supposed to be magical aspects of it? Was I supposed to be left with the feeling that there was going to be a sequel, and that this was a fantastical novel? I just don't know. And I feel like the synopsis is incredibly misleading, not very true to the actual story-line. First of all. The writing. I understand what the author was trying to do with it. The MC, Gwendolyn, has been in and out of mental institutions since she was 12 years old. Her naivete about the world, and her social awkwardness felt very refreshing in the beginning of the story. But then it quickly morphed into a stream of consciousness that is so hard to follow. The dialogue was choppy, the details were told through the eyes of someone who just doesn't understand the world and the people in it. It was true to a character who has had problems with her mental health. However, it just didn't work for me. Her thoughts were confusing, hectic, and a complete mess. Just like she was. It didn't really endear me to her character, especially with her bipolar moods and utter ignorance about everyone and everything. Second of all. "The romance." I was not a fan of any kind of romance or love interest in this story. The little drama with James and Lane seemed to be there just to create jealousy. And Peter was a psycho. Seriously. I didn't swoon over him; I didn't have a good feeling about him. I don't know where the author was trying to go with him. I just didn't trust him. He's manipulative, dangerous, and possessive. And not in a good way! I didn't feel the chemistry between them, and their relationship just felt.. odd. It was just as confusing as the messed-up plot and characters. Third of all. The secondary characters. They didn't feel three-dimensional. Not to mention, I just didn't get why all of them were needed in the story. Namely, James and Lane (and even Orchid). People have found comparisons between them and people from the original Peter Pan story, so maybe that's why they were in there. But they didn't add anything to the story, nor did they provide the MC with strong relationships. Fourth of all. The plot. This plot was confusing as hell; it was a jumbled mess of nonsense dialogue, characters who seemed to be thrown in there randomly to create angst and drama, and the flashbacks/memories that were tossed in to add to the MC's mental problems were puzzling. I still don't understand where it all ties in and why the book was ended like that. Fifth of all. I am just so damn conflicted right now. I don't even know what the hell I read. I have never in my life been so confused after finishing a book. I don't even know if I liked it. Am I just completely missing the point? Am I so stupid that I'm overlooking the message of the story? Maybe it's just me. In fact, I seem sure of this. The book has five star reviews on Goodreads, so what the hell did I get from this that's got me so confused that others seemed to understand and love? Girl Lost was one of those books that I'm probably going to be in the minority about. I don't even know how to rate it. This was a completely different retake on the popular story of Peter Pan. But I don't think it worked. At least, not for me. AND THIS IS A STANDALONE. Yup, I give up on ever wondering what the author wanted to tell people.

It's funny, I feel like this book was the one that Milan was most interested in writing-the other stories were a way to set this one up. And while this one was good, it also felt like the most...conventional of the three, at least somewhat. Insofar as Milan's characters are ever fully conventional, at least. Having said that, everything I enjoyed about the previous books (especially the appropriate use of history not only as widow dressing, but as plot!) remains true here as well.

There are parts of this book that are great, but then there's the fact that I walked away from it for months and wasn't the least bit curious what happened. I did come back and finish it and I have mixed feelings. I think JK's an amazing writer and in I love some of the characters, but I didn't really care get amped up about the heart of the story being the contents of another book. Not sure I'm terribly interested in continuing this series.

The men in this book are fucking idiots. Arin is in competition with Ronan for the title "Most Painfully Moronic". Ronan is so hurt over being friend zoned that he throws tantrums every chance he gets. She wasn't interested before and she's not interested now. But he has to blame some other guy for ruining his claim to her. I get that this is not the most progressive society, but come on. Even his sister is hurt that Kestrel didn't choose her brother and I'm like, "So years worth of friendship mean nothing. You'd rather have everyone be unhappy settling for less. Your brother will realize that the woman he loves doesn't love him back and he's wasting his time when he could be looking for someone else or, I don't know, just find happiness with himself?" It's a soap drama in here with the cliche misunderstandings and the lies. Especially Arin when he constantly criticizes Kestrel for being cold-hearted just because she has to marry the prince. I want to slap Arin and scream, "You are at fucking war. There's no time for you to be obtuse because your dick hurts!" I mean, Kestrel is trying to overthrow a tyrant and bring about a new era of peace. But all Arin cares is getting his dick wet not understanding the imminent danger if they're caught showing their true feeeeeelings. Honestly, he is the largest threat to freeing the Herrani people. Just fuck this guy. Kill him off (but I know he's protected by plot armor). I don't find these men attractive when they are the biggest hindrance to this story. This book would have been astronomically better if Kestrel was allowed to go all out with the political intrigue and maneuvering. She's too good and I still can't believe she's being held back by a petty romance. What's even more insulting is that Kestrel couldn't see the injustice of racism, slavery, and imperialism without the power of luuuurrrve. Are you saying these things are okay as long as you aren't sexually attracted to someone oppressed? Cover Review: Generic. The use of the sword for the "I" is meh. It's obvious that the sword's photoshopped in. To be fair, the cover matches the tone of the story. I can't anything seriously. I can't make sense of the choices.

**3.5 Stars** State of Wonder was very well written. I found myself in Manaus then the Amazon right along with Marina. The book did have a slower start which is why it took me longer than normal to read it. However, when it did get a "jump start" the book really took off. I was a little disappointed with the ending. It was a mixture of unhappy and happy and I would have preferred one or the other, rather than the mix. On a whole, it is a book I would recommend to certain people, but not to everyone.

Gideon was another win for me. I admit, he loved Jacob more, but it was pretty close. Gideon is a powerful, acient of the the demon race, the oldest still alive. I knew from the start it was going to be much different than reading Jabobs thoughts. Gideon has lived so long, too long to really remember what it is like to love and feel. He's use to keeping everything personal bottled up, even from himself. It takes Magdelegna (Legna) to sooth him, and even that wasn't easy. After reading Jacobs story I was dying to know what Gideon and Legna's past was. Why was Legna so hostile towards him, and how would their story prevale. I was excited to get into it, and was satisified with such a great tale these two have made. I'm a sucker for mysterious, lonely male characters, and Gideon is certianlly that. Legna was also a great character. She's the sister of the Demon alpha named Noah(Who's story I'm BEGGING to read!) She's the most beautiful demoness, with a great personility and a calming pressence. She's also a mind demon, the baby of the family and pretty much misjudged. She grows beautifully in this story, and I hope to see more of them throughout the series. As series go, this is a new favorite for me. I look forward to each new book, and recommed it to all paranormal romance lovers!

Blog post: http://sonichreads.tumblr.com/post/16... Review: Despite Anna and the French Kiss being a shit book, I continued on because I forgot everything in Stephanie Perkins's books. I don't hate Lola and the Boy Next Door, but I don't think that this book was good in anyway at all. Let's just say that I'm cold-hearted and harsh on books, but did you see other books that I gave 5 stars? Yeah. Lola and the Boy Next Door would not stand out except for its writing. It was better than Anna and the French Kiss and of course I had quite a time with it. It was pretty enjoyable, not boring but not phenomenal. I did really like the writing and that's why this book did not stay at one star from me. Sure enough, this is the part where I complain. First off, I don't get why this book always and ALWAYS brings up the age gap between Lola and her boyfriend. You know, I really HATE when things are being repeated. It's really annoying and boring and uncomfortable at a certain subject such as this one. Most relationships stay strong because of trust that both sides give each other, but I really did not see any from this book. Lola was a liar from the first time she met Max and she kept on lying to him despite Max not trusting her, their relationship remained the same. Which is odd. There were trust issues surrounding this relationship and Lola still had the balls to say that Max was going to be the one. Right. Your ass. Unlike Anna and the French Kiss, this book isn't about cheating but almost. Basically this is like St. Clair's point of view excluding the cheating. Lola certainly wanted to be with Max but kept leading Cricket on. What is it about Perkins's books that always put the love interest in the nicest way possible whereas the other guys were sort of a dick or maybe hanging naked girls on their walls? Lola was not what I like as a character. She was so immature and whiny. What the hell. I'm not too sure if I like Cricket but where the fuck did the author get her inspiration from and name him Cricket? Seriously. Overall: I did not expect anything better from this book. The characters are okay. The plot was terrible. Wouldn't recommend.

This one fell flat. I enjoyed the descriptions of the landscape and national parks (especially Zion because we just visited last fall and it was incredible! ), but the two sections of the book didn't connect well, the dialogue was boring, and the story line was too slow for my taste.

I was a little underwhelmed :( Thoughts: From what I've read, a lot of people think that the book starts off slowly and picks up its pace toward the end. I disagree. In my opinion it's the other way around, and after the first 150 pages or so, the story just lost it's pacing for me. Nothing seemed to be happening really and after the excitement of Gollum and the Trolls and Spiders, it all seemed to get a little dull. I wanted MORE from the characters! Bilbo was funny and had me chuckling, and Gollum just gets all the love heart eyes from me in the world, but other than that I didn't really feel like I knew many of the characters. I wanted more backstory. The songs were fun, if not a little tedious towards the end. It's become evidently clear that I'm not too good at putting words to a tune in my head - I more read them as poetry and they didn't really add much to the story because of that. I loved the world that Tolkien created. And some of his concepts were fascinating to me! But once again I felt they were lacking in explanation or portrayal - I wanted to experience things like Thunder Battles and The Elven Kingdoms more than I was allowed to. I liked the character development in Bilbo. The fact that we got to see him evolve from a Hobbit who loved nothing more than his kettle into a stealth burglar, was pretty awesome. I liked the narration style - it was like being transported back into childhood and listening to someone tell me a fascinating tale of mystery and magic ... very clever. Overall I found the Hobbit to be a readable book, but definitely one intended originally for children. It lacked in vital things such as character development and back story in my opinion, and would have gotten four stars if it had kept up the excitement and pace that it had at the beginning, all the way to the end. See what I thought of the movie adaptation here: The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey
Great book, I compared it to the Hobbit in terms of awesomeness.

I loved the premise of this one: four waves of destruction have wiped 7 billion people off the planet. Only the lucky--or unlucky--have survived. No one knows what the 5th wave is, but surely it must be horrific. The only thing the survivors know is that the aliens are wearing human faces and it's impossible to know who to trust. It's bleak, it's scary, and I was excited to dive in. But given everything I just said, this book was somehow more cerebral than action-y. The characters often waxed philosophical about humanity and what it means to survive than actually showing us how they survived. Don't get me wrong, though: there was action, especially in the last quarter or so of the book. Perhaps I got spoiled (irreparably damaged?) by books such as Ilsa J. Bick's Ashes where there's an apocalyptic hellscape I would not be able to survive in for longer than two seconds, and just when she gets you good and terrified over the state of the planet, she slams her foot on the gas and doesn't let up until you careen into a cliff (and then are left rocking back and forth in a corner for a year until you can get the next installment). I never felt that anxious or worried during The 5th Wave. Which probably says more about me than the book! Ultimately, this one just wasn't for me, methinks. There's a movie in the works, though, I hear; it'd make a killer movie. And I'll be first in line at the theatre!

This is a swoon worthy story that left me with a huge smile on my face and I loved every single second of reading this one! Simon and Abby are so obviously perfect for each other that I wanted to just skip past all the obstacles and get right to their happily ever after! Simon is such a delicious bundle of yummy male and the fact that he's a single father just makes him that much more irresistible. His interactions with his daughter Hayden were so sweet that I couldn't get enough of them together. This is hands down one of the most beautiful and touching love stories I've read in quite a while and this is a perfect story for anyone who's looking for something uplifting to read. Sweet love story. Well written with great characters. Funny and romantic. I recommend it to all romance readers. Two thumbs up!

1%: Jack is very annoying. He narrates in a way such that he knows he's in a book ... it really irritates me the way he tells the reader not to continue reading, but tempts them to at the same time. Posted to Almost Grown-up: After reading Divergent, I felt like I started foaming at the mouth with want every time the word Insurgent was mentioned. That's probably a bit creepy, but I friggin' LOVED Divergent and was beyond excited to continue reading a new favorite series. The day Insurgent came out found me walk-jogging into the nearest bookstore to buy my own copy. We catch up with Tris nearly immediately after her would-be initiation day and the battle that took place there. To be perfectly honest, I am both glad and and disappointed that I couldn't make time to reread Divergent beforehand, so I wasn't bothered by any reported continuity errors, but I found myself struggling to recall the exact events that are referred to throughout Insurgent. My reading of Insurgent was a somewhat confused one. Tris, Tobias (Four), and others that they travel with move around a lot. My feelings... and essentially ratings then started to fluctuate wildly. After less than ideal circumstances, Tris and Four are now together. But their relationship no longer feels like a healthy one. It seems they argue as much as they do anything else and Four starts pulling one of my least favorite behaviors, occasionally adopting an "I know best" attitude. Fortunately, it's not a constant thing for him, so it only irritated me and didn't make me hate him. Tris becomes a character who starts to feel a bit flat to me as well. Her Divergence and aptitude for other factions seems like an excuse to make her a little too much of the hero. Certain scenes have other characters turning to Tris for advice because she had an aptitude for Erudite, so despite her age, lack of training or experience in that faction, lack of insider knowledge, and lack of seniority even within her own faction, clearly she's the best one to make a plan. It felt like a stretch. The long slog through the middle of the novel moving from faction to faction had me somewhat bored. The difference between those scenes and the action is marked. Because adventure and action is where Veronica Roth's writing really shines. Those were the scenes that had me wide-eyed, frantically turning to the next page. Those were the scenes that had me completely in their thrall and pulled the Insurgent's rating up for me. And that ending... hoo boy. What a cliffhanger. Let's just say that I can't wait for the next novel. Overall rating: 3.5/5. Not as much of a WOW as Divergent, but a decent follow-up.

She carries a gun in a specially made purse just in case although she's getting careless. This is a fraction of what we now know about her. (See? I shouldn't already know all this on page 6.) But what did the book in for me was this line on said page six: "It took awhile to get there on foot, since I was trying to stay out of sight and to avoid breaking an ankle in my new, over-the-knee, high-heeled boots. I'd bought them because they matched the cute leather mini the salesgirl had talked me into, and I'd planned to wow them at the club after work, but they weren't exactly made for speed." There is so much wrong with these two sentences aside from the stilted writing. Why do so many urban fantasy heroines dress like hookers? Why would she wear this sleazy outfit to work (where she had been at the start of the scene) which is a travel agency where presumably customers come in? Why wouldn't she change she was done for the day? Wearing this to work and later wowing them at the club? Not keeping a low profile. Why would you wear such an impractical outfit with people out there trying to kill you who nearly succeeded once. Why wouldn't you take the boots off so you could run faster since your life depends on it? So clearly she's an idiot and more worried about what she looks like than staying alive. I am not reading this book.

I'd decided to take a pass on Soulprint, or at least wait for reviews to come out. The title sounded New-Agey and the plot like sci-fi. Then I read a rave review on Goodreads from Ashley of Nose Graze and decided to give this book a try for review. I'm so glad I did. Soulprint is an excellent thriller with a super-cool premise, but it's also a story with philosophical themes, well-developed characters, and a touching romance. There are sci-fi aspects, but if you're not a fan of that, the science isn't a huge part of the story. What I loved most was the way the book ingeniously blends something age-old -- the idea that souls can be reincarnated -- with something speculative and high-tech -- the idea that souls can be analyzed like DNA and then tracked when they are reborn in a new body. Alina, the main character, knows she is the reincarnated soul of June, a notorious murderer. As such, she's spent her life in a high security prison. The book begins in action, with Alina being broken out of prison by people whose motives aren't immediately apparent, and I was gripped right away. Once Alina is broken out, the story slows down. She learns more about the people who've helped her and what their motivations are -- or are they being completely honest with her? She also begins to feel June's presence within her -- or is she imagining it? This slowdown in pace was an interesting narrative choice for a thriller-y story, but it also offers some breathing room for character development and the exploration of some of Soulprint's themes, questions like: Are we a product of our pasts? Do we have free will? What is the nature of the soul, and could those qualities that make us individual and unique carry on after our physical bodies are gone? I think that Soulprint has a little something for every reader: an intriguing scientific premise, a daring prison break, some interesting philosophical questions, and a sweet romance. Ashley's right -- give it a try! I received an advance copy of this book for review. You can read my full review here on YA Romantics

This Song Will Save Your Life tells a story of a young girl named Elise who has been drowned by her issues and insecurities of having no friends and never fitting in. This caused her to change and reinvent herself into someone like them, but her attempts were unsuccessful. Driven by frustration and sorrow, she thinks of a better way of solving her problems. And with that, she ends up with an even more scarring life experience to carry on her shoulders. But fate stepped in as she accidentally stumbles into the best underground party in the world that made her experience new things, and eventually changed her life This book tackles not only the usual inequalities of the hierarchical high school world, but also issues about bullying and it's severe effects to those who people involved. We've heard that a few time before, but what makes this book a stand out for me is that Elise, although she wants to become like everybody else, refuses to listen to the kind of music popular today. It's the one thing she's not willing to let go or change. That was the beam of light in the darkness that surrounds Elise, which became even brighter when she discovers her love for DJing. Speaking of Elise, there were times that I really had been exasperated with her behavior and her choices. Maybe because I have never felt what she felt, but still, I got irked sometimes. But most of the times, I do get why she acts that way. So for the most part, Leila Sales has created relatable Elise. The other characters, especially Vicks and Mel, were pretty awesome as well. They were their own, exploding with personality and individuality. But I don't want to talk about Char, or Pippa, or Emily. The other characters felt like small extras in a big film due. For the plot, it was okay. I still have mixed feelings for it. I liked it in general, but I'm not sure if I liked some of the little things that happened on the sidelines. I am still a little skeptical with the ending because of what happened to Elise at school, what happened to Alex, or even Pippa or Char. There were a lot of loose ends that I feel were essential for Elise's characters growth, and even for the satisfaction of the readers. But all in all Leila Sales has delivered something good. A good coming-of-age stories for those who feel like they don't belong. Plus, the title and cover is amazing!

John Steinbeck makes his characters so realistic and easy to relate to. Lennie and George are ranch hands in constant search of work. The problem they have keeping a position once they find one, is due to the mental state of Lennie. He is strong and more than capable of hard labor, but his child-like mind causes him to react with fear and rage when misunderstood. George is Lennie's friend and tries to cover his back when things go wrong. He promises Lennie that one day they will have enough money to buy a place of their own and live off the fat of the land ... raising rabbits. Lennie loves to feel soft things and catches mice to feel their soft fur. He is mesmerized by a litter of pups and wants to constantly stroke and pet one he has picked out to keep. He inadvertently kills these tiny animals because of his rough handling, and worries that George won't let him tend to the rabbits they one day plan to raise. When Lennie has a run-in with the wife of Curley (another rancher) he can't resist her soft hair and ends up breaking her neck. Lennie hides, waiting for George. He knows that they will have to leave again quick, in search of another place to work, because of the BAD trouble he has caused. In the end George finds Lennie and calms him down, telling him to look way out on the horizon and picture the future life they have planned together. Then George shoots Lennie before the angry ranchers catch up to them and take matters into their own hands. George knows this is the only way to peacefully put an end to Lennie's troubled life. There are several other characters that interact with Lennie and George. Each one can be studied to show that Lennie wasn't the only one suffering. There is the black stable boy, Crooks, who is lonely and has a memorable line saying, "A guy goes nuts if he ain't got nobody. Don't make no difference who the guy is, long's he's with you." Then there is Candy, who had to have his dog shot after it became stiff and old. Now that was one sad scene, foreshadowing the end, where George is faced with his difficult decision. This is a short but 'meaty' book that will leave you thinking. There are many similarities between the characters and overlapping situations. Told by a master storyteller, Steinbeck has a knack for painting a picture of humanity, true to the times.
Triumph of mediocrity.

I think I liked this one even better than the first in the series, which I really liked. Plot-wise this book isn't quite as directed as Nexus. There are a lot of separate, only marginally-related plots going. But all of that is totally fine if the book is read as part of the trilogy, as it is meant to be. The only true criticism I have for the book is the number of overly-convenient plot devices built from Nexus-connectivity. That said, as sweeping as the vision of post-human evolution was in the first book, this one was even more mind-blowing and inspiring. Lots of interesting technology was brought up, perplexing ethical dilemmas explored, and scarier evils revealed. It was a really good read that made me think a lot. I'm excited to finish the trilogy!

Disappointing sequel to Anne of Green Gables. You know those episodes of Gilmore Girls where Lorelai and Rory were reduced to bit players and the writers instead turned their attention to the townsfolk of Stars Hollow (Taylor, Miss Patti, Jackson, etc.)? Anne of Avonlea is a bit like that. Anne doesn't get a storyline of her own: she just gets to play match-maker to a lonely woman and act as nursemaid to a rascal of a small boy. Worse still, the whole thing feels contrived and overwritten. I'm hoping the next book in the series, Anne of the Island, will be a return to the form of Green Gables. (Side note: Should I make comparing literary classics to WB shows a recurring motif in my book reviews? Next time: the uncanny similarities between Faulkner and Dawson's Creek! ...okay, no.)

Love Love Love Love Love! Charlotte Bronte is a genius! This isn't a book I would normally be crazy about because it's so long and descriptive but she did it so well. For a time I was sad that I didn't have to read this in High School but now that I think about it, I don't think I was old enough to grasp everything that this book has to offer. It's much more than a love story, it's a coming of age tale and its fantastic! On a side note, I wasn't exactly convinced of Jane and Mr. Rochester's love at first. It seemed almost unbelievable and a little too much for such a young girl. But besides that little mishap, I loved it! "I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will." "Life appears to me too short to be spent in nursing animosity or registering wrongs."

I gave up trying at 160 pages of 314, which I think is a decent amount to have read in order to decide if you're going to like a book or not. So, initially I picked this book up because of all the incredible hype it was getting on goodreads/tumblr/booktube. Hype hadn't lead me wrong with Six of Crows and A Darker Shade of Magic, but I suppose for every Captive Prince, there's a Twilight. This book was a recipe of everything I love: a gunslinger female lead, magical desert horses, an adventure quest. I think right after I bought the book, I discovered the author was white. That was my first red flag. Because the world-building in this book reads like every stereotype of Middle Eastern culture. Amani's hometown is so dramatically awful, with things like abusive men taking multiple wives, child brides, etc, that it is basically the "barbaric brown people" trope personified. And Amani herself is, of course, special because she has blue eyes. Her love interest Jin is from a peaceful place which seems to be loosely based on Asian culture. The more I read, I was honestly shocked that so few people seem to have read this and thought it was okay. I'm all for mixing different real world cultural aspects with fantasy, but when you're only using the bad parts to set up conflict, it feels very two dimensional, and, honestly, damaging. So now if we take these elements away, what are we left with? Nothing that makes up for it. I was genuinely slogging through this book. The writing is mediocre. I hate to go at someone who is a debut author, who I'm sure worked hard at this, but man, you could tell it was someone's first book. It followed what I think of as Disney physics. Meaning action would jump from one point to another, leaving you questioning how. And sometimes something would happen with impossible results: like in Tangled when Flynn's horse is jumping from rooftop to rooftop. It's a cartoon, you can do that! But I'm probably supposed to find things that happen in this book at least vaguely believable (not talking about the magic), and yet. No. Also, the plot in general was...? So it starts off with Amani trying to win money in a shooting tournament to help fund her way out of her shitty town, so she can go live with an aunt she's never met in a city she's never seen. She ends up basically wasting a ton of the money she'd saved just entering the tournament, and doesn't win because it's rigged, etc. So the whole first chunk of this book is just her trying to get out of her town-- jumping in because I HAVE to comment on the weird, inexplicable train thing. Amani has guards who are after her in her hometown, because she helped a wanted man, Jin. So she escapes them and then buys a ticket to take a train to go to her aunt. Her cousin just HAPPENS to be on the same train as her, and just hates her because ?? and alerts guards from her town that she's on the train, who are also on it because ?? And the whole thing is just so contrived and ? Anyway, so the plot is that she wants to go somewhere she thinks might be relatively safer than where she lived, even though Jin keeps telling her it's terrible there. This is literally the whole plot of the first 160+ pages, them just traveling to a place. I felt like I was reading Harry Potter and friends camping again, or Roland and Susan in The Dark Tower hunting that damn deer. Like please get on with the story. And maybe something more interesting happens later, but man, I can only take so much. My TBR pile is too big to waste time on stuff that can't even catch me in the first hundred pages. Hard pass on this series.

I had pretty high hopes going into this one, and while they weren't met I do think this was a solid novel. There are a lot of good things this book has going, but I still wouldn't rate it above a three as far as my personal enjoyment goes. You see, this is one of those books that is renowned for being so terrifying and mind blowing, and it really isn't. This is not a scary book at all. Not once did I feel remotely creeped out by this book, and that was the biggest disappointment to me. NASA has run out of funding so they come up with the brilliant plan to hold a contest that brings three teens from around the world to the moon for 172 hours. We end up with Mia from Norway, who wants to have a famous band and has no interest in going to the moon, Midori from Japan, looking to rebel, and Antoine from Paris, who is completely unremarkable in any way, seeming as I read this book hours ago and have already forgotten him. Once they get to the moon it seems things might be more sinister than they thought. Another huge issues I had with this book was the set up. It takes the characters over 150 pages to get to the moon, and in a 350 page book that is a huge amount. Those first 150 pages are completely set up. Don't get me wrong, taking time to set up your characters and their lives is great. In this case, it didn't work. Because of all this set up, I quickly lost interest in the initially intriguing story. These characters are developed, but they aren't interesting. I never connected to them in the slightest, which made it hard to care about the things happening to them. Other than that, the writing was good and the premise is still cool, even if the execution was a bit off. I know there are people who will really enjoy this book, so I would encourage you to read other reviews if you are on the fence and determine if this is your brand of "scary". This book undoubtedly has its good moments but was just okay for me.
I don't think I would even enjoy this one. Sorry not sorry.

I couldn't finish. Like legit, I could not go one. Somehow Rose lost all sense she gained from the 4th book which I kind of enjoyed and just turned plain stupid. Why is she so obsessed with Dimitri, does she not remember how cold he was? Does she not remember that he pretty much held her hostage and made her forget WHY she was trying to kill him? IS SHE THAT STUPID? So why is this book all about her journey to saving Dimitri. FUCK, Dimitri, I don't know she didn't just stay with Adrian who's nice and treated her well. UGH, I'm so mad how she treated Adrian, usually I do not root for the side piece (which is what Adrian was), usually I'm always Team Guy She Dated First and usually get mad when she chooses the side piece. This is NOT THE CASE Adrian is BAMF, he's awesome, he's funny, sure he has his vices and he's not all perfect like the perfect Dimitri who became a Strigoi but at least he had depth! Dimitri did not. He was just perfect and boring and whatever, honestly, Rose deserves to be alone. She's so selfish, she continuously gets her friends in trouble, she continuously doesn't give a fuck about anybody else but herself. I went from loving her during the first book and progressively I started hating her more. By the 5th book, I started rooting that someone, maybe her friends would just put her out of her misery OR that she actually starts giving a fuck about her friends and supposedly the "love of her life". She doesn't. I'm done with this series. I stopped at 30% of this book and I knew that it doesn't get better from this. Rose somehow gets stupider and everyone else continues to let Rose go downwards spiral of selfishness. But it's okay because Rose is SOOO AWESOME, she's such a great warrior blah blah, who gives a fuck. I no longer care what happens with Rose which I find out she somehow SAVES Dimitri. UGH, Richelle Mead should have just let Dimitri die or stay a Strigoi.

"Whoever had decided that school should start so early in the morning and last all day long needed to be hunted down and forced to watch hours of educational television without the aid of caffeine." I met this author at a movie convention and bought this book, had it signed, planned to read it soon...but then it sat on my shelves for years for some reason. That's the story of my life with books. The writing style is simple and humorous, which should be enjoyable for the middle school age. It was a little too simplified for my tastes, but the story was good enough to stay interesting. I would have liked a bit more complication, but again it's middle school age, so that's more forgivable under that circumstance. Vlad is a hybrid who goes to school like any other normal child, but he soon finds out that he is being unfairly judged by a vampire council I wanted to strangle. There's a few oddball characters where you're not sure if they're trustworthy or not, but all ended up okay on the last pages. Basically a fun book with several cute moments, it works to be a quick read and nothing more. The series may develop more - I have a few other books to read in it - and I'll continue to see if the plotline improves a bit as he gets older.

Update: Ummmm wtf past me?!?!?! Why the heck did I rate this 3 stars?? This book deserves all the stars!!! I love the characters so much, especially Cinder! Augh apparently I just had really bad book taste two years ago... I was hesitant to read this book at first. The overall concept seemed really creative, but I am not necessary a fan of fairytale retellings. Also, I have a hard time reading books from 3rd person POV. But wow, am I glad I decided to give it a try! Cinder still has the key concepts of Cinderella, but at the same time it is so different. Cinder is a cyborg, and a mechanic. I expected her to seem "not human" when I was reading the book, so I was surprised when I found that the author did a really good job of not making that whole thing too weird. "I'm sure I'll feel much more grateful when I find a guy who thinks complex wiring in a girl is a turn-on." I actually grew to think that the whole "part robot" thing is pretty badass. I also love that she lives in China! I've never read a book with China as the main setting, and it was a whole new and exciting experience. I actually learned a lot cultural-wise. The book is really exciting throughout the book, but a little predictable. As soon as she decided to not tell Prince Kai (love interest) that she was a cyborg, I kind of foresaw how that whole thing was going to play out. There were enough other surprises to keep it interesting, though. Overall, I think was a great book! The ending was suspenseful, so I can't wait to read the next book!

Well, now that I'm done with this book, I wonder why it doesn't receive more hype than a few craps I've read for the past couple of years or so because All Our Yesterdays is pretty good. More accurately, it's a pretty good efforts by a debut author, Cristin Terill. I tend to be very selective of reading any time-travel books because they can be mind-blowingly awesome (until it can cause me insomnia) or just purely bad. All Our Yesterdays surprisingly sits close towards the mind-blowingly awesome category which is a first for me. The blurb simply gives practically everything away and to be honest, I could predict the ending from miles away. Also, I didn't feel invested in any of the characters. I was frustrated not because the evils that a character has done (because we didn't really get to know how he transitioned from an innocent braniac into a ruthless scientist), but I was frustrated at how weak-willed the characters who supposed to finish him behave. Yeah, I know the author went around saying how if they are weak, they would kill him at the first sight blablabla but as the fate of the world is resting on their shoulders, they did a lame job of trying to save the humanity. As if that's not a strong enough motivation. The world building was pretty weak too. "How's outside? Bad?" "Worse." Don't give me that shit. Details matter. Otherwise, how would the readers truly understand the dire of the situation. And I swear two of the chapters had a wrong heading. It was confusing as hell. Ugh. Overall, I know this may sound like a negative review but trust me, it's actually a pretty good book. It kept me awake until 3 in the morning. I can't remember when was the last time a book managed to do that but I think it was years ago. So yeah. Although I would suggest you watch Loop (film) or/and Stein:Gate (anime) if you're looking for a better time travel story.

** spoiler alert ** FTC : I bought this book because I needed to read it. These thoughts are my own. OK, I'm always surprised to discover this but there are people who have never read these books...I know, it horrifies me too. Due to this fact (and my belief that this is a series worth reading and not worth spoiling), I'm going to review the final chapter of this series in a Q & A format to give enough away to make you want to read it without spoiling anything for newbies to the series and people who have been waiting a long damn time for the culmination of Cat and Bones story. Can I read book this out of series order? No, you really can't. This story wraps up the story of Cat's heritage, answers questions I didn't even know I had and shows how far Cat and Bones relationship has progressed. Did the ending make you feel happy? Yes. The ending was not one I predicted, nor one I thought I would want, but I think it was perfect to what is the ending of their love story. Is Bones's still dreamy? I wanted to punch Bones at multiple points in this book. The one thing I respected in this series is Jeaniene Frost's consistency of character; there is no massive character change to either of them because they fell in love, they stayed the same, and it was who they were that got them through all the shit that love brought with it. Bones is a selfish bastard and what he wants, with no apologies and no excuses, is only to keep Cat safe. Is everyone in it? Yup, the whole gang. This the book that sews all the loose threads together, that has all the final show-downs, that puts the characters through the ultimate ringer .... honestly, there were times that I hoped all would turn out OK because it certainly didn't look like it would. What was my favorite scene? There is a scene around a third in where I literally would have killed Bones for Cat ... he doesn't tell her part of his plan and the fall out is devastating. I disliked him for it but then he explained; I went away from that scene with a less romanticized view of him but I loved their relationship even more for it. It is a fab book. Favorite character? (not Bones!) Ian. It will always be Ian. Can Ian get a book? Doesn't even have to have a HEA, I just want to read more! Did it make you feel all the feelz? I laughed, I cried, I cringed and I sat with my heart in my mouth waiting for all the characters I adored to (hopefully) get through the book OK; I read this book in 2 hours and I couldn't have put it down if I tried. Sum it up in three words. Thrilling, exciting and sexy. Read it... or start reading the series. I insist.

More like a 3,7... I guess? It could have been better. There are a lot of good stuffs in this book but they are pretty mediocre. It wasn't tense enough even with all the actions involved and it also wasn't emotional enough, contrary to what I expect from a book. There are also a lot of familiar elements in this book. The world building reminded me of The Winner's Curse, the spying & rebelling against the empire reminded me of The Young Elites, the trials reminded me of The Hunger Games, and the Augurs reminded me of Silent Brothers from The Mortal Instrument. I don't know if it's true and even if it is, it's okay for a writer to be inspired. It was just weird to me to see all the elements from other books I read seemed to be pieced together in this book. Now on to the good stuff. I actually enjoyed it. The world building was slow but gave me a clear image. It's complicated but not overly confusing. I also like how the stories of Elias and Laia slowly intertwined. And I love the character developments! I'm all for character development. Laia started out as a weak, defenseless, family girl who was faced with no choice but to save his brother. She didn't suddenly become so brave and kick-ass or whatever. She took her time being afraid, suspecting people, distrusting and trusting people, and slowly she pushed herself to stand up and be brave. And even in her bravest stance, I still got to see her inner conflict. It feels real. Her attraction to both Keenan and Elias also feels real. You spend time with attractive boys who always try to protect you, you get attracted. It's only natural and doesn't seem slutty at all. Elias is a built-up soldier with rebellious mind and a loving heart. I understand his character from the very beginning of the story. Those traits are so contradictory that he's always torn between sides. He always calculate the consequences of his actions, thinking whether his action is more good than bad before he actually do things. He can make up his minds and he's damn rational! I'm so glad he rarely let his instinct takes over and screws up. In this book, he went to a lot of hard stuffs. And I mean, really hard. He was pushed far beyond his limits and hit rock bottom but he could always compose himself when needed. I also like the way the writer portray him as an actual emerging adult guy with a male brain. I usually hate love triangle and avoid it when I can, but Elias's isn't actually a love triangle. He got attracted to the only female companion he has since childhood who happened to be very attractive but he actually liked Laia. He and Helene have always been together but they are very different and they think about things differently. With Laia, he can open up and be himself. And it's fun to read! What I don't really like is the Augurs. It's just annoying that they already know the future. They talk to people as if he's giving them choices but all they do is just pulling the strings so the people do exactly what has to be done. As they have seen in the future. The only thing I like from them is when they read Elias' mind. It was fun and silly. Every time Elias has mocking and murderous thought, Cain countered it immediately. I cracked a laugh every time it happened. Anyway, I'll definitely wait for the second book.

Nick's 5th grade Language Arts teacher is serious about words--she believes the dictionary is the highest authority--but Nick decides to shake up her classroom (and eventually the school, the town, the country, and the English language) by inventing a new word! This is a short, interesting story about the power of a simple idea. Despite the Big Questions it raises about language and authority, it's not very deep. Still, a good read for habitual and reluctant readers alike.

It starts off worrisome: Lydia has a friend, Grant, who is really into her. She knows it, isn't into him, and is trying to avoid hurting him. (This is icky, but pretty normal for teenagers.) And he believes, as does Lydia's grandfather, that there is a Great Big Secret in the woods. Obviously they are correct, and it seems likely that when Lydia finds this out she and Grant will have an adventure together and she will reconsider him. There is a secret, Lydia does find out, and Grant does not appear again in book 1. How pleasant! There is of course insta-love with a Boy With A Mysterious Past, and a quickly and pleasantly dispensed with triangle with Lydia's great-uncle (she realises he's her great-uncle, or will be, that she likes BWAMP, and tells him she's not interested and sets him up with her great-aunt). The book is fine, but like many other first books in a series lately, the author seems to think that this means "one great big story, split up into three books" and not "three separate stories, each with their own plot with an ending, plus an overarching plot to cover them all". As time travel books are always based on some level of coincidence, I do not mind that Lydia just so happened to go to just the relevant time in her personal history, though some people found this implausible.

The charming cover and Swoon Reads imprint drew me to this novel, and while it had a cute premise, several things in the execution just didn't work for me. Knowing two friends who met and flirted their way through a college creative writing class (and have been married for some time with four kids! ), I was ready to see a cute love story emerge. Instead, because the two main characters spent so much time being passively nudged together by everyone else, I never really felt like the plot was moving until at least 2/3 through. They ostensibly shared an interest in nerdy things like Buffy, yet aside from a couple fleeting references when they did interact, readers weren't really *shown* their connection; instead, we are told repeatedly how perfect everyone else (even their grumpy creative writing classmate Victor) knows they are for each other. After a while, I was half convinced that the deep dark secret that was keeping Gabe from reciprocating Lea's interest was that he was possibly on the autism spectrum (which would have been an interesting story in itself, a la The Rosie Project), but no, it was more of a younger version of my least favorite romance novel trope, the Big Misunderstanding. It might have all been a little more understandable if we'd gotten these reasons from the protagonists themselves, but even the characters who knew the issue didn't actually speak of it until way too late in the novel to be a convincing excuse for all the secrecy. And these characters felt much younger than the college students they were supposed to be. I do have to give props to Lea for trying to move on when a series of maddeningly conflicting signals reaches new heights and depths, but again, that was late to the story. I did also appreciate a range of sexual orientations in the peripheral characters, present without comment, which is important. I'm not giving this a star rating because I rarely finish books that don't hook me in the first 50 pages or so, but I wanted to dig into what didn't work about the story for me as I puzzle out my own writing journey. And really, it was just interesting enough to keep me reading in spite of my reservations, but I have no idea what a fair star rating would be in this case.

However, I am trying to read more and tend to the blog more often. I am also thinking about starting Top 5 Wednesdays, but let me know what you think. I am not hating on the author, the fandom or the series and am, in fact, hopeful for the future books in this series. Please do not attack me for my review. I am not invalidating your opinions about this book or the TMI series in general. I wasn't underwhelmed by this book because I knew, going in, that the majority of people who have read City of Bones, as well as the other books in TMI series, say that this is the weakest of Cassandra Clare's books. The writing style had some major issues, such as intentionally vague writing, info dumps, and intensive background stories. Many of these are unavoidable when establishing the world in a fantasy book, specifically the first book in a series. However, (and I will get more specific in the spoilery section of this review) there were some stylistic things that I didn't jive with. I also didn't love as many of the characters as I thought I would, specifically Isabelle, Raphael, Jace, and Luke. Isabelle was a real let down for me, character-wise, which I will talk more about the spoilery section. Finally, I feel like this book could have been shorter. There was a lot of time spent between important plot points where characters are struggling to find or fight their way out of situations that could have been condensed. Ultimately, I have a lot of hope for later books and honestly think that they can get better so I am going to push myself to read the next couple in the series and see how I feel. I hate to say it, but for City of Bones, I prefer the adaptations over the book itself. **Spoilery Section** So the first and primary thing that has been said about City of Bones is that Cassandra Clare's writing style in this book is the weakest, which I agree with. In the beginning of the novel, Jace's info dumps were the most annoying to me. Not because Clare was providing the reader with an immense amount of information at once, which was admittedly overwhelming. No, the info dumps annoyed me because Jace intentionally left Clary out of the loop until it was absolutely necessary or they were in a life-threatening situation. This got on my nerves because a significant amount of the novel's beginning chapters were spent in Clary's head as she is trying to figure out a part of the Shadowhunter world, or her past, that she didn't understand. Rather than immediately clearing this misunderstanding up, Jace waits for Clary to get good and agitated before he tells her some important and revealing piece of information. The writing began to frustrate me more towards the end, but for a different reason. It was a combination of writing cliches that got to me. The first cliche was the "yes you are, no I'm not" banter or the "pining love interest" that goes on between Clary and Jace while Alec is recovering in the Institute. The second cliche (that lasted a little bit longer than the first) was the "intentionally vague dialogue (usually between someone evil and the protagonist) that is supposed to propel the story and create a super intense climax when the reality of the situation is revealed." This one came when Clary and Hodge were having their "showdown" of sorts. I think that I was more annoyed by these because they came one after another, followed by Luke's massive backstory dump. I feel like there must have been a better way to frame these conversations other than the use of writing cliches. Now for the characters. I was very disappointed by the character of Isabelle in this first novel. She was very whiny and didn't really have much character development. She kind of felt like the dumb blonde that was given a little too much power, which is really unfortunate. The actress that is currently playing Isabelle on the TV Show has all of Isabelle's quirks (like her inability to cook and her affinity towards clothing and fashion) but she also radiates power. She holds herself in battle and wears more revealing outfits because she wants to and she is confident enough in herself that she feels comfortable in that type of clothing. I didn't get any of this from book Isabelle, and as she is one of four prominent female characters, it made me sad that she didn't seem a little bit stronger. Raphael was the same way. I felt that his character was a little underdeveloped and I didn't enjoy how little time we got to spend with him. He transforms from a vampire in hiding to an all out bloodthirsty leader in no time at all, with very little development in between. Finally, Luke a little of a let down too. Less character wise but more because of how little time we actually get to spend with him in the book. Most of the time, Clary thinks about him and her mom and then moves on. Only closer to the end does he become a prominent character and even then, he has a massive backstory dump that turned me off from him a little. In the end, I have very high hopes that this series is going to get really good. I wish, however, that I could just skip over the beginning couple of books and fast forward to where the writing style has developed and the story has fleshed itself out. I might save the next book to get me out of a reading slump, but I think I want to at least give the next book a shot. At the moment, I don't know how dedicated I can get to a series that is massive and rather intensive. Overall: 2 3/4 stars out of 5 stars 65% out of 100% -Jaime

It begins right where World After left off--Raffe with Penryn in his arms, flying, and Paige sitting on Beliel's body which is being carried by scorpion-tailed locusts. While Word After left me disappointed, I'm not gonna lie so did this. While WA was good for the last 30%, this whole book was a mix of really good/really disappointing. The character development in this book is very profound. Penryn has always been a self-reliant and strong female character but in this final instalment, Susan Ee takes her badass quality to a whole new level. Raffe, on the other hand, has always been a fierce believer but in this book, the battle between his responsibilities and his heart gets tougher. He's not just an archangel; he's a warrior. The story, pacing and my overall excitement gives this book 3 stars however, there were many disappointing scenes. The romance in this series has always been subtle yet powerful. I really enjoyed their relationship because of their intense chemistry but at some parts I was disappointed. Especially when they're lying in bed together, it turned a bit too desperate for me. She moved his hand so it would be on her nipple?????? I didn't find it at all sexy or steamy but slightly creeped out at Penryn's actions and Raffes response. Penryn used to be smart, but lost most of it as the story progressed. She let herself be manipulated and used for the most pathetic of reasons. She was seriously a TSTL character with Beliel, she knew he was manipulative but she still let herself be tricked by him, all so she could spy on more of Raffe's memories. Her actions probably resulted in the deaths of dozens of humans, those hellions she released must have killed a few people when they escaped, but that thought never crossed her mind. Also, why was Paige the chosen one when it came to the locusts? How could she control them? Where did that power and ability to come from? Did Doc engineer it that way? If so, how? And why Paige? I felt like it was only put in to have that whole dramatic moment where Penryn was told her sister would be their saviour. That one page where Layla comes back on their side was way too convenient. One minute she was happy with being evil and then she turns back around to coincide with Raffe and Penryn needing help. I felt like a better ending would have been Raffe returning back to heaven, taking all the angels with him , as he originally promised with Penryn. Overall, an unsatifsying ending to what could have been a decent series.

Find more reviews, plus book discussions and giveaways on my blog, YA Romantics Me Since You was a moving story of a family reeling after a terrible tragedy. I got this as an e-ARC and just started reading without remembering anything about the story. The book begins in a first person POV narrated by Rowan, a slightly rebellious sixteen year old girl. After a few chapters, there's a sudden POV shift into a third person present chapter narrated by Rowan's father. At that point I thought the book was going to be one of those Jodi Picoult style multiple POV books that look at different sides of a tragedy from different people involved. (That would have been interesting, actually, but was not the case.) As I read further, I began to suspect that this first tragic event wasn't the only tragedy, but just the inciting event, so to speak. So I'm guessing this rather strange POV shift was included because Rowan's father is present at that first tragic event, while Rowan is not. Still, I found this single lapse into a different POV a little odd and awkward. I sort of wish her father either been given more chapters to narrate, or none at all. (Since the scene in question was videotaped AND another character who's important to the plot was present, that could have been a way to let the reader know what happened.) That small quibble aside, this is a poignant story of a family dealing with and trying to move forward after a senseless and horrible loss. And I was pleased that one of my favorite parts of the story -- something that I thought was just added for atmosphere -- ended up having a lot of significance to the plot. I loved the fact that Rowan had a job at a dry cleaners, and loved the funny little details about the customers and the work. When, toward the end, I began to realize the part her job would play, I was touched and impressed. I also really liked the fact that romance was NOT presented as a magical antidote to sorrow and loss, and that the story didn't try to fast forward through the recovery process and rush the characters to a happily ever after. There were a few moments of speechifying and statistics quoting, but overall, this felt authentic and real to me. Me Since You reminded me a little bit of The Beginning of After by Jennifer Castle. If you're a fan of YA books about grief and loss, you should definitely add this one to your TBR.

Your ability to enjoy this book will depend greatly on how willing you are to suspend disbelief. Much of the "pleasure" of reading it stems from: the anxiety of wondering if and how Grace will get herself out of this situation and learning about the twisted game Jack has created for her. My girlfriend who doesn't typically read fiction listened to portions of the audiobook with me on the way to Thanksgiving and said the story made her very anxious in a bad way yet she also simply had to know how it turned out. This book makes numerous mentions of Agatha Christie and reads like a classic mystery mixed together with a Lifetime thriller (with a dash of FSoG if Christian Grey was actually a psychopath and if the infamous red room wasn't so much a "fun" pain room so much as a psychological torture pain room). The audiobook narrator was absolutely superb ; I especially enjoyed the urgency and emotion she injected into her reading, as well as her flawless ability to do the different voices in the book including different British accents for differently classed characters. I believe the audiobook truly enhanced the reading experience for this one. Great for people who keep wanting psychological thrillers, especially ones with likeable protagonists you root for Also worth noting: a crucial secondary character has Down syndrome. I'm not well-versed enough to comment on how successfully the author portrays Millie but I liked that she played an important role in the story.

Finding out who you are, who you love and how their view of the world is vastly different from your own - it's called growing up - and it's magnificent, terrifying and mind-explodingly beautiful. This is the second novel by Rainbow Rowell I've read, and has become one of my favorites so far this year. Maybe it is due to the fact is is set in an era when I grew up, maybe it's because Eleanor is a red head too, or the fact the main characters are a little weird, a little on the periphery of the High School pecking order. Or just because of the slow burn of the growing and undeniable passion they have for each other - whatever the reason, 'Eleanor and Park' spoke to me on so many levels that I can't squee enough. Rainbow's writing style is effortless and never pulled me from the narration. I completed the book in one sitting, totally engrossed in the drama of High School life. Miss Rowell has the ability to create beautifully flawed and realistic characters that you have no other option but to embrace in all their glory. She tackles issues like body image and bullying through the eyes of the main characters that ring true to your own experiences. It's a love story, so yes the outcome is predictable, but the path the story takes is beautiful. With moments that could have been taken straight out of my childhood diary, I loved how this book traveled the road of innocence, identity and the angst that a teen feels of - let's be honest - just about everything. I don't want to spoil the book by discussing any more, but it is enough to say that this books gets top marks from me and is a must read recommendation. Rainbow Rowell's awesomeness at its best.
