I'm reading this again (never a good sign), and finding it as strange as I found it the first time, and the second time, and I don't know how many times at this point, actually, and I'm reminded of something I came across years ago -- a brief speculation about how each of each of Austen's heroes would gift wrap a present. (Henry Tilney would put a lot of finesse on the bow, Darcy would just hire someone to do it for him, etc.) It was an adorable, casual thing, I think from somebody's letters, and I can't seem to find it again. In honor of my most recent visit to Mansfield Park, here's my own attempt at something similar. The refreshing beverage each Austen heroine would bring you on a hot summer day: Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth Bennet: Chilled Perrier with lemon. Sense and Sensibility, Elinor Dashwood: Plain ice water. And a coaster. Persuasion, Anne Elliot: Hot tea. (Oh, did you want something cool? Suffering builds character.) Emma, Emma Woodhouse: An overlarge glass of chardonnay. Lady Susan, Susan Vernon: I don't know what it is but it probably has a roofie in it. Northanger Abbey, Catherine Morland: A Frappucino that she ran out and got you from Starbucks. Mansfield Park, Fanny Price: Lukewarm tapwater. Because she is the LAMEST creation ever to have a story built around her. And this is what I think gives the book such fascinating jagged edges -- that the warmest emotion you're likely to feel for the heroine is pity. The flaws in the secondary characters are severe, but not always offensive, and they're certainly more entertaining. The secondaries are so much more fun that you're almost as punished as Fanny herself when you try to root for her. Even the author doesn't seem to buy it, distancing the reader from the moments at the end when Edmund finally decides he's in love with Fanny, and instead just informing us that it happened. Of all her books I think it's the darkest (excepting maybe Lady Susan) and probably the least comedic, but for all that, hard to take seriously. So the question, I guess, is whether we're meant to. That's what keeps me interested on the umpteenth read.

Sigh. So happy with this one. One of the best KA reads in a long time. I think I've learned how to enjoy a KA book. I'm not a very patient reader and I do not like long descriptions of rooms, outfit, makeup or mundane activities like grocery shopping. These parts I skipped. I seem to becoming an expert in picking parts with pertinent information. Cher came across rough to me at first, but as the book progressed, she grew on me ... or maybe her speech pattern softened. I don't know. What I do know is I liked the evolution of her relationship with Merry. First as friends ... and then as a couple. The shift in their relationship from friends to lovers was a bumpy one because both of them had their own baggage. What I liked in this book, we get a lot of Merry's POV so we knew exactly where his head was, otherwise a lot of things he did would have been considered a dick move. I think Cher's son Ethan was a little too perfect, but I did enjoy mother and son's relationship. I really liked that Cher was different--she was a straight talker, a fighter, she can definitely talk shit with the guys, and I enjoyed her funny quips with Merry, making her man laugh. The theme really was about "Holding on." Merry was a bit different from other KA heroes. He was alpha and badass, but he definitely had a vulnerable side. Besides loving Cher and Merry together, what really made this book click for me was we get lots of scenes with our past heroes of the Burg --Mike, Colt, Tanner, Cal and especially Ryker. God, I loved Ryker ... he's one crazy mofo. For me, I like guys talking business and shit with each other more than the female posse gatherings talking about outfits and makeup which can get old. There were several good conflicts interwoven into the storyline although there were a few spots that dragged, but not enough for me get impatient ... (remember I skipped long descriptions). Best of all, KA gave us what us fans have been clamoring for a time. A kidnapping! The title "Hold On" came full circle and I felt those words at that climactic moment. It was also emotional when something happened to a certain character. Ryker And the epilogue? Classic KA and a fantastic end to the series. Well done.

One day while I was at work, my mom texted me. She works as a librarian and she knows how much I love Holmes pastiches. She saw this one and thought of me. Sorry mom, but I really didn't like it. Not enough to one star it, but just really annoying. For a while, I thought three stars. Then 2.5. Finally two. Now, I'm hovering around 1.5. My first dud of the year, man. We should celebrate this! (sarcasm) There were just a few things I had a problem with, and I'll try to list them as they came up to me while I was reading. Keep in mind, I read this in one sitting, so I really didn't have any time to just sit there and put it aside. I made myself read it with a brief break to read my chapter for the buddy read I'm doing. 1) The writing. I realized it from the very first page, honestly. Holmes and Watson were too familiar for my liking. The dialogue came out stilted no matter who it was with. The writing wasn't even close to Victorian. It wasn't like there was any attempt at all. I mean, if you're going to make it like modern writing, then make it a modern book. I'd love to read a Holmes pastiche set in modern times like in BBC's Sherlock! Then, don't even get me started on the random French. I don't know a lick of French, so I had to keep a tab for Google Translate to help myself through full sentences that were just in French without a translation. Even random words weren't translated. Do you know how annoying it is to have that? I expect it in classic books, but one that was published just last year? It doesn't work for me. 2) Holmes. Yeah, no. It wasn't Holmes. It was some odd caricature of him. I'm all for making him softer and more approachable, but he was just wrong. I can't even describe it because it was just a gut feeling I had from the first few chapters, that only deepened when I got further into the book. 3) The mystery. I didn't like it. At all. It just felt too random and I didn't enjoy it at all. I can't really describe what I didn't like, but I found I didn't care about anything. Not the kids, the people, what happened, the random French people who were there. Nope. Nothing. So, I'm giving this a generous 1.5 rating even though I didn't even bother reading the last couple chapters. Just skimmed. I don't think I'm going to continue with this series, especially since the next one involved a secret from Holmes' past that's likely related to some woman.

You can find this review and others on my blog http://www.shades0fpaper.wordpress.com "But there is one part of this that hurts. The carefree, normal part. The part of me that was lost when we first moved and that I'll never get back." I have to say I've heard nothing about this book before I decided to pick it up, and I honestly don't know why. This was my second Ashley Elston's novel I've read, and after loving This is Our Story, I wanted to pick up another book by her, so this was one I was intrigued by. And even though I didn't adore it as much as I liked her other novel, I have to say it was still a pretty good book and I enjoyed reading that type of plot. I believe I have never read a book where our main character was in a witness protection program (there was one episode in Criminal Minds and I found it so interesting but no books), so reading through the eyes of someone who is in one was quite unique and intriguing (even though it probably wasn't 100% accurate but still). There was also this whole mystery surrounding the main character Meg and her family and the reason why they were in that program. I really loved that atmosphere, it made me want to keep reading to discover what happened and why they were running away from, so that was pretty cool! "He hugs me tight while I look behind him, scanning faces like I did a few seconds ago. And like I will do for the rest of my life." I have to say sometimes I wanted to strangle Meg, but I think she was a very real character other times. I loved the relationship with her sister (she was super adorable) and even though there was a lot of drama with the family, I have to say her interactions with her little sister were pretty nice. You could see how they cared about each other and I love to read stories about sisterhood (even though it wasn't the main focus on the novel). I also really enjoyed the romance and her love interest. Usually ships are a hit or miss to me (mostly hits but there were other times where I hate the couples!) but I really like Ethan! There's a bit insta love-ish at first, but I really enjoyed how the author made them friends before turning them into lovers (I'M LIVING FOR THOSE STORIES WHEN THEY'RE DONE RIGHT) and also Ethan was a really cute guy who worried so much about Meg and honestly, he wasn't mean or anything. "Don't forget who is a friend and who is a foe. And don't forget, sometimes a person can be both." What I have to add is that it was a bit predictable to me. Now me being me I knew I had 90% chances to discover the whole plot twist before it actually happened, and I was right. I knew most of those things, so they didn't surprise me as much as if I probably wouldn't know (duh). There were a couple of things that felt quite obvious and so I was like "well... okay", BUT there was something I didn't know that had to do with the things I guessed, so that's why I didn't lower my rating that much, because I still enjoyed the story. And after that ending... I really want to continue reading the second installment because I've already had a few theories and I'm super pumped to figure everything out!

It had character depth for all of them, showing the issues with the marriages and then just in general. God, the character depth. It was gorgeous. Then, there was the mystery. It was completely brilliant and well woven. It ticked all my boxes for things I want in a period murder mystery. This book was nothing like it. Characters felt terribly off. There was barely any depth, and when it was attempted, it was incredibly awkward. The plot was plodding, even though I knew what was going to happen. Too many side stories. I know, she was trying to keep period accurate. But that, for me, killed it. She could have had tangents and side stories, but I just do not care about a letter that Lady Catherine wrote or Elizabeth's relationship with her old friend Charlotte or Mr. Collins or whatever. I don't care. It's not relevant to the plot or mystery in any way. I'd say, skip the book. Watch the miniseries.

2.5 Hearts Review written for MM Good Book Reviews http://mmgoodbookreviews.wordpress.com/ I love reading BDSM related books but this was an odd one for me. We have a murder case that escalates into serial murders bdsm related. We have a Detective who upon investigating for the murder/s he gets intrigues by the lifestyle. We have a lifestyle Doctor who is consulting the police, who falls for the intrigued Detective and decides to show him the ropes. And we have a murderer who seems to get into the victims houses as a guest, slowly closing in on the Detective and the Doctor. The basic line of this book is pretty awesome. The idea behind it all is fantastic, intriguing, gripping even. But the end result just slipped from my fingers as elusive as water. There were passages and scenes which I loved and had me either laughing or gasping or simply enjoying. But as many such passages there were, there were more to make me halt and think "seriously" disbelieving what I'd been reading, or even making me feel bored. First of all my huge issue was with the detective work for this story. The murderer was obvious to me the moment he was mentioned. The conviction he did it was made stronger when Detective Gavin finally got around and questioned him. From that moment on I simply couldn't stand the police work, or lack thereof. There were glaring events and evidence that should have the police pressing on the murder and cracking him way before the half of the book was reached and the end result was that it got tiresome waiting for the inevitable. The ending itself was no surprise and cause only an eye roll from me. Annoyance and frustration were the main emotions caused by the entire police plot. Second issue that had me reeling was the lead character himself. Gavin started as a deeply closeted man, never one having tried even being with a man, married and not even thinking of shattering that illusion. In the matter of a week, or was it two, he goes from married to divorced and from virgin/closeted to diving into homosexuality and submission vigorously. He had never once told a soul about his sexuality for thirty years, yet he not only confides in his new partner, whom he knows nothing about and has just met, but he also goes ahead and tells her about the lifestyle he's agreed to. The inconsistency of that had me quite unbalanced trying to figure this character out. In addition with his horrible detective work, he never much gained higher status than plain stupid in my eyes. As for his submitting to Ben, the way he went from total newbie to "yes, Sir" in seconds, oh Dear Lord. What a turn off. The rest of the book simply felt like a big textbook on BDSM, too clinical and detached to get into and with so many rules and justifications of everything being done and said that had me bored and yawning endlessly. As I said there were only few scenes that made me feel something other than boredom in this book and it was such a shame. Bottom end I didn't got close to the characters at all. There was a wall keeping at arm's length despite the book being narrated by Gavin. I didn't get to feel his feelings or get into what he was getting because the language use for the narration was as I already mention quite clinical. Even when the most gruesome event happened that should have had Gavin's mind reeling and us shaking with pain and despair it failed to ruse more than an eyebrow. What should have been the highlight of the book, the point that would break any reader into sobs and skin-crawling and gut-wrenching was lost in a lack of passion and a detachment you could not overcome. For me this book failed its mission leaving me an odd taste and feeling as if I was in school and being forced to read a subject that while I'm interested in, it can't hold my interest for more than five minutes. Confession: When I was a teenager I sold movie tickets from a glass booth like the one on the cover, part of an old art-deco theater with red velvet seats built in the 30s. I loved that job. And in my off time, I volunteered with the homeless. So when I read the synopsis for this book I got a WEE bit excited! This IS an amazing story, but unfortunately the bizarre formatting makes it anything but readable. The story is told as the memories and diary entries of a dozen people, but instead of devoting on chapter to each, the author changes POV several times in every scene. So each page, at times, will have three or four different people speaking. Combined with the sheer number of narrators, and the fact that each one is coming from a different time, the overall effect is nothing but a confused, chaotic cacophony. For me, at least, it made the entire book unreadable. I have trouble believing that not one editor spoke up and said how hard this makes the story to follow. So I'm disappointed, because this story is just right up my alley. Too bad it was hidden in the chaos.

Fantastic concept, horrible execution. I know it's a translation, and that's why I persevered longer than it really deserved, but the narration was poor - it didn't flow, it had no spark to it, and it meandered far too often. Every time we got inside a character's head for a flashback or extended bit of introspection, my eyes glazed over and I came out of those dense, dry paragraphs forgetting where I was. The characters were as flat as they were unlikable, so much so that I found myself wishing the Black Rock Witch would just let loose and end it all. As for the concept of Black Spring and project Hex itself, I give Heuvelt full credit for trying to bring several classic horror tropes into the 21st century, but the attempt just didn't work for me. There were far too many leaps of logic required to make the town work, and far too little understanding of the human condition to make the project believable - everything that was happening to 'break' the story to the world, I would have expected decades ago, and I can't believe the government wouldn't take more drastic measures to keep new people out. As for the Black Rock Witch, she was a cool concept with a great backstory. I found myself wanting to know more about who she was, about what really happened to her son, how she came back to curse the town, and where the original settlers went. Like the story of the Roanoke Colony, it was the mystery and the speculation that made her tale so compelling. As much as I appreciated what Heuvelt was trying to do with his reversal of the trope, the story that reminded me that horror works best when the monsters are kept in the shadows, teasingly glimpsed, but held back for a climactic reveal. I admit, I skimmed a good chunk of the second half, just to see how it ended . but the final few chapters did nothing to redeem the book. Disappointing.

This and other reviews can be found on The Psychotic Nerd Actual Rating: 2.5 MY THOUGHTS I didn't really think this was going to be my kind of book. Ballerinas and drama just didn't sound like a me book. But my Goodreads friends left positive reviews and the authors will be at a convention I'm going to later this year, so I thought I would give it a try. Sadly, I was right about this not being a me book. I wanted to enjoy it, and I did like parts, but I'm not a fan of books with a ton of drama. Gigi, Bette, and June are students at an elite ballet school. Gigi is the new student, but her talent allows her the lead role. Bette has always been in the shadow of her successful sister and has been attending the school for years, was expecting the role herself. And June's controlling mother is pressuring her to get a lead role or else June will have to leave the school and give up dancing. But all June can land are understudy roles. These ballerinas will do anything to get on top and they will go to monstrous lengths to get there. The characters are a big part of this book. It's told from all three points of view: Gigi, Bette, and June. Sadly, I disliked almost all of the characters. The only character I liked was Gigi. Gigi is such a sweetheart and I think she deserves the roles she got, and absolutely did not deserve any of the horrible things people did to her. Yeah, I hated everyone that was mean to Gigi. Bette was an absolute bitch. Yeah, she has her own problems she has to deal with and some aspects of her situation suck, but she's still a bitch. June was okay at points, but June still is not a nice girl. Yeah, she was pressured, but Gigi sees June as a friend and it's horrible how June doesn't care what happens to Gigi. I do like the fact that this book have a diverse cast (Yay!) and that it deals with tough issues. All of the girls have other issues their are dealing with. For example: anorexia is within this book. It is important to have these tough subjects within books. I was interested in the plot of this book, but at the same time, I really wanted to stop reading. I have such a hard time with drama in books. It makes me hate almost all the characters, like I said before, and it makes me very very frustrated before I want the few characters I actually like to be happy. I kept reading this book, because I did want to know what will happen next, but these ballerinas were horrible! I just want Gigi to be happy!! IN CONCLUSION Okay, so this book was not for me. I think some people will enjoy, but there was too much drama! This book stressed me out so much and I do not think I will be picking up the sequel, even if I want to make sure that Gigi will be happy. I don't think I can go through all that drama again.

Here's the thing about Life and Death: I appreciated it more than I liked it...hence the 2.5 star rating. So instead of focusing on the things that didn't work for me, let me tell you why I appreciated it. Stephenie Meyer's Life and Death: Twilight Reimagined is a reimagining of her original Twilight novel; a gender swap to be exact. And if you don't know what Twilight is, then you've been living under a rock. I read this for pure enjoyment. Perhaps to be reminded of how Twilight once made me feel. You see, Twilight was a huge part my growing up/ fangirling/ falling in love with books experience back when it was THE book to read. It will forever have a special place in my heart, because of those Twi-hard years. While I gave up waiting for Midnight Sun a long time ago, it was nice to get this little treat. So naturally I was curious to pick this one up and relive that experience. At first it was difficult to separate it from Twilight. Yes, I know it's essentially the same spiel, but I wanted to experience it as its own story rather than a recycling of the familiar novel. It was hard not to read Beau as Bella and think of the characters as brand new creations, despite the slight differences. Being so familiar with the original tale is probably what kept me from getting more of a reading thrill. It wasn't as exciting, because I knew what was going to happen. And maybe other readers felt the same way. Part of what makes a reading experience so exhilarating is the unknown; those chapters that keep you guessing to the very end. I was missing that unchartered territory with Life and Death. Nevertheless, the author managed to put an interesting perspective on the whole damsel in distress trope and shed new light on the vampire/human relationship. Beau and Edythe are not identical to Bella and Edward and a fun twist was added that automatically sets the whole story a little more apart from the original plot. I liked that. I will end with this: Life and Death is for lovers of Twilight. It was predictable yet entertaining. Twi-hards will know what to expect. So thanks Stephenie Meyer, for this little addition to a much loved series. It was an enjoyable transition read in between other books and brought back some waves of nostalgia.

Hands down, my favorite "middle book" of 2012. I wouldn't have said so last year after reading DIVERGENT (Indeed, DIVERGENT wasn't even my favorite dystopian of 2011), but this year, INSURGENT blew me away. If I had to hazard a guess, I'd say this is my favorite dystopian series. Is it any wonder it's been selling so well to everyone looking for something similar to THE HUNGER GAMES? I can't tell you how many people I've loaned my copies too (Seriously. They're BATTERED. ), but everyone agrees that this series is far and away the cream of the crop! I think what appeals to me most about this series is that, where THE HUNGER GAMES had holes and gaps that Suzanne Collins brushed past or never filled in, The Divergent Trilogy has yet to have these issues. Granted, we're still one book away from the end, so things may change, but for now, I feel comfortable saying that this series feels much "fuller." I especially like how healthy the relationship between the two main characters is! There's no love triangle, there's no will they/won't they angst, there's no abuse. These characters get together in the first book and are still together come INSURGENT. True, they have problems, but they work them out and grow together. I applaud Roth for this strong relationship model that teens need to see!

That's why I didn't mind the face paced romance, even though I usually prefer slow built up romance. It's the kind of book that will make you think about a lot of things. It might make you ask yourself what you'd do if you had 24 hours left before you die. Did you do all the things you wanted to do? Did you reach all the things you wanted to reach? Are you happy about the last conversations you had with your loved ones? Million of questions went through my mind as I read this beautifully written story. It might be the type of book that will make you want to use your time better, that will make you want to get out and do all the things that you are scared of. Who knows? It might have that kind of impact on you. I know I couldn't stop wondering if I am using my time and if I am really living my life to the fullest or if there's anything that I am missing. It may sound a little dramatic but this book really managed to make me reconsider a lot of things and I think if a story is able to make you want to change your entire life it's definitely a good one. I know most of us will have a different experience with this book. Some might feel the same as I did when I first read it, some others may just enjoy the characters and wish they had gotten a much happier ending. Personally, I am happy that this book had such a huge impact on me and I know for sure I am going to re-read this one many, many times.

Natalie's got confidence and then some, and has no reservations about going after a man, even if it's only for a night of fun. But there's something about the quiet, somewhat grumpy, tattooed man at the farmer's market every week that makes her fumble and ramble. She may love the Brie he makes, but she's interested in far more than just Oscar's handcrafted cheese. When her advertising company picks up the small town where Oscar lives for a project, Natalie's all over the job, mixing business trips with pleasure trips. But as much as she enjoys her time with her country man, she's a city girl at heart. Can they find compromise somewhere in between the two extremes? First, I know, I know, the title and cover may be a bit . unusual. But trust me, this book is worth the read! Cream of the Crop was such a delightful read. It's not so light that there's not some angst/emotions popping up, but it's still relatively fluffy and fun - and I mean that in the best possible way. I very much enjoyed Clayton's writing style (and will be reading more of her books in the future), as well as Natalie's spunk and sass. Natalie's a take-no-shit and give-no-fucks kind of woman, and I loved her for that. She fully accepts that yes, she is plus-sized, but she's damn beautiful and she has the confidence to take what she wants out of life. She wasn't always that way; her backstory includes a douchebag POS ex-boyfriend who really did a number on her when she was graduating high school (controlling, verbally and emotionally abusive, made her believe she was never enough, etc., etc.). But after leaving him, she picked herself up and set her mind on a career where she kicks ass and a mindset that dares the world to call her fat and belittle her for her size. I could truly connect to some of Natalie's early struggles about herself, and while I can't say I'm to the give-no-fucks level that Natalie is (yet), I loved seeing such a heroine in print. Because we can't forget that everyone needs to be able to see parts of themselves in books. And no, this is not the story of the fat girl finding herself - and love - after losing weight. Nope, not at all. Natalie is an unapologetic size 18 from start to finish. She's happy with herself. Which I also loved because far too often when there is a "heavier" heroine, much of her character arc revolves around her losing the weight and suddenly being beautiful. Fuck that shit. Lose the weight if you want to be healthier, I have nothing against that. But a person isn't ugly because they're fat and beautiful once they're skinny; that's society's BS talking. Let's see, I laughed and smiled during a lot of this book. I could relate to Natalie and loved her attitude and confidence. What else? Oh! The chemistry between Natalie and Oscar is fantastic; this is quite a hot read, whether they're simply kissing or getting busy on any available surface. The only complaint I have is minor: I do wish we could have gotten Oscar's POV thrown in. I don't mind 1st POV in my romance novels, but I do prefer if it's dual 1st POV so we can get the full picture and experience of the couple. The epilogue was done from Oscar's POV, which was interesting since the rest of the book was entirely from Natalie, but I would have liked to see Oscar's POV mixed in a bit; maybe not every other chapter, but at the very least a few times during the course of the story. This was my first Clayton novel but it will not be my last. Fun and relatable and sexy as hell, Cream of the Crop reads like a good romcom. 4 1/2 STARS! And so we come to Partials by Dan Wells, a novel that has been sat on my YA shelf for quite some time - the backlog on that particular to read shelf is long because there is SO much great YA fiction around these days - and Partials is a great addition to all of those. In it we meet Kira, a young girl and a clever one. One of a handful of survivors of "the release" the community resides trapped on Long Island...and they are slowly dying out. No baby survives past three days. When her best friend falls pregnant, Kira is bound and determined to find a cure and save the baby - but her only hope may not be human at all.... I rather loved this book. Ok, you do have to suspend disbelief a little bit at just how clever scientifically Kira is at 16 years old at first, but even allowing for that this is a great read. The "Partials" part human who were created to win a war and then turned on the full humans are very well imagined and the splinters within Kira's own community are cleverly done. The supporting cast of characters are all well drawn, and you will quickly be enveloped into their world. There is adventure to be had here, and a touch of romance, with some imaginative science thrown in for good measure. The standard does not dip for the entire book and the writing flows extremely well - easy to read but very involving, its a definite plus to the genre and I look forward to picking up "Fragments" the next in the series soon. It resides on my shelf and I'm feeling that it won't be there for too much longer.

I don't often find a book I want to read again after the first initial inhalation of its story and characters. I don't want to pore over events that shape the narrative, linger over the words spoken and the feelings felt by the different characters. It's a rare book that engages me to the extent that I will read and reread because every time I do, I find something more to take away from it.Cold Magic, the first book in the Spirit Walker trilogy, is one such rare book. I found myself reading as slowly as I could so that the pleasure that came from reading it would last a longer time. And when I did finish the book, I immediately went and looked up the author to see when the next installment is coming out because I don't know if I can wait until it does and...well, there is no release date yet. Boo. Cold Magic fascinates because of the detail with which the alternate world is created. The history, the people, the mythos - it is all so exquisitely detailed that the reader will find herself swept away with it but at the same time, in some detached manner, breathless at the superb skill of the author. The story is not built on a shaky foundation which is loosened by a logical question or attempts at reason. It is solidly woven, binding together different parts of the world to create a gorgeous tapestry, a setting in which the wonderful characters of the book can exist. There are two women: Cat and Bee. Girls, really. Both twenty. Usually when you have two characters, there is a lack of balance between them. One is deemed more important than the other. It is a testament to Ms. Elliot's writing that despite the story being told in the first person (Cat), Bee is just as much intriguing and an equally strong character as Cat. Neither of them are perfect but both have been characterized in a manner that transcends their otherworldliness and makes them relatable to the ordinary reader curled up by a fireplace (or not). The other characters are just as strongly hewn. Their individuality, whether they are present for a chapter or two, is very present. I've said it before, side characters and their characterizations are very important to the success of a novel and Ms. Elliot delivers wonderfully on those counts. The romance is surprising with its presence and all the more compelling for its element of unexpectedness. Another strength of the novel comes from its pacing. The entire novel is like a race. Tensions increase as the finish line is approached, the sense of danger skitters across your skin and you (no matter how much you try not to) read as fast as you can in desperation to see what happens next. The story has many layers, it's a complex interweaving of different dynasties, different times and different hopes. It is unpredictable to its last page and I'm so running out of superlatives right now. This was a brilliant premise to what promises to be an awesome trilogy. If you are interested in steam-punk, strong heroines, friendship and sizzling romance, read this. Even if you aren't interested in any of those things, read this anyway. It's too good to miss.

*Back-dating reviews based on random things I wrote at the time. I just wrote about the three as a whole rather than each book* So, I finally read them. Initially, I wasn't going to - based on everything I'd heard, I figured I'd not like it. On the flipside, I also believe you shouldn't slate a book until you've read it, so once I saw the books floating around the house I thought there was no harm in borrowing them and seeing if I could work out what all the fuss was about. I really can see why it's so popular, but I really dislike most of those reasons. The unrealistic sex, the scale and perfection of everything, the timescale alone infuriates me. This was always my pet hate in fanfictions: guy meets girl, it's instantaneously obvious they'll get together and end up together forever - that's exactly what this book does. Despite it being ludicrous at many moments, I'd rattled through the books so quickly that I just had to know what happened, otherwise it'd niggle at me until I found out. The main theme in the plot that honestly infuriated me was the fact that it all spiraled from jealousy or longing surrounding Anastasia. I'm not saying if you're plain and understated you aren't attractive - far from it - but literally everyone they meet is either instantaneously smitten with Christian, therefore jealous of her, or wants her. No, not going to happen. I understand it's fiction, and I understand it's fantasy, but this has classic cliche fanfiction written all over it. My other issue is Christian. Why I was most annoyed was that - based on reading the first book alone - people I know were romanticising him and praying for their own little Christian Grey. He is a control freak, a bully and no amount of money or pretty hair can change that. This is only forgiven because he's said to be beautiful and unfathomably rich. Would an ordinary guy get away with that behaviour? No, he wouldn't. The idea anyone would romanticise such a horrid person - the negatives veiled by the fact he has money and speaks to lovingly of her - is crazy to me. Just because someone can tell you you're beautiful and genuinely cares for you doesn't mean you should take shit from them. And Anastasia. Dear, sweet Anastasia needs a reality check. Your first boyfriend. Your first everything. A quote sticks out following the announcement of their ridiculously quick proposal: "I love him and he loves me. He wants to marry me and there will never be anyone else for me." Anyone else says this about their first boyfriend and everyone would take them as a sappy teenager in love, but because he's a billionaire that's okay. There's a reason they're popular and it's because they pander to the perfection and ideals in love. Boy meets girl, they fall in love, she fixes him, they get married, they live happily ever after. There are obviously more tumultuous times created through Christian's past, and that's one of the few factors that remotely peaked my interest. But, even then, it was very predictable. Did anyone really not see it coming that Jack was part of the foster family? It's hard to give it credit where it's due, because I can't work out where it is. The writing style was juvenile, the plot wasn't great, the characters weren't very good. She's taken an intelligent girl and presented her as a pushover, someone who'll take a beating from a pretty face. She takes too much shit without knowing that he has a past because he is essentially rich and attractive. This ramble is pointless and it's not really going anywhere. Overall, I can see why it's so popular but that's because it's just very vanilla, plain and tailored to the mainstream. This isn't even a BDSM book, like I had been told, this is a book about a couple coming from two sexual extremes to find a balance and fall in love. Nothing they actually do is extreme and I find it surprising that anyone reading this thinks so. And, a rant dedicated to the reason it's so popular - the sex. I've had issues with EL James' style of writing throughout the whole book. I found it quite juvenile and repetitive. The Inner Goddess drove me crazy and the fact she would put dashes between words to form a description rather than choose one suitable word infuriated me. But when it came to the sex scenes, it feels more innocent. Ana being inexperienced could be one reason to use such poor vocabulary on anatomy - "my sex" and "there" are pretty juvenile ways to describe the female anatomy, as is "his length" for Christian. The other reason I think that really drove the poor language is the author herself. She's notably embarrassed in interviews when she's questioned about sex, and it seems even in her writing - in her own fantasy - she can't write anything crude through a certain shyness. I suppose that makes shy newcomers feel better about reading it; they'd be less embarrassed reading this than reading about cocks and other similar words. I think that had Anastasia been more dominating in the relationship, it wouldn't have been as successful. I, personally, didn't like Anastasia and her pushover nature when it came to sex. I felt she was blinded by beauty and money, despite her saying it's not about the money. She wouldn't have done anything like this for a beautiful bum now, would she? So, the loose language is my main theory as to why it goes down so well. Mix that in with an irresistible billionaire with a troubled past, the fact that you know they're going to end up together happily ever after and BAM! There you have it. That's why it sells. The sex itself has its pros and cons. One key pro is that it creates an atmosphere that avoids a wham, bam, thank you mam scenario. Christian worships every inch of her body almost constantly and it always builds up before sex. That, again, is another reason I think this book has done so well. I, however, did not like it. Not to mention the sex itself is unrealistic. For one, Anastasia is a virgin with no gag reflex. Not unheard of, but mighty convenient. She experiences her first orgasm, if I remember correctly, by him playing with her nipples. Does that even happen? Even if she was sensitive enough for that to happen in the first place, the more sex she has, the less sensational this should feel. Yet it doesn't. It can still get her off completely. And, just throwing it out there, she always comes first and he comes soon after. Sometimes they even come together! There was even an instance in which she couldn't come because she was distracted by thoughts on life, yet Christian says "come" and she does. Again, I understand this is fantasy but the sheer inaccuracy of this annoyed me continuously throughout the series. I'm glad he found his release, I'm glad you crumbled around him, but once in a while he's going to come just before you do and probably roll over and go to sleep. To the BDSM aspect... I think this has been greatly skewed in promotion and what I hear from other people. This is not a BDSM book. 50 Shades of Grey deals with a Dominant and a virgin essentially falling in love and finding a happy medium between two extremely contrasting sexual lifestyles. In turn, it's middle of the road. In fact, it's normal. Spanking isn't taboo, nor are vibrators, handcuffs or any of the objects they used. If they were, you wouldn't be able to buy them on your local high street, nor would they be advertised in shop windows. The issue is Christian as a character. He has defined his sexual desires by his past, though they were really founded through Elena, and then adapted to fit his past. The author, with or without meaning to, puts forward the idea that Christian is only into BDSM because he is damaged, and that is an issue people I know who are into BDSM really have with these books. BDSM is a preference, it is not a sign of emotional baggage or a damaged past, yet EL James really makes the link between his childhood and his sexual desires. His baggage is what causes his stalker nature, his possessive needs and his inability to trust Ana to be safe without him being around. These can be tailored to his damage, but BDSM cannot. tl;dr I rate this series in a similar way to Twilight - there are so many great erotic (and vampire) books out there, so why did this one break through? It's usually the watered down, easily digestible books that break it and, more often than not, they're terrible representations of the genre they become the poster boy of. These books, like the series they spiraled from, are poorly written, have a terrible plot and awful characters. It is completely unrealistic in every sense and, while pandering to dreamers and fantasy is fine in books, this takes the absolute piss. I think the massive rant was me trying to be reasonable, when it's a long-winded way of saying this is a horrid book. You ask for any erotica nowadays and this will be the top recommendation. It shouldn't be. Not by a long shot.

I was pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed this read. I'm a list maker, so buckle down for some pros and cons! Pros: This was my first Bracken read, and I must say- I was blow away by how well she crafts character voice in this story. Prosper felt like a *real* person. He absolutely shined in this novel. I love how this normalizes diversity for younger readers. We have a mixed girl, whose parent's races aren't even mention until over half way through. Her mother is also somewhere on the queer spectrum, which again was hardly an issue of notice for the children and treated like a regular part of life. Just how race and sexuality should be handled. The atmosphere was exceptional. From the orange-knit pumpkin sweaters to the deep fried, sugar-and-cinnamon coated Silence Cakes, fall and Halloween are everywhere. Most of the story takes place within a haunted house, but we also get to visit a fall festival, a creepy basement, a graveyard, and scariest of all: middle school. The dynamic relationship between Alastor and Proper was my favorite part of the whole story. Just read and see! The world building was quite good. I enjoyed learning about the town and family history, as well as the multi-demimsions the fiends and other such creatures came from. Cons: I really don't have any serious issues with this book. The only thing that bothered me (again- a minor irritation) was the author's use of anecdotes to start nearly every new scene. Its a fancy little writers tool I enjoy every now and then, but felt it was over used here. Overall, this is a really great, middle grade halloween read!

I am a sucker for fairy tales, traditional or re-told. Let it be known that I grew up on the Disney princesses (Cinderella, Sleeping Beauty, Belle, Ariel, and so on). I lived and breathed this stuff. My mom likes to retell a certain story where I was dressed up as a fairy, walking around the house with a wand. When I came upon her on all fours, scrubbing the tiles of the bathroom floor, what did I say? "Mommy, you're so lucky. You get to be Cinderella." Yeah. That was me. And my love for fairy tales never faded. I started reading the original, often much more gruesome tales as I got older, took a few classes on traditional folklore in college, and wrote numerous papers, by choice, about these fascinating tales. So SISTERS RED, for me, had a certain level of appeal that not all books do initially. This is more a re-imagining of Little Red Riding Hood than it is a retelling, but it is fast paced and packs a punch. Scarlett and Rosie live in a world where there is not just one big bad wolf, but hundreds. They are strong female leads, battling this evil and doing their best to protect the otherwise naive and unaware. It was the layered pieces of this tale that made it successful for me though: the bond of sisterhood, the desire to want more from life, the butterfly-inducing feeling of first love. This tale is certainly inspired by Little Red Riding Hood, but at its core it is a story about sisters who grow closer as they grow apart - if that makes sense. Jackson Pearce keeps the tension and action high in this novel, and you'll occasionally hear a snippet of the original tale woven in. Such as "the better to see you with," or "you mustn't stray from the path." These little pieces, slipped into the otherwise modern tale, are such a nice touch. They made me smile. If you dig fairy tales and girls kicking butt, you'll likely enjoy this read! Originally reviewed here

dnf @ 53% I tried with this book. I honestly did. While I wasn't enjoying the beginning, I was really hoping that if I got farther enough that the novel would get better. (Warning: spoiler part may be ranty & if you like this book I am in no means trying to offend you. If you don't wanna hear it, then don't read it.) I have not read a lot of books which talk about important issues like suicide, so this book is definitely valuable in that case. But while reading it, it almost felt like Jay Asher was glamorizing suicide. I mean, seriously? Hannah Baker definitely went through a lot of problems with her life, and I am definitely not disregarding that or trying to belittle that. She felt like she had reason to commit suicide and I am NOT going against that fact. But what I found as a problem in this book that Hannah, literally BLAMES these people for her suicide. "I committed suicide because YOU spread a rumor about me and YOU pretended to be my friend". No. No. Stop. I understand that these people hurt you, and in the end, you felt helpless against them. But it's one thing to to tell them to change their behaviors and another thing to commit suicide to prove a point that THEY made you do this. While reading the novel, I kinda despised Hannah. All Hannah did was repeat the same things over and over again, continuously emphasizing that her suicide was this person's fault. Honestly. Read this quote, directly from the book: "And yet the whole time Courtney was using me, she thought she was polishing up her image in my eyes. Can you say... backfire?" What? What does this line mean? "Backfire"? Are you seriously saying that you killing yourself is revenge at her for using you? "I'm gonna kill myself. That'll show her." That is LITERALLY what the line translates to. To me, Hannah was just such an annoying character. Every single time she kept repeating 'you're to blame for MY death' she was being too dramatic. I know I am supposed to feel depressed for her, as this is a SUICIDE novel, but I just couldn't. Hannah was petty, overly emotional, and literally committed suicide to make a point to others and I just don't condone that. Maybe Jay Asher wanted to make this book relatable for suicidal people, but after reading reviews from ACTUAL people who had thoughts of suicide, they confirmed my suspicion that this book was just written based on the overall generalization of suicide. It's kind of like The Fault in Our Stars-- that book is based on the overgeneralization of cancer and a lot of ACTUAL people with cancer can't relate to it. Like I said before. This book glamorizes suicide and I really don't think it's okay. Another thing I disliked about this book was the writing. Besides the fact that I found the entire book to be problematic, the book just seemed to drag on forever. The book is written in a fashion thought to be of how teenagers talk, and I found it SO annoying. Lines were literally repeated over and over. All the characters kept repeating questions instead of any actual answers being provided. Clay: "Why did you do this Hannah..... Why didn't you do this" LITERALLY THE ENTIRE NOVEL (well at least up to the point I read to). Anyways, reading further would just kinda be like torturing myself, because I could not connect to Hannah in any way at all and I just could not read it. I found it boring. Simple as that. Anyways, despite finding this book to be extremely problematic, the only reason I decided to read it was so I could watch the Netflix series. I'm still gonna give the show a try, because maybe the problems that were emphasized in the book are not as prominent in the show. Again, I never EVER want anyone to misunderstand my dislike for this book as belittlement for anyone who actually has suicidal thoughts. Everyone SHOULD think before they act/speak. Although it seems as Jay Asher TRIED to send out that message, it came out completely malformed to me. It seemed more like a girl blaming a bunch of people for her choice, rather than teaching them to think before acting.
Wish-fulfillment, time travel, vampires. The main character spends most of the book saying: "But what if I don't want to be your awesome magic princess-oracle?"

I'm really torn here. As a librarian, I should be firm on the stance that the book is always better than the movie/tv show, but having watched the show before picking up the novels, I'm rather partial to the show. It's also made me root for characters that I just can't bring myself to get fully behind in the books (Jaime Lannister, I'm looking at you - I really like that thing you've got going on with Brienne on the show, but if I have to hear one more time how much you have the hots for your sister, I'm going to scream). On the other hand, sometimes getting inside a character's head is a great benefit for a reader. So I was familiar with the author. She writes about serious issues. This book was a New York Times bestseller (Fiction, 2011). http://www.librarything.com/work/1022... 1/30/12 (as posted at my GR group): I finally finished reading Sing You Home by Jodi Picoult. I don't know why they gave the book that title. It's about Zoe, a music therapist, but most of the story centers around the disposition of 3 frozen embryos after the divorce of the parents of those embryos, Zoe and Max. After Zoe and Max divorce, Zoe discovers that she's gay and she marries Vanessa. The gay couple want to use those embryos. Max decides he wants those embryos. Therefore, much of the story is about the court case and the pros and cons. That slowed my reading down because court cases can be boring at times. Another thing about the book is that it's told by three different narrators, Zoe, Max, and Vanessa. That annoyed me because I kept forgetting who was doing the narrating, even though the text was different for each one. In spite of the above drawbacks, I'd say it was a good story, well-written. I like reading Jody Picoult's observations about life and people through the thoughts of her characters. (They speak in the first-person, "I".) She fleshes out her characters well.

Hear that? It's no big deal--just the sounds of my heart-breaking and my weeping echoing through my house. I'll be fine. Really, I will--*sobs* I expected a lot of things from The Score. I mean, Dean Heywood-Di Laurentis is manwhore who finds himself fascinated with a feisty, dramatic blonde who is not interested in him. At least, not for a second time. Fun, right? Except, she can't stop thinking about him and when his perfect world is rocked, the time comes for them to decide whether the future is there for both of them--together. I was utterly amused on more than one occasion--Twilight references, Wayne Gretzky paperweights, Winston, oh, my! It was also hold-the-phone HOT. As in, panties disintegrating, ovaries exploding, temperature rising S. E. X. Y. I need a cold shower, a fan, a man, something. Because, whoa! But then, it was shattering. Heart-dropping, you're killing me, I can't go on sad. That's what I mean. I was so invested in this story and these characters, and what happened? Did. Not. Expect. It. Oh, and add Can. Not. Handle. It to that, too. Because I cried. Oh, yes, I surely died. And even now, writing this review, I have a pit in my stomach and a feeling like I might not be okay again. Except I will. Because while Elle Kennedy effectively stomped on my fucking heart (thanks for that, Ms. Kennedy), she also healed it. With a sweet, hopeful, funny and scorching, sizzling, sexy hot ending. With a surprising bombshell to boot. Eek! I can't say I was expecting that, and I am reserving the right to hold judgment until book four, Tucker's book, comes out, and we can see how it plays out. Right now, I'm excitedly apprehensive. And intrigued. And desperate for more. Oh, and in need of some more damn tissues. *Sobs* ~ Beth, 5 stars Dean Di-Laurentis is a manwhore--rich, privileged and accustomed to getting what he wants, Dean lives the high life and the high life is good to Dean. When Allie Hayes blows into his life like some kind of hurricane, she's a force to be reckoned with and Dean has no idea what he's in for. One wild night of the hottest sex Dean has ever known, and he's convinced that he needs more. Allie's not like other girls. She doesn't roll over and just give Dean whatever he asks for. She's not really interested in a relationship with him so much as she's interested in using him as a rebound and then moving on with her life. The fact that the sex is amazing is just a bonus--a bonus she's not entirely inclined to walk away from just yet, despite the fact she's a "nester" and Dean doesn't do commitment. Still, they navigate their way through their unorthodox relationship and before long, they're both in over their heads. I LOVED Allie and Dean. They were playful and fun and fucking hysterical. I laughed--loudly, and for a fair amount of time--like a crazy person at my Kindle. They were also Kindle melting hot; the fun and playful nature of their relationship translated to their bedroom activities in a way that was sexy and a little bit wild, but with so much heart--sometimes it took my breathe away. There were scenes...*sigh*, I'm still recovering from some of those scenes. Dean was unexpectedly sweet and smart, and Allie was so strong and plucky. I loved them. I loved...everything. It all just worked for me. And then it broke my heart. Like, seriously broke my heart. I was distraught. I ached for Dean and then, later, for Allie. My heart felt so bruised and shattered for them but I could not have been more proud of both of them as they rallied. They showed so much growth and character. So much fucking heart. God, I loved them so much! If I haven't already made my point clear, allow me to spell it out for you: READ THIS BOOK. Emotional and hilarious, heartbreaking and heartwarming--it's a rollercoaster ride for your feels but it's worth every peak and valley. ~ Shelly, 5 stars Gorgeous, hockey player, man whore Dean Heyward-Di Laurentis is all about living the college life, and that means getting into as many woman as he wants. Literally. He was happy with the life he lived, until Allie knocked him on his ass and changed the way he lived. All Allie wanted to do is keep living her life despite having to make one of the hardest decisions of her young life, and yet, what she found instead was comfort in the last guy she ever thought of...Dean. These two had me sighing, laughing, clenching my thighs, rolling my eyes and wanting to smack some sense into them at times. I loved their chemistry!! Allie's determination to not fall into the pit called Dean again was hilarious! Dirty Dean, as I like to call him, left no stone unturned in trying to convince Allie to give him a second chance. Allie and Dean have their highs and lows, they come to realize their goals in life have changed and, at some point, they will have to make decisions that will definitely change their relationship. ** spoiler alert ** I thought this book was okay.The parts about what the North Koreans thought about the outside world were interesting. Kim's internal conflict between wanting to tell her students the truth about the world, and the desire to not make her students lives harder was fascinating. Kim talks about how, in North Korea, you are always being monitored by someone, and seditious thinking can be very dangerous. If the students learn the truth, then instead of believing sincerely the DPRK's propoganda, they will have to pretend to believe, which will be much riskier. Given this, is it ethical to dump truth on them, especially knowing that it may make you, the Westerner, feel better than the amount of good it will do them? It's unlikely Kim's students will band together, start a revolution, and overthrow Kim Jung Un. More likely is the possibility that they will simply find it more difficult to behave in the ways necessary for their survival, and they will therefore be at greater risk of being sent to the gulags Kim so abhors. It was also very interesting to learn about the huge list of topics that were verboten for the teachers to discuss. Basically, the missionaries are playing the long game. They are not focused on immediate results but on results two or three generations in the future. Therefore, they are very careful to try and obey the rules laid down by the North Korean "counterparts," though they still try to sneak in some veiled Christian stuff. This kind of super-subtle proselytizing is really the only kind possible, taking into account the balance necessary between educating/evangelizing the North Korean students, while being permitted to stay in country. One of the things that bothered me about the memoir is Kim's seeming unfamiliarity with Christianity. She is posing as a fellow missionary to her coworkers, but she is actually an atheist. Kim lashed out at one of the missionaries for saying that life on earth is temporary and their focus is on the North Korean's eternal lives. Kim responded angrily asked "How could you possibly look at people in gulags and tell them that it is temporary?" - the implication being that the missionaries were not doing what should be done and were in fact doing something incorrect. However, this is the only way the missionaries would be allowed to continue working in North Korea, and Kim herself is doing nothing different from what the missionaries are doing. I think Kim is misunderstanding the focus on eternal life as a focus ONLY on eternal life. "This reminded me of Ruth's claims that God has his reasons, and the sufferings of North Koreans were a temporary stage on the way to heaven. Gulags, then, served a purpose in the name of Jesus, much the way my students were taught to follow their Great Leader despite the famine. Or rather, because of the famine, which was reinterpreted as a form of martyrdom, necessary to the building of a powerful and prosperous nation." These two things are not automatically linked. Saying the first DOES NOT MEAN you are also saying the second. Kim has made a huge assumption here, and she gives no evidence to support her interpretation of what Ruth said earlier. This is particularly ironic, because this comes after a long discussion of how foreign the idea of giving supporting evidence is to her North Korean students. The fact that Kim could live with the missionaries for so long and not grasp this makes me question her ability to grasp the psychology of the boys she taught. Kim does mention, however, that she was raised and remains atheist, so perhaps more of a shared culture exists between her and the students then between her and the missionaries, making her insights into the students more well-founded. Kim also frustrated me when she acknowledged that her publishing this book would upset her former coworkers. Instead of making a case for why she felt she had to publish, or what publishing would do in a positive way, she says she hopes her coworkers will forgive her because they believe that God made her, and that therefore God also knew about her betrayal and made that happen too. This is, again, a weird misunderstanding of Christianity. Christians believe in free will, and therefore in responsibility for your actions. To receive forgiveness, you need repentance. It's entirely possible the missionaries might believe that God let this happen to test them, or that God sent her to test them, but that's not the basis on which anyone should seek forgiveness. It is kind of offensive that she would say she hopes they forgive her because they believe God made her, especially because she is an atheist. Why argue for forgiveness based on a premise you yourself don't accept? Does Kim even believe she needs forgiveness? I feel like Kim's lack of respect for Christianity really informs this book. She argues against things people didn't say (or at least, that she didn't report them saying), she uses misunderstood doctrine to demand forgiveness for endangering PUST's future, portrays Christians as gullible, and participates in one of Christianity's most important rituals, communion, without regard for whether that's appropriate. I would not participate in another relgion's rituals or ceremonies, because even though I don't believe in them, they do, and it's disrepectful to them to treat them as meaningless or make-believe in front of them.

Have I ever mentioned how much I love portal fantasies? Seriously, they're one of my favourite things, second (or third, really) only to cats and cake. This book is not a portal fantasy. It's a post-portal fantasy (postal fantasy? ); Seanan McGuire describes what happens to you after you fell through into a different world - a world in which you felt at home - and then came back. It's a great idea and it allows McGuire to say a lot of clever and insightful things about the genre (have you ever wondered why it's usually girls who fall into other worlds? there is a brilliant explanation for that in this book). And also tell a brilliant story about broken people who don't belong. Those are always good. The story focuses on Nancy, who has been to the (well, more of an an) Underworld, but unfortunately stumbled back into our world and now has trouble adjusting (really she just wants to find her way back), so her loving but also a bit selfish parents send her off to a "school" for "troubled teens" (in reality a haven for people just like Nancy - it's kind of like the X-Men school). Once she arrives, people start to die, and that becomes the plot. It's a bit like a detective story, except the characters don't do that much of the detecting - so let's say that it's more like a Harry Potter book: weird shit goes down and the protagonists stumble through the plot trying to get their bearings. This is the only fault I can find - Nancy and a group of people who eventually would probably become her friends (the plot unfolds over the course of just a couple of days from her arrival) mostly walk around feeling scared and don't do that much (it's probably realistic, but really, who reads books for realism? Other than that: A+ book, the fantasy part of the plot is great, the different worlds that other pupils have fallen into are quite interesting, there's great representation (an asexual character! a trans man! ), bits of wisdom thrown here and there... Yeah. If only the protagonists did a bit more (or maybe if it was a fully-fledged novel and the action could unfold over a couple more hundred pages? The book doesn't feel rushed, but I would lie if I said I wouldn't spend more time with those characters).

While reading this book, I had two diverging thoughts: This could never happen-rounding of people and treating them like criminals simply because they might be dangerous in the future? It's the whole "innocent before proven guilty" phrase, but completely backwards. I know this will never happen, especially because it is too ration, unjust, and mostly because it's accusations based on mere assumptions. This could actually happen- maybe it isn't as relevant now in today's world ruled by order and justice, but unjust actions and cruel treatments of people of different race, religion, and class is not fictional. There are world wars and death written and recorded in text books, written into songs, and made into movies based on true events. Human beings are fragile creatures, and the blame game has not been and probably will not ever go out of style. Maybe this exact situation hasn't occurred (yet), it doesn't mean that the thought is far fetched. With these two thoughts mingling in my mind, it made reading this book really interesting. For once, I was really scared and a lot of the scenes made me feel really anxious. I really like Davy! Even before she had the kill gene, she seemed like a really sweet girl who treated everyone around her with respect despite the fact that she's a prodigy. So when people started to turn on her and treat her as if she was less than a human being, it really made me mad. Her ex-boyfriend, Zac, is a complete asshole (despite the fact that I think he does care about her and still loves her) and let's not getting into the worst friend in the world, Tori-hated her-ugh. I really admire how well she pulled herself together, and knew when to stand up for herself and knew when to back down. She's really rational and strong, and I don't know if I could have been that level headed if I were in her shoes. I really liked Mitchell, Gil, and especially Sean. The romance between these two were great because Sean didn't see Davy as a damsel in distress, he recognizes her strength and pushes her to be stronger and I admire that. Yes, there are times where he saves her but there are also times where she saves him. I did enjoy the first half of this book-it was more emotional- more than the second, but the second half is definitely more action packed. The ending left me with the calm before the storm feeling, and I couldn't help getting a The Darkest Minds and Divergent vibe while reading this book. Now keep in mind I HATE IT when people compare books, but for me, I didn't think that Uninvited's plot line is similar to TDM and Divergent but I got similar feelings while reading this book. TDM because of the helplessness of it all, and how people will look the other way despite knowing what they are doing/seeing is wrong. Also, how these kids have to defend themselves against a cruel government system. For Divergent, Davy reminds me a bit of Tris because she is seen as a weakling and everyone thinks they can take advantage of her but she proves to be more than their ignorant opinions of her. I loved both TDM and Divergent, and now I can say that I also really liked Uninvited as well, bring on the sequel!

I liked this book for what it was to me: an easy, quick read that I could enjoy without much thought. I have a dark feeling about the future books in the series, but I liked the lack of a love triangle in this one. I adore books about faerie courts. The idea of a magic "blight" was fascinating to me, and I appreciate a character who can accept when she's been outmatched. There were times where I knew other YA protagonists would have been sassy so as to wave their Look How Rebellious I Am flag, but Fayre kept her mouth blessedly shut. My goodness, though. It had its problems: I rolled my eyes the second I read Fayre's name. Fayre? In a book about faeries? My You're Trying Too Hard meter was ding-dinging all over the place. On page two. So, this girl is captured because she killed a faerie. Her punishment? To be taken out of a miserable life of poverty to a sprawling, beautiful mansion with unlimited food and maid service. Fayre wants to paint? Well by god, she can paint. Fayre's worried about her promise to take care of her family? No worries - they've been glamoured and live a happier life, too. ... What happened to committing a huge crime? Almost every single person in this story likes or forgives Fayre way, way too easily. She murders someone's friend? Oh, she'll get some snarky comments for a single day, but she'll be forgiven the next. I was so completely confused the first or second night she's living in the mansion and goes to dinner. Tamlin (her eventual boytoy who was introduced in the story as a monster that screams "MURDERER!!!") and Lucien (her boytoy's friend) are her brand-new captors and despite the awkward reason for being there, Lucien offers Tamlin encouraging flirting tips...after he'd snarked at Fayre. Okay? Things happen to Fayre, for the most part. Her piece scoots around the board because people decide to make a move that happens to involve her. She goes with it. She pulls on her badass britches by the end of the story, but it takes a good long while. That said, though, it was sort of refreshing to read about someone who didn't constantly feel like she was at war with the world. Sometimes I get the impression that YA novelists feel as if their protagonists need to keep up a perpetual stone wall: they need to be stern, excellent in all things, and bristle at the slightest challenge. That's annoying, imo. Characters possessing a bit more passivity should not be considered weak or uninteresting. I also know that the scenes in the manor were a bit filler-ish, but they felt ridiculously refreshing to me. How wonderful to just soak up a location, to establish relationships, to have a long stretch of relative downtime instead of PLOT PLOT PLOT ACTION ACTION ACTION. I'm pretty sick of the need to emulate Michael Bay in YA novels. Again, I think novelists have the idea that no one can ever be happy for longer than a page. Unless a new conflict is unfolding, no one is happy. And while I get the reasoning, I'm just so pleased to come across a novel that didn't feel the need to bombard me with ten thousand twists and turns. Can we also say that there were some racy-ass scenes in this book for teens? I would feel icky handing this to someone under 17. Don't get me wrong -- I personally enjoyed it -- but nah, I'll pass on recommending this to any one of my students. I don't think I could bear the thought of them having to read those (short, let's be real) scenes. I'm surprised I had this much to say. There's more too, I guess, but it's not worth mentioning. Sarah J. Maas is still not on my go-to list; I think her writing lacks something lyrical and it feels too simple. However, this book was there when I needed it.

Review: Complete Faith is the sequel to Morning Report and gives us the relationship between Noah and Tommy that many readers had been hoping for at the end of that book. But it doesn't give us a lot of angst and pain, or crisis, or mystery, or much of the drama that makes a good book great. So, this one is a good story that is actually a bit above average in the audiobook format due to narrator Aaron Pickering who, as usual, does an excellent job. His vocalizations of the various characters hit a range of tones and accents, and when he uses his hot, sexy voice to narrate the hot, sex-filled scenes between couples, it sounds so realistic that I feel like I'm being a voyeur. The story involves Tommy, 23-year-old hand on the Lost Cow Ranch, gay and in the closet and a virgin because his parents are super-religious and he's so fearful they'll find out about him that he's kept a tight rein on his behavior. And it involves Noah, the pastor of the gay-friendly church which Luke's family has turned to after their previous pastor proved himself to be a gay-bashing bigot. Noah is 35 years old and is totally smitten by Tommy so when Tommy is finally ready for his first kiss, it's Noah who's there for him. And it's Noah who gives Tommy more firsts, including the courage to come out to his parents. That, of course, doesn't go well, but Tommy wasn't expecting it to, and he's now living on the ranch so the impact isn't great, other than on his heart. The story progresses with other friends and ranch hands having their own struggles, Tommy having some minor trouble with one of the bullies he went to school with, then the usual ranch issues. One dramatic crisis involves flash flooding on the ranch and Luke and Simon as the characters most affected, but considering that the story is about Noah and Tommy, there really wasn't a major crisis involving them. The potential was there in a few different ways. One, with Tommy's parents being so cold to him, and another time when Tommy had a severe case of the flu I thought it might turn out to be something worse, and even a third time when he was driving to Noah's in a bad storm, I kept expecting something major to happen to him, but none of those things was ever more than mundane. Even the age gap wasn't made a focal point in any way. The main drama occurred toward the end of the story and involved Noah's position as pastor of his church being threatened, but again, it was not a huge issue and was resolved quite simply. So overall, I'm going to give this one 3.5 hearts-- 3 for the story and an extra .5 for the narration. But I am looking forward to listening to the next audiobook in the series because these are nice stories with a sweet romance and sometimes I like it when things to go smoothly for the guys. He says, "Do I look gay to you?" Because suddenly he's thinking that maybe he should. That maybe he should have put on a pink button-up and popped the collar or something. And sandals. He should definitely be wearing sandals. She says, "What?" But then he remembers, he's hot no matter what he's wearing so he says, "What what?" Which only makes the girl flush more and turn to face the window. That happens not even a couple of hours after he finds out about his butt-boinking adventures of the night before. Doesn't even spend so much time angst-ing about the turn in his preference in bed partners. When you say embrace, dude really embraces. He then meets Vance the mysterious texter, has sober sex, and falls head over fucking heels he scares himself. Gunnar has issues, however, that he doesn't have the inclination to invest a fraction of his awesomeness in sorting out. This is when the story shifts and becomes more than just a funny take on the usual GFY. This is when you realize that it's not only a boy meets boy romance but also Gunnar's painful but necessary journey to the land of the feels. You see, Gunnar has only ever loved one person in his life - his equally pompous jackass of a brother - and the sentiment is not even reciprocated, something Gunnar knows and just shrugs about. He doesn't love his parents, or their dog, or his friends, or any of his bed flings. It's not that he wants not to feel anything for these people, it's just that he doesn't. There's just nothing there. When his friend almost OD'd on pills, his first thought was how inconvenient it would be to find a new roommate. And as unfeeling as that may sound, I completely get what he means. I know how it is when all you feel about the majority of people around you is meh. Not trying hard not to give a shit meh or even Vulkan-ish emotions are alien to us meh. It's just good old fashioned meh. I mean, there's like and appreciation and fondness and everything, but just not that deep, I'll grieve so hard when you die kind of love. I bet I'm not making sense. Moving on. This not really feeling things practice has worked pretty well for Gunnar in the past so when he suddenly starts getting all "I have feels" with Vance, he gets unsurprisingly idiotic about it. Add in some family stuff and Gunnar is swimming in so many emotions it's not even funny. The angst is not overdone, though. The humorous narration balances shit out. The supporting characters are also well developed and important to the story and it's nice to have a non-MC be instrumental to the emotional development of the MC. I loved this book/story/online fic. I loved that it's free. I loved that the characters talk like how my internet saturated mind thinks people their age talk. I liked Vance though I'd have appreciated to have known him more. I loved the roommates and their unabashed insistence in being fag hags. And I loved loved loved Gunnar. Unfeeling asshole or not, I'd totally want to grab some Raspberry While Chocolate Latte, non-fat, with an extra shot with this goddamned sexy chameleon.

Looking for Alaska is the second book of John Green's that I read and absolutely loved. After reading The Fault in Our Stars, I was fascinated by John Green's writing and decided that I definitely have to check out his other books as well. It's safe to say that that was a very wise decision. Looking for Alaska is a story about enigmatic girl Alaska Young. The protagonist of the novel, Miles Halter, tells the story of his experience at Culver Creek Boarding School, where he meets his new friends, Chip "The Colonel", Takumi, Lara and the mysterious Alaska. Together, they go through usual high school problems, such as finding yourself or life's meaning, smoking and drinking illegally and planning possibly the funniest pranks Culver Creek has heard of. Although Miles isn't the popular type, or even the type that has had a lot of friends in school, he quickly becomes wrapped in his new friends' world, being drawn to Alaska with an incredible force. Alaska is intelligent, funny and attractive and Miles falls for her hard. The only thing standing in his way is Alaska's boyfriend, Jake. Even so, Miles continues to pursuit Alaska, even if he knows they won't be more than friends. With Alaska's mood swings, Miles desperation continues to grow. Does he love this unpredictable girl or not? While they continue to go as friends, Miles' questions shatter his peace and start to affect the others as well. But one night, one sudden event will change everything around Miles and The Colonel. The world Miles thought he knew gets taken away from him in an instant. Nothing will ever be the same. As it was to be expected with one of John Green's books, Looking for Alaska left me with a bitter taste. It also possibly left me heartbroken. At times it was very funny while other times it was truly sad. The worst kind of sadness you can possibly feel is the one where something hurts you so much and still you can't cry and let it all out. Instead you keep it in and it eats at your soul. My experience with Looking for Alaska was very similar to this worst kind of sadness. However, I loved this book. I thought it was amazing, heartbreaking, funny and sad. I loved Alaska Young and I loved The Colonel. I didn't think that there would be the problem of life and death in this book but I was obviously wrong, as it turns out this is one of John Green's main themes. I did like the whole meaning-of-life topic and even the one of finding-your-true-self and I appreciated the realistic outcome of the book.
