Daikichi is a thirty year old bachelor who notices a six year old girl he doesn't recognize when he attends his grandfather's funeral. He finds out that she is the illegitimate daughter of his grandfather (and thus technically his aunt), and as much a surprise to the rest of the family as to him. Despite having just lost her father Rin is treated as an inconvenience and when the family sits down to "discuss" her future, clearly already having made up their mind to ship her off to wherever will take her, Daikichi decides to take care of her himself. Bunny Drop is a slice of life story that grows from the consequences of Daikichi's decision. It focuses on day-to-day life and discussions of "mundane" concerns. For some this may sound boring but the characters are thoroughly engaging, things are well paced, and real attachment forms as we follow along with their lives. Daikichi is in over his head but willing to learn and compromise, and Rin is a largely independent child who none-the-less is still only six, with all the wonder, weaknesses and needs that go along with it. This first volume sets the stage nicely, and sets up developments and questions to be explored in future volumes. The art is simplistic, but very well done and the style suits the story being told. I really hesitate to bring this up here, but it's been a big enough issue for some that a small warning is appropriate before people start reading. Without getting into specific spoilers, the series is much different in the second half, and that has "ruined the series" for a lot of readers. I still think the series as a whole is wonderful and well worth reading, but I understand the complaint and felt it worth mentioning. Bunny Drop is a charming tale of an unprepared yet caring bachelor who suddenly becomes a father, and of growing up for both him and his "aunt."

Upon rereading this, I took a star away, as for me this truly warrants a one star review. The Historian is a long winded slog that is a terrible mystery/vampire novel, a decent travelogue of 1970s Eastern Europe, and borrows the method of Dracula without nearing any of that book's execution. I'm into long winded tales, I'm into books set in the past, I'm into books about books, and characters as scholars or playing at scholars: Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell is one of my all time favorite books, and if I'm after a "smart" guilty pleasure I'll still enjoy picking up The Club Dumas. So this should totally be in my wheelhouse, but it was honestly even more of a chore the second time around. First the good: Kostova did a lot of research and travel to the places in her novel and it shows. The sense of place as we hop round Europe is quite good, especially with regard to Istanbul, Budapest, and Romania. Kostova has nice attention to detail for the travelogue oriented parts, and here, that detail is necessary, lends itself to establishing atmosphere and scene, and is altogether welcome and accomplished. That's all I've got for the good. Now for the frustrating, infuriating, weak and downright dull parts. First problem: the first narrator is entirely pointless. She has no personality to speak of, and has very little page time. Her entire reason for being is to ask her father questions, and then read from his series of letters. She has a few moments of action near the end, but she herself does nothing in those moments. You care nothing about her, indeed you almost forget she exists, how little she is seen or heard versus the letters/conversations of her father, and because Kostova pretty much has one voice for all of the characters, she is entirely unmemorable. This leads to another two part downfall of the book: switching between multiple pasts with little payoff, and poorly using an epistolary format throughout. Because the first narrator is more or less pointless, the entire timeline of her past (because she is writing from the present to describe her past encounter that mostly describes her father's past) means very little to the reader. The portion that we care to read is Paul's past, his research and journeys and trials and tribulations shared with Helen. Paul and especially Helen are far more compelling characters. The third last we get is Rossi's, which informs Paul and Helen in their past as they piece together clues and facts. I could deal with this, but the problem is we are supposed to be gathering all this through letters that Paul has provided his nameless daughter. But the long winded prose and sentences, the extra details in what should be moments of action or fear don't fit at all with letter writing. Kostova cannot use the epistolary format authentically, and doesn't seem to care that the reader will find the set up unbelievable. And because how Paul writes letters sounds like how the narrator talks (and sounds like Rossi's letters as well), I found it that much harder to swallow, especially after reading Stoker's take so recently and how well he was able to pull it off, and be true to character voices AND to making a letter sound like a letter. If Kostova had excised the unnecessary first narrator, and removed the epistolary format, and centered the narrative around Paul and Helen with the flashbacks/letters of Rossi, the book probably would have been two stars for me. But it would still only go up a star because... DRACULA IS BARELY IN IT AND HIS ROLE AND MOTIVATIONS ARE ASININE. It is not good that the research and scholarship of Dracula is far more interesting than the character itself once he finally arrives. And what good is it to give us such rich history of Vlad Tepes/Vlad Dracul, the Order of the Dragon and the secret knights of the Sultan opposed to him for all eternity, his cults, folklore, songs, if it comes to naught in creating a worthwhile, significant character when he appears in the flesh on the page? The idea of (and fear and pursuit of) Dracula is far better than Dracula himself, which is entirely a let down and very deflating. And what is Dracula's master plan? What is his motivation behind leaving creepy little books as calling cards and having his fiendish flunkies kill cats and third tier side characters? Why have these historians been toiling and pursuing him? Because he needs an expert librarian to catalogue his extensive, ancient library. That's it. DRACULA WANTS A PERSONAL LIBRARIAN (Oh and take over the world of course, but we're told little about that.) And I thought Stoker's Dracula was absent, but at least he built the horror and tension needed to believe in his cruelty and malice. Here we are told in letters and research about young Vlad Dracul's impaling oriented exploits, but its all undone by the dry, overstuffed language of the discoveries and the absence of any impaler like activities in the main narrative (Paul's daughter and Paul's). Why even be Vlad the Impaler if he never impales anyone??? Kostova's Dracula is entirely neutered when he appears on page, and ultimately undoes any charm or creativity about the historical research into the background of Dracula. If I felt the climax of Stoker's Dracula was a bit weak, the climax to The Historian for all intents and purposes does not exist, that's how bad / short / stupid / unsatisfying it was for me. Not to be overly crude, but if I was going to suffer through all Kostova's masturbatory prose and poor execution (with a side of mice travelogue), I was expecting one hell of a climax at the end, some reason for reading this. But there's no pay off, there's no there there. Fortunately I will never need to read this book again: it's two readings too many as it is.

They definitely had insta-love but I understand why. Maddy has never experienced human contact with a boy her age and I completely understand why it would be so easy for her to fall head over heels for the first boy she sees. So the insta-love didn't bother me. I love the way Maddy always talks about reading books and she talks about a lot of different classics throughout the story. I love how she talks about rereading her favorite books backwards and suddenly the characters go from knowledge to doubt and coming of age stories become stories about losing your way. It's such an interesting perspective on things. "I was happy before I met him. But I'm alive now, and those are not the same thing." This book is filled with beautiful, wonderful quotes. That's the #1 reason why I still enjoyed this book as much as I did. This book felt like reading Maddy's diary, especially with all the little diagrams and charts throughout the book. It was very cute and unique. I also love how she describes meeting Olly like the Big Bang theory happening in outer space. There was nothing and then in one single moment there was everything. I love that. It's such a beautiful way to think. I just wish the ending was better. The big reveal at the end didn't blow my mind, it just pissed me off. It kind of ruins the purpose of the entire book. And those last few pages, I just wanted a better conclusion. She didn't even tell Olly everything she had figured out at the end and that pissed me off. I wanted to see his reaction too. It's kind of a big fucking deal. How could her Mom even do that to her? I get that she was grieving over the death of her husband and son, but eighteen years later and you still haven't told her the truth? That's a joke. She saw first hand the pain that this "disease" was putting Maddy through and she didn't care. She's so selfish, it just pisses me off. If the ending wasn't so terrible this book would have easily been a 4.5 and it would've been one of my favorites.

Real rating: 3.5 stars I went into Turtles All the Way Down with much trepidation. I tend to feel that John Green bites off more than he can chew in his novels. In past novels, he would try to expound very "deep, philosophical" themes. Worse than this, he loves using the Manic Pixie Girl tropes. So I started this novel expecting to be hit by these two problems. Instead, I was pleasantly surprised. Aza/Writing Aza is probably the best John Green protagonist I've encountered. She grappled with so many internal demons. She also had her external battles that resulted because of those internal demons. Her mental illness was so written in such a realistic way that reading it caused me anxiety. It felt so real, in ways that John Green's books have never really made me feel. It was because of these issues that those deep, philosophical thoughts that are a staple of John Green novels felt substantial. Aza seems like a character that could actually have these thoughts. She had seen so much, been through so much, that when she had thoughts like, "Anybody can look at you. It's quite rare to find someone who sees the same world you see," I didn't scoff. Instead, I mulled it over. Davis/Romance I didn't consider Davis a main character. I say this because I feel like this was not a romance novel by any means. This is a book about Aza and Aza's war against her thoughts. Davis is merely a side character, pushed into the wings most of the time (and rightly so). Yet, I need to point out how cute he is. He is not perfect, he is sad, he is confused. But he is so eloquent. His love of astronomy and his thoughts on it was heart wrenching. My heart broke a bit when he said favorite star was his favorite solely because it was seeing 12 year old light, light in which his mom was still alive. Like, first of all, ouch. But let me just thank John Green for not making this a love story. He put the idea out there but he didn't push it. He let Aza take center stage. I loved how the story was all entwined. The way both conflicts merged into one at some points. Though it wasn't 4 star worthy, I will say this is the best John Green novel I've read so far.

This book came with so many glowing recommendations from people I trust that I must admit I was disappointed with it. It's good, but has enough failings not to be a masterpiece, as proclaimed by Jane Smiley, Margaret Forster et al. In the tradition of Heart of Darkness and Mosquito Coast, it's about an authoritarian Baptist missionary who drags his wife and four daughters off to a village in the depths of the Congo to convert the ignorant natives. The year is 1959, just before the Congo gains independence from Belgium, only for Patrice Lumumba, the newly-elected President, to be assassinated with the help of the CIA, and the country turned over to the murderous Mobutu. So of course you can tell in advance it's all going to end badly. The story of the destruction of the family is told in turn by Nathan Price's wife and daughters. It's long -- 600 pages -- and it took me till about page 300 to really get absorbed in it. Unfortunately I felt most of the last 150 pages were a mistake and should have been left out, or at least drastically trimmed. The good: the vivid, lyrical descriptions of life in the jungle, and the different viewpoints of four all-American girls struggling to come to terms with a totally alien way of life. I also liked the way the heroine of the story, Leah (clearly Kingsolver's alter ego) gradually comes to understand and appreciate the spiritual richness of the Congolese way of life despite unimaginable material poverty. The bad: unfortunately, instead of ending the book when the mother finally finds the courage to abandon her increasingly autocratic and cruel husband, marching off into the jungle with daughters in tow, Kingsolver tacks on 150 pages following the girls over the next 30 years. This second half of the book is an increasingly didactic rant about the harm done to Africa by Western capitalist exploitation -- something which had been made clear enough in allegorical fashion in the first half of the book. Perhaps this kind of laying-it-on-with-a-trowel is considered to be necessary for American audiences, who are probably completely ignorant of the atrocities committed by their own government in the name of democracy (or rather capitalism). But for me it detracted from the subtlety and force of the first half of the book. Also, there was no sense of character development in this part of the book -- the sisters remain essentially the same people at 50 as they were at sixteen, with life experiences apparently doing little to change the way they think or behave, and they deteriorate into stereotypes. For example the eldest sister Rachel, the stereotyped bigoted white woman living off the toil of others, is still saying "Jeez, man oh man" at 50, just as she did at the beginning of the book -- and is still just as insensitive and woefully ignorant of politics, despite living and running a business in Africa, where political upheaval is constant. At one point she tells Leah that Ronald Reagan is "keeping us safe from socialist dictators". When Leah asks which ones, Rachel replies, "I don't know. Karl Marx! Isn't he still in charge of Russia?" -- thus giving Leah the opportunity to deliver a patronising political lecture. It could have been so much better if it had been 150 pages shorter, with just a postscript revealing the different fates of the girls after they escape from their father. For a lesson in how to write a political novel with a soul, look no further than Matthew Kneale's English Passengers, or Barry Unsworth's masterpiece Sacred Hunger.

This book made me suspicious of the ice cream truck that patrols my neighborhood. That should be enough to tell you that it's an effective thriller, but I'll give you a little bit more... Some sick bastard drives a stolen Mercedes through a crowd of people waiting outside of a job fair. It's a massacre. He kills eight, injures countless more. He gets away with it. The detective in charge of the case, Bill Hodges, retires years later. He's haunted by the case he couldn't close. He watches daytime TV and flirts with the notion of putting a bullet through his brain. It's not uncommon, he assures himself, for retired police to swallow a bullet. Something about it seems like the predetermined final chapter in his life... Then he gets a letter in the mail with a familiar smiley face on the envelope. It's a letter from the killer he couldn't catch, Mr. Mercedes himself. The madman taunts Hodges, even mentions Hodges putting a gun to his head, as if he's been watching all this time... He assures Hodges that he has no intention of creating another bloodbath--once was enough--and tells Hodges to just go ahead and end his life already. Except, instead of delivering the final nail into Hodges' coffin, Mr. Mercedes has accidentally given the old detective a reason to go on living. Hodges begins the investigation anew, all the while knowing that somewhere the killer is watching him and plotting his next attack. In addition to following the likable Det. Ret. Hodges, the book also gives the killer almost equal coverage throughout the book. Mr. Mercedes is an incredibly messed up young man. Cold, hateful, and evil in way that feels all too real. He patrols Hodges' neighborhood in an ice cream truck, smiling to the kiddies who come bouncing up to his ride, all the while contemplating poisoning the ice cream and killing every kid on his route. It's a disturbing character made all the more disturbing because the book lets us get into the killer's head--a place we would rather not be. This is Stephen King's first full-on crime thriller and he navigates the new territory quite well. But I gotta admit to a lack of surprises in the twists and turns of the plot. For much of the book, I could anticipate what was going to happen next. This could've wrecked the book if the characters weren't so interesting. I really like Hodges and the other good people he rallies to his cause. And the villain is strong and weird enough to carry his part of the book. I think that in the long run, this will be considered to be 'minor' King. In a way, that only makes sense. This is the author who brought us The Shining, The Stand, The Green Mile, The Dark Tower series, and so on. A crime thriller about the killer that got away appears considerably less ambitious by comparison. But this is looking at things the wrong way. Stephen King is 66 years old and he's been writing since the 1970s. At an age when other artists would rather retire or simply repeat the kind of hits that made them popular in the first place, King is trying something new and he's doing it successfully. Something about that gives me hope. Stephen King is one of the few masters who will never go quietly into the night. He remains brave and bold and I thank him for that.

This review originally posted at More Than Just Magic So you may have heard of this book by now. It is the YA book of the spring. Everyone is talking about it. And with good reason. The 5th Wave has been compared to The Walking Dead, The Hunger Games, The Road, The Passage, Ender's Game....The list goes on and on. Is it similar to any/all of these titles? Yes. Will knowing that in any way prepare you for what you are about to read? Absolutely not. The 5th Wave is one of those action packed, edge of your seat reads. I was so absorbed in this book I couldn't do anything else until I was done reading. It consumed me. And when I wasn't reading I was constantly thinking about the book. It made my heart race and it made me genuinely afraid of alien attacks. Seriously. This is how we're going to die. These aliens were so direct, so cold and calculating. Each different wave was a completely plausible event. No techno babble or science fiction fantasies. No nonsense. Think of all those terrible monsters throughout science fiction history. The Daleks. The Borg. These aliens are that level of terrifying. They will stop at nothing to achieve their ultimate goal - total alienation of our species. In the middle of all that fear however I really fell in love with Cassie. I thought she was an incredibly complex character. She was brave. Braver than I could ever be. But she wasn't invincible or fearless. She was scared for her life and nervous about trusting anyone. More than once she considers hiding/running. But these fears make her stronger because they are motivated by the love she has for her family rather than self interest. In a way she reminded me of Katniss. She was brave and held herself together pretty well, but her concern and fear for the safety of her family was her central motivator. When I started reading I didn't realize the book was going to shift perspectives. I was perfectly happy just reading about things from Cassie's point of view. But I like multiple perspectives. I like looking at stories from different angles and seeing how a particular event (or series of events) effects people differently. And I think Yancey's choice to go that route for The 5th Wave was a smart one. I do think however that the perspectives that weren't Cassie were a little under developed. Those sections were shorter and snappier and you just didn't connect with those characters in the same way. They were still captivating and had me hanging out to their every word but they weren't as fleshed out as I would have liked. Above all I loved all the questions this book asked about humanity itself. What makes someone human? Is it simply biological or is it something deeper? Something more abstract? And when it comes time for humanity to make its last stand will we stand together or will fear get the better of us? Recommendation: A fantastic edge of your seat ride that will have you watching the sky for our inevitable invasion. Easily one of the best alien adventures I have ever read.

I found this sly and sneaky. I think it's Sam's way of "being" with Sookie. We all know he's always had a "thing" for her and though she's often found him attractive, the "thing"'s never been reciprocated. So, to me this is just his excuse to parade Sookie around as his "girlfriend." I like Sam, don't get me wrong, but I don't think he is the right one for Sookie and feel like the author just put them together to be spiteful to the fans who've made her a fortune. The fact that Sookie kissed Sam (for his Mom's benefit. Right.) while she's with Eric makes me sick. Also, I thought the animal shelter scene was a bit excessive -- even for a series that's known for its blood and gore. And Quinn just shows up out of the freaking blue. This is one weird story. I was quivering with rage at Achilles for letting Patroclus go in the end (Because how arrogant was this cowardly little punk? He did not deserve Patroclus). The rest of this, however, simply retold bits of a story that I already knew. I should warn you that I have issues with historical fiction--I find that the real meat of these historical stories gets lost in minute details that make these kinds of novels drag on and on... so take my opinion for whatever it's worth.

You'd always feel a little cheated the next week how easily the hero or heroine overcame whatever peril was placed in their paths, but then forget about it as the next cliffhanger ending grabbed your attention. This book was one whole lousy cliffhanger ending after the other. Mild spoiler alert. I was really entertained by this story. Although since I read this, my opinions slightly changed mostly due to the short story I just finished last night following Travis and Abby's wedding , I was still entertained and kind of enjoyed it. Basically the story is a fun, hot, steamy scenes, with so many clichees I couldn't even count, and with characters who simply mesmerized me with their idiotic actions. At first, I thought Travis would be a bit more dangerous and mysterious, but his character turned out to be flawed, yet addicting. Okay, I admit I fell for the compulsive and controlling bad boy act, and I'm not totally proud. Abby, on the other hand, started out as being this all-american-girl, nice and sweet, but there were times when I hated her mood swings so much that I almost closed the book. I am still baffled by authors who think that by making their leading ladies shy and in need of constant protection, the love story will follow the already known and predictable pattern "girl meets boy, girl need rescue, boy saves girl, they live happily ever after". To be honest, this is not what makes a book remarkable, yes it gets it off the shelves, but it will not remain as a memorable story in the heads of avid readers. I am sick of female characters who have random strong moments that give me hope that maybe they could kick some ass, and in the end I'm left with small, naive girls who let the man of their dreams decide their lives. But letting the cynicism aside, Travis'character and the whole love story had me going and reading page after page. I am not completely happy with how everything turned out, but as a whole I liked it.

Why am I just reading this book now? I've read so many Alexa Riley books I can't believe I'm just reading thin now. It's OTT crazy possessive alpha smut as always but I'm loving it. Carter (who is Carter?) is serving eight years in prison for murder the book opens four years into his sentence with a twenty year old Layla visiting him. She's written him hundreds of letters and not heard a word back, he used to be her bodyguard, a bodyguard she fell in love with. Layla has no idea what happened that night. 'All I have is this giant blank spot in my mind driving me insane. One second I have a perfect life and the next I wake up in the hospital covered in bruises, with my mother missing, along with my bodyguard.' Not only does Layla not get any answers Carter but he tells her he threw her letters and she's to get gone. With that she takes off and starts a new life. Four years later Carter is released and we all know where he's heading. I loved this book, yes Carter is completely OTT and obsessed but I can't wait for more.

This one was lots of fun and it met my expectations. The plot reminded me of Chamber of Secrets but I must say the Gatekeeper was an unusual threat. If Harry's fatal flaw was saving his near ones, James carries the weight of the world on his shoulders. The book borrows characters from the original series but doesn't let it dominate the story. They serve a minor role, give you a link to the past but it never overshadows the present story world and its problems. We learn more about Merlin, I was fascinated by his legend and how this could affect present day Hogwarts. James has a lot on his plate : Are his loyalties in the right place? What if he's wrong? Is any deviation of history a sign of trouble? How blurry are the lines between good and bad, if there are any... Father issues were a part of Harry Potter and James has his own. Harry still gets a Butterbeer for his parenting skills. Saving the best for last, I was dazzled by Scorpius and would love to see more of him.

I was so excited in the beginning: in my whole life I was contemplating issues such as if I could save only one of my parents, which one would it be- then the same for my kids and so on. Silly, I know, but still. And here is this book by this author whose Kite Runner I wanted to read before anyone heard about it at all, and he writes about this. Wow. (My edition was 500 pages, so this point was followed by some long troublesome reading.) The book stopped being about the siblings. Instead, a parade of completely non-interesting characters marches through the book and I just keep turning the pages to find Pari and Abdullah and sisterly-brotherly love. Only the last chapter gives me this scenario, but it's all upside down. Usually I wouldn't mind if a story doesn't have a happy ending, but in this case I feel I was robbed of a story - or the writer didn't have the words. In which case, why did he bother starting at all? Ps. I'm afraid this isn't good story-telling at all. This is getting lost in details and completely missing the point. If you want a good story-teller, read Maugham or Jenniver Niven for example.

If I have one regret about my reading life it's that I didn't read this book in 2000. I was a teenager. I just moved to the US all by myself and was about to attend American High School for a year. My life was a mess and I wanted to start anew. Nothing prepared for what I was about to experience and I did all the wrong things and went the wrong way about the whole thing. If I had only read this book back then maybe I would've gotten my priorities right. Also it is written in such a simple language that my teenage self wouldn't struggle with it. It would give me the courage to explore more. As it was, I started reading in English with some big complicated book that made me dizzy and I eventually abandoned it. It was 2000! This book was huge then, I believe. I went to a bookshop and asked someone there to recommend me a book. I explained I came to the US, just started American High School, that I felt very lonely and that books made me happy. Why the idiot working there didn't just give me 'The Perks of Being a Wallflower', I will never know but I hope he got sacked eventually. Mind you, I wasn't somewhere along the Bible belt, where he might've been worried of causing scandal by giving me this book. It was New Hampshire! Live free or die! Of course, reading it now, in 2012, when I'm a seemingly well-adjusted adult living in London and not afraid of tackling even the most complex books in English, was not exactly a mind-blowing experience. I still felt the power and allure it would've had for me if I read it at a right time but could also see it for what it was - bit of a naive coming of age story written in a language that was too simple if it was supposed to belong to Charlie - the English class prodigy. There was a lot of: "I was sad. I cried. I was happy. I cried. And then I just cried for no reason." But you know what, there is one lesson in it that you should remember. Friends are important. And the friends you make when you're young are usually the friends you keep for life. So choose wise. And also here is a note for half of the people on the internets: Charlie was NOT autistic. I know people tend to call 'autistic' anything they consider weird but Charlie was the opposite of autistic. Autism is not characterized by higher than normal appreciation of literature or being oversensitive to people's feelings and super-perceptive when it comes to emotions. People, autism is more or less the opposite of that. If you need to give Charlie a label, make it PTSD and stop embarrassing yourselves.

After reviewing Howl's Moving Castle, I began to research the author. It said there was a sequel to HMC, and I just had to grab it! The book is called Castle in The Air. It's POV is not Sophie, Howl, Calcifer, or any of the cast you read in the first book. It's of a boy named Abdullah who lives South of Kingsbury. He sells rugs and always daydreams about being a prince and meeting a beautiful woman in a garden. One day, a man sold him a magic flying carpet. While sleeping on it, the carpet takes him to a wonderful garden. He meets a beautiful girl and thinks it a dream based on his daily daydream. The princess calls herself Flower-in-the-Night (seriously, that's the love interests name. I know right?) Abdullah figures out it's reality, and they plan to elope together. Once she's almost to the carpet, WHOOP! A Djinn picks her up in his big claws and carries her to an unknown place. He embarks on a journey featuring a cranky genie, black cat with her kitten, stubborn carpet, and a dishonest (yet) honest soldier. Where is Sophie, her husband Howl, and everyone else you ask? They're all stuck in the plot as secondary characters. Lettie (Sophies sister) and her husband Ben Suliman are also shown and they help the journey move forward. Michael is sadly not mentioned. (I really like him, darn it!). Howl and Sophie also present their little newborn Morgan. Such a happy/dysfunctional family. *sigh* The first critique I have to give is how slow the plot moves. It's not a book that will stick out in your mind in the future, but it's a cute read. I give this book four stars. It lost one point for how slow the plot progressed. Otherwise it's very nice and I recommend it.

3.5 stars rounded up. I've always liked Tessa Dare's books, but even more, I like her. I may or may not have fist-pumped when I read the "nevertheless, she persisted" clapback at Mitch McConnell. This read like a historical romance, but I found myself questioning the accuracy of various aspects. Accuracy issues aren't new to historical romances, though. I just didn't feel tuned into the setting, and I'm not even referring to the modern-day references, e.g. "fake news!" (which I actually enjoyed). Many of the mores, behaviors, and conversations didn't seem grounded in their time. Reading this, you may even wonder whether Dare should just try her hand at contemporaries. Ultimately though, I think her style brings charm and relatability to historical romance. I can shrug it off because I know what I'm going to get. However, others readers may struggle. There are many things to love about this book and Dare's writing. But in the end, I didn't love the love story, and that is the gist of my complicated feelings. I wasn't able to focus or feel as much. I liked Ash more than Emma, and it's very rare for me to like the hero more than heroine. Not that Emma wasn't likable! She had admirable qualities, but she wasn't as easy to connect with. Ash wasn't supposed to be likable, at least not for awhile, but I have a weakness for grumpy heroes. His protectiveness, his vulnerability, his strength - they were swoon-worthy. He won my heart. The book didn't always hold my attention, but that may have been influenced by my current mood and the fact that I read more contemporary and m/m nowadays. This is an enjoyable book, with enjoyable characters and enjoyable banter. If you won't be put off by the issues that I mentioned, I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it.

Oh my word! Gah! This book is infuriating, uplifting, realistic and oh did I mention infuriating? Honestly, I am so torn over how to rate this book that I'm going to do my first ever review without providing a rating. After reading this book, I was forced to consider how to rate and review books. The story itself was intriguing, but I couldn't stomach the characters at all. I wasn't fully invested in the characters and it made me not care as much as I should about the outcome of the plot. That being said, I think the author did a great job of portraying a victim of psychological abuse and what that does to the person's feelings of self-worth. The plot centers on Grace and her emotionally abusive douchebag of a boyfriend Noah. The book opens with this Romeo allowing Grace to service him after he snuck off to another room of a party where another girl performed oral sex on him. Noah admits that he's been cheating on Grace and pretty much brags about it to her. Because Grace seemingly has a death wish, she takes Noah back pretty much immediately (even agreeing to go for lunch with his mom the next day?!) and the abuse continues. I had a hard time understanding Grace's initial attraction to Noah. The story includes flashbacks with Grace leaving her nice guy boyfriend for bad boy Noah. However, he came off more as an obnoxious a-hole than a bad boy. He tells her on their first outing together to shut up and calls swirling fireworks "spermies" (be still my heart, gag). There didn't seem to be much of a honeymoon period for these two. As you can tell, I wasn't a fan of Noah (which readers aren't supposed to be) and to be honest Grace bothered me as well. It wasn't her doormat behavior that bugged me because I was able to empathize that she was damaged to the point that she basically let Noah walk all over her. It was her self-righteousness that got to me, i.e. calling other girls sluts, wanting to beat other women up for her boyfriend hitting on them, her constant insistence of being a "good girl." Jake was by far my favorite of the book and I'm glad the author included a guy that readers could fall in love with. The way he healed Grace was touching and once their relationship took center stage, the book was a much easier read. This book handled a tough subject and I respect the author for trying to bring attention to victims of emotional abuse. There are books that romanticize bad boys who treat women like crap and it was refreshing to see a depiction of when that kind of behavior has serious repercussions. Considering the book garnered such an emotional response from me, I would definitely say it's worth a look. The author took me on an emotional roller coaster and the novel will likely stay with me for a while.

I don't feel right giving this one a rating, because I'm not really qualified to. This is not really a review, more of an experiment. An outsider's view of a romance novel. The last time I read a straightforward romance novel was as a teenager. I picked it at random from the library. As I recall, it was about an orchid hunter who falls in love with his adopted sister's long-lost twin. It was accidentally hilarious. But it left me prejudiced against romance novels for a long time. Now, I did enjoy Sookie Stackhouse books up to a point before the vampire pop culture explosion reached critical mass and I began to find them tedious, and I've read and enjoyed things like Jane Eyre, Pride and Prejudice, and Water for Elephants. It's just books marketed specifically as romance I avoid. Yet the joy some people get from romance novels is often so ecstatic, that I began to wonder again whether I was missing out. Surely it couldn't be the most popular and profitable genre for nothing. Maybe it's unfairly maligned because it's "women's fiction". Trying it out again required a little research into what would be a good typical romance book, and this one was very well reviewed and set in the regency time period. The Regency seems to be the most popular time period for historical romances, popularized in the twentieth century by Georgette Heyer, or so I'm told by Wikipedia. I prepared myself to suspend my disbelief somewhat and forgive historical inaccuracies and a certain level of cheese. I couldn't always do so. But I finished the book, so it must have been doing something right. Even though I could see where it was going, I wanted to know how it ended. Here are the things I liked about it: The Heroine was 28, and pretty shrewd for a virgin. She was kind of a badass sometimes. She straight up shot a man.I forgave the historical inaccuracies of her feminist tendencies, because it's a nice change from the typical female of that era. I hate the Fanny Price type. There were some pretty funny scenes in it, it had a sort of romantic comedy vibe for a while, and cute back-and-forth between the leads. some of the love scenes worked, at first. When they kiss in the thunderstorm, even as I was thinking, oh, how cliche, they're kissing in the rain, I thought it was romantic. And when he speaks Italian? HOT.I think I have to be in the right state of mind, like I'm watching a hollywood movie. I'm still not certain if it was the book that fell apart or if I just couldn't stay in the right frame of mind for the duration. Or if I couldn't stop myself from thinking about things too much. Such as, hey, this rake that's been sleeping exclusively with prostitutes since he was 13...shouldn't he have ALL THE DISEASES? Am I just supposed to ignore these thoughts and be swept up in the romance? Penicillin wasn't discovered until 1928. Here are some other things that just didn't work for me: I couldn't believe that such a smart woman would let herself be drawn to such a red flag of a human being like Lord Dain. We're shown that Jessica understands men more than she should, having raised brothers and cousins, and having a libertine Grandmama, but she is aware that Dain is a rake, and keeps spending time with him, UNCHAPERONED, when she knows what could transpire. She has admirers even though she's reaching spinster age, could marry anyone if she wanted to get married, and is knows that lust is no basis for a good relationship, but she gets involved with him anyway. Like Jane Eyre, the book starts with some background about Lord Dain's childhood, so we fully understand how twisted his psyche is. I forgave his bitterness for a while. But I really couldn't get past the prostitutes. A man who has been with prostitutes his whole adult life wouldn't really be an excellent lover. He's never had to try. Love doesn't just magically make you good at cunnilingus all of a sudden. ( Plus, aforementioned, ALL THE DISEASES) And someone who has had no love in their entire life, has a good probability of being a sociopath. I don't know, he's in his thirties, maybe the love of a good woman isn't enough to fix him at this point? Maybe I shouldn't go to this genre for realism. You don't just plan on shooting someone in the arm in the 19th century, with a 19th century gun, and count on it going through without shattering bone or hitting some nerve or getting infected and killing a man. There is no guarantee he'd survive. People in the 21st century wouldn't even risk that, you could give the person chronic health problems. The injured man does have a dead arm for a while but it turns out to be psychosomatic, which I totally saw coming. It was cured by LOVE AND TRUST. Eventually the love scenes became tedious. They all had different locations and positions, but used similar language. How many different ways can you plunder a mouth? Always with the plundering and surrendering, etc. But the one in the churchyard kind of icked me out. Not necessarily because of all the gravestones, but that it was kind of rapey. Dain has an abuser's mentality, he was trying to control Jess, but she found a way to win that round of sex by telling him "I love you". If she hadn't been into it, though, I feel like he probably would have just gone ahead anyway. That damn kid practically ruined the whole thing. I was nervous about when he'd show up, because you don't just mention an illegitimate brat out of nowhere early on in a story without that coming up again at some point. He comes up again in the last act to redeem the Hero some more. The Hero being just a little boy inside is a theme that was repeated througout the story, and when he suddenly comes to terms with every thing that's broken within himself, sees himself in his son, and wants to help him, it makes sense, but it's all very rushed. The ending felt pretty sloppy, we're expected to believe that emotionally scarred boy is just fine now, won't try to murder their newborn, Dain is completely changed, and their baby is going to be born healthy--syphilis, what syphilis? Maybe someone can tell me how well this particular book represents the whole of the genre, is it worth it to read any kind of romance or should I just not bother if Lord of Scoundrels didn't win me over?

So OBVIOUSLY I was excited when I saw the summary for Jane Steele because HELLO, I have so much love for Jane Eyre and to have this be inspired by it, but with a murderous Jane, I just could not resist! And I'm so glad I picked this up, because it was SO GOOD! I mean, wow, I was a bit anxious when I started it because of said love for Jane Eyre, and the fact that I was wondering whether or not I would be able to connect to a character who murdered people, but I ended up very much loving Jane Steele as a character and I'm really glad that it wasn't just mindless killing but I could understand why she did what she did. And in some cases I definitely cheared her on because holy wow, EVIL people! Jane definitely has a hard life, it starts with a less than ideal childhood, a complicated family situation and then boarding school, which as in Jane Eyre, is just not run by nice people. I cannot even begin to imagine how you can get out of something like that and still have a shred of humanity left in you, but Jane managed. And in the hardships she makes a friend, but then they flee together and things go South again after that. Which is how she finally ends up at Highgate again and the real fun can begin because YES I SHIPPED IT! I mean, I love Jane for her strength and her loyalty and that she's willing to just do anything for the people she loves and has a strong sense of what is right. And when she met Mr. Thornfield, Sardar Singh and Sahjara, I was just happy that she was finally with people who appreciated her, and Sahjara is an adorable little girl who has been through a lot, it made my heart happy to see her and Jane interact. But now let's talk about Mr. Thornfield: I totally adore this man. He has this amazing big heart and sees all the good in Jane and her flaws and just takes it all. I loved his sardonic humour and the way he is with Sahjara, because you can just feel his love for the people at Highgate shining through in the thing she says. I loved that he and Jane both have dark things in their past, but together they find a way to deal with them. Basically, they were just better together and I totally shipped it and wanted to yell JUST KISS ALREADY and had tears in my eyes and just ALL the feelings. So yes, I'd definitely recommend you read Jane Steele. I love the voice that Lyndsay Faye gives Jane and the whole mystery surrounding Highgate and Mr. Thornfield. And I had lots of feelings over the romance and the ending totally made me smile because what Jane describes must be the best feeling ever! My rating: 5 stars

I very rarely abandon novels about halfway through; usually, I manage to judge by the first thirty to fifty pages whether a book would be worth my time or not (I do not rate unfinished novels, which is why you'll never find a one-star rating on my "read" list). A Tale of Two Cities started off interestingly enough, with (the protagonist?) Mr Lorry undertaking a voyage from London to Paris with the object of "recalling" an individual to life. The two cities of the title are portrayed in the bleak, vivid ensuing passages of an expert writer, but I feel Dickens comes short as a storyteller. True, his characters are richly and distinctively drawn -perhaps even to a fault, where his figures may come off as caricatures- but I found there was little drive and direction to the narrative. There was no one prominent or likable enough to root for as a protagonist, mainly because Dickens consistently jumped about sometimes-irrelevant characters (what was Jerry Cruncher's role in the story?) The author was apparently paid per word for his novels, which would explain why he not only included some seemingly meaningless scenes in the novel, but also why they felt terribly dragged out. These aspects made the novel a laborious task for me. This was my first attempt at Dickens, and based on A Tale of Two Cities, it will be my last for some while. Either this was one of his weaker efforts, or I belong to a literary minority not particularly fond of Dickens (...or maybe the novel would've eventually picked up had I kept reading?)

He's rude when he doesn't need to be and he has anger management issues, but he's never even slightly violent toward Jess or another woman. He just can't stand paparazzi. He's also portrayed by the media as a womanizer. In reality, Jack is a sweet guy with a hard past and trust issues, hence why he tries to push people away before making the "mistake" of trusting them. That doesn't work with Jess, because she's one tough girl. Jess' attitude toward Jack and everything else, crazy paparazzi included, is what made this story so fun to read. That and the beautiful romance, which includes "hate to love", "friends to love" and a lot of longing and wanting and waiting for the right moment. Kill me now and I'll die a happy girl!! The glamorous life of Hollywood's rich and famous was portrayed well enough throughout the story, although some details seemed too distant from reality, mainly in the end of the book. I know a lot about celebrities and I can't see them doing what Jess and Jack did when they arrived at that party. Last but not least, there's a pet that won my heart: Leo, the pig. He's adorable. Just. Adorable. I wanted to hug him all the time. Leo made me smile, but also made me tear up because his story gets pretty sad toward the end. I can't say I'm happy with the author's decision when it comes to Leo, but I understand what was done and why it was done. *sad face* Aside from that crying moment, this was a book that made me laugh and smile a lot. So go get it if you're looking for something that will bring a bit of joy to your hard day, week, month or year. I wrestled with the possibility of a more generous 1.5/2 stars, but I think I'd rather be honest and brave potential criticism for it. I feel a little harsh giving this such a low rating, but I feel like I'm with (relatively) popular opinion here in finding it disappointing - we sit through the Games twice for the sake of a revolution-centred finale, and never really see it. The pacing, the saving grace of the previous two books, was very poor here - very little happens for the first 20 chapters or so, followed by a sudden rush of action at the end, making the whole thing too confused and rushed for even the most dramatic events to have much impact. There are a few deaths, but they don't prove particularly moving since they're presented so plainly. It seems like the author wanted to throw a few minor characters away to give a sense of brutality in the conflict, but I didn't care for the characters, or for that matter the way they died, enough to care. The way that it's very slow for the first three quarters, then there's a bit of action at the end, is similar to Catching Fire, but unlike the latter I didn't find it satisfactory to redeem the book as a whole, yet alone provide an effective finale for the whole trilogy. The whole story could have been told in two books at most, but YA loves its trilogies (and they're worth more money to publishers! ), so this choice isn't exactly surprising. Katniss does not have a culmination of character as I might have hoped - she carries on having almost no power, and remains a poster-girl for the revolution rather than being directly involved, spending large swathes of the book performing publicity exercises. We expected a story about a teenage girl finding her inner strength and overthrowing a dystopian government, but instead we see her ordered around by minor characters (who also disappoint the expectations made in the previous book) and, lacking agency throughout, and, as usual, dressing up in various outfits for the sake of image, the same way the Capitol already made her do. The rebels continue to rely on staging events for promotion rather than letting our narrator see any real action. Even when it looks like she will be in the thick of it, it's all for show after all and the story carries on in the same vein. We are mostly stuck underground, not in the thick of it at all; and, when she finally is in the action when she reaches the Capitol, it's very short lived and, once again, she doesn't actually get to do much more than witness the destruction. Never reaching President Snow's mansion, while perhaps realistic, is the culmination of the series' disappointments. As is par for the course with these, there was plenty of uncompelling, plot-jarring romance as well. Katniss can't make her mind up until the end of the very book between the two of them, essentially leaving Peeta and Gale to battle it out. The epilogue which 'sorts it out' for us wasn't the most terrible, but was a pretty typical, mediocre afterthought that will inevitably satisfy some fans and make other readers grown: think the Harry Potter epilogue, the only difference being that Harry can move on while Katniss and Peeta are still suffering aftershocks - so, like the Potter epilogue, but less heartwarming. I don't think reading it as an audiobook is to blame because I've really enjoyed other audiobooks I've read, and the quality of the recording was alright. Most of my problems are with the story, at any rate, not the writing (which obviously suffers in audiobook form when you can't review it as carefully). Also, it wasn't the worst book I've ever read, but for God's sake, I can't think of a single think I really liked except maybe for the part at the very end when she realises she needs Peeta more than Gale - I didn't care whom she ended up with, but I liked how she reasoned it . For a two-star book I can usually think of one or two things, but I wouldn't have finished this if I wasn't determined to finish the series. I'm sick of this series and glad it's over, and I've finally finished it (at least Collins had the sense not to add any 'midquel' novellas, as YA authors are wont to do). I'm also glad the hype is effectively over now. I suppose, for me, the lesson learnt is to marathon series in the future in case that makes them easier to get through, but also that I should probably steer clear of overly-hyped YA trilogies like this one as a whole.

Willowdean is your average teenage girl, but with the confidence that will knock your socks off. Yes, she still has insecurities, but she loves herself despite that. Willow is fat. She knows it, everyone else knows it, but she isn't ashamed about her weight. When she discovers a Miss Blue Bonnet Pageant form in her late aunt's dresser drawer, she decides to enter. In Willow's town, the pageant is a huge deal. Most girls spend their whole lives dreaming of this pageant. What was once a pageant in honor of Willow's aunt has turned into something that Willow must not only do for herself, but for girls like her everywhere. To the girls who aren't up to society's "standards," but are happy anyways. Willowdean has always been fine with her body. Her confidence begins to falter when a very handsome boy, who just so happens to have a crush on, shows interest in her. How on Earth could a boy like Bo like someone like Willow? Even after their ups and downs, Willow pushes Bo away. All because she fears what others will think if they saw them together. On top of this, Willow is in a fight with her best friend, Ellen, which leaves her with no one to talk to. While the relationship problems between Bo and Willow and the drama between Ellen and Willow seem petty to me, it made sense. These kids are all in high school and they are portrayed flawlessly. This is high school. The ups and downs, the drama, the relationships, the insecurities, and doubts are all high school. While some may have some problems with the way the events in story unfold, I think Murphy did a fantastic and a very realistic job of portraying high school. I strongly connected with this story, as I struggle with my body image every day. Some days I'm happy with my body, while other days I don't want to look in the mirror. I have definitely learned over the last year that happy and healthy is so much more than "skinny." Size does not determine your level of happiness. You must learn to love yourself on the inside before you love yourself on the outside. This book only confirmed all of that. Dumplin' is a story of learning to love oneself and finding what you are truly made of. Do yourself a favor and read this book today.

I think it would be great for others to go in as I did, with only a "You gotta read this book," and nothing more. I don't know if there is any other book quite like this one in existence, so even the Sherlock comparison is dangerous since it might give the wrong idea, depending on what a potential reader thinks when they hear "Sherlock". The copy of "The Name of the Rose" that I read (which I received virtually free and in perfect condition via BookMooch! Score!) included extensive author's notes at the end. Some of these notes I found myself skimming because the topics became too specific for me to follow. But other areas of the notes were fascinating, giving me new perspectives on writing and the relationship between books, authors, and readers, as well as illuminating (not in the 14th century sense!) the genesis of this story (I can't help all the Christian words, after reading such a long book dealing with the topic, it's like breathing out my influences after breathing in the book). I found some of the author's opinions to be slightly insulting (at one point it almost seemed he was saying, "Wow, even idiots like my book!") or wearying (writing a pleasurable book without supporting escapism? EVERY book I read is an escape if I enjoy it, so, dear author, you have failed in that respect) but at other times I was impressed by his open honesty (particularly when he mentioned using the story-within-a-story method in order to feel safe). The end notes were excellent overall and a worthwhile chaser after the main event. Now that I've read the book, I really want to watch the movie. Bloody shame it's not on a streaming service like Netflix! If only there was a blu-ray swapping service akin to BookMooch that I could use :)

She may be prophesied to be this great mage but she has to work really hard to master her abilities. I enjoyed the parts of the book where she was at Eton passing as a boy for safety reasons. She is something of a tomboy and has had an unusual upbringing which made it plausible. I enjoyed the relationship between Iolanthe and Titus. While Titus is attracted to her right away, the romance develops at a slower pace because of more pressing concerns (and the fact that she has to pretend to be Archer Fairfax, a fellow student at Eton). I also liked the friendships that Iolanthe developed with the other boys at Eton, especially with Kashkari. I look forward to seeing more of the secondary characters. They added much needed humor at times. As much fun as her life at Eton was, I really found myself intrigued by the magical world too. To help her learn to harness the elements she hasn't mastered yet, Titus trains her in The Crucible, a place that reminded me of the Holodeck from Star Trek. The entrance is through a book of fairy tales and you have to proceed through various levels, fighting dragons and wyverns and other challenges. I also found their mode of transportation to be interesting. People "vault" from place to place but they can only vault certain distances and so many times in a day. It reminded me of apparating and disapparating from the Harry Potter books. While the book has excellent world building, I thought it read like a page turner and didn't get bogged down in detail. It was easy to catch on to the rules of the magical world and it also helped that part of the book was set in historical London too. I definitely had some questions that were not answered at the end of the book though I have some suspicions about the Bane. He is really a mysterious figure for most of the story and doesn't get as much page time as the creepy Inquisitor. I found her to be very menacing and she added suspense to the story whenever she appeared. I thought this was a strong beginning to the Elemental Trilogy and I am definitely looking forward to the next book. The Burning Sky is an entertaining blend of humor, suspense, and fantasy with engaging characters. I think this book would appeal to fans of Rae Carson, Chantress by Amy Butler Greenfield, Poison by Bridget Zinn, and other teen fantasy.

Having heard so many amazing things about Megan Whalen Turner's The Queen's Thief series, I finally snatched up the THE THIEF. After bragging that he "can steal anything," Gen ends up in the King's prisons, only to later be selected by the King's scholar, the magus, to accompany him on a journey to seek out-and steal-and invaluable ancient treasure. I found the beginning of this one a little slow, but the second half made up for it tenfold. Talk about twists and turns and surprises. (Like Jellicoe Road, I would tell hesitant readers to give this one ~100p before quitting.) Gen's voice is blunt and humorous-he's lazy, and yet completely sympathetic, likely because he does have the skills to back up his bragging (and then some). He's also one of my favorite types of narrators: an unreliable one. This fantasy world is rich and evocative-an almost Greek-like setting, but with a unique series of gods/goddesses and their own histories-and the character development is top notch. None of the characters we start out with as a reader are left unchanged by the end. I've heard the second and third installments in this series are where the story really shines, so after a thoroughly enjoyable tale in THE THIEF, I'm pumped to pick up THE QUEEN OF ATTOLIA. It's difficult to rate a book of short stories, for me. They can be so different from each other, so that one is totally to your taste and another is not. Throw in some poetry too, and there's even more opportunity to leave people cold (I don't know many people who aren't picky about poetry). So the good, first: this is pretty typically Gaiman's work, wry and dark and twisted, rich with implications and things lurking in the shadows. His stories all flow well, so that it all leads logically on to the ending (which is not to say that the endings are predictable, though familiarity with Neil Gaiman's imagination might give you a pretty good idea). The bad: I did find it a mite too familiar. That might partially be because I read the introductions to each story first -- always something of great interest to me, but it does flavour how you're going to experience the story. Secondly, Neil Gaiman's poetry pretty much doesn't do it for me. And thirdly, the opinions on "trigger warnings", from which Gaiman took his title, were... fairly typically as though he had not actually discussed them with anyone. I'm a big advocate for them, and I think most quibbles against them are nonsense; sure, life itself doesn't have trigger warnings. And? Why should that stop us from giving other people notice when we can? "Here be bad things" is something, but triggers are so different for different people... Stick a label on the story like you do nutrition information on food: not everyone will read it, but those who can benefit from the additional knowledge and preparation. And not "this product may contain nuts, soy or dairy products", but "this product does contain nuts" or "this product was manufactured in a factory which also processes nuts". Actual, precise information about common triggers. It's not going to cover every eventuality, and we can't pretend it will, but it would make sense to try. And not just by saying "these stories end badly for at least one person in them". All in all, that sounds very critical. I did enjoy reading the stories, though, and I think Gaiman does clever things with the form. I'm just a bit too used to his kind of cleverness.

I reviewed this book with my blogmate Celeste and our good friend Sim over at The Book Hookup we decided to rate this 1 billion stars, but the ratings max out at 5...so it's a 5 star. And that means top shelf here at The Book Hookup. First Thoughts: Celeste: HOLD. ME. I don't think I can write a review that will do this book justice. It was so good. I had all the feels from book 1, Charade, but now I have ALL THE FEELS. Sim: This book!!! It ripped my heart out... Loved it!! Ana: This book brought the ugly cry, the heartbreak and the flails...it had it all! Plot, Pacing and Style: Celeste: In this installment of the Games series these characters, Delaney and Adrian, are so very broken. And when I say broken, I mean broken. They have had so much tragedy in their lives. I was broken hearted for them. Delaney's goal was to track down Adrian to find some peace from an incident that changed their lives in the worst way possible. But, Delaney never expected to fall for Adrian. The story of their love was so powerful - I couldn't help but be moved. The pacing was perfect: slow and steady, which was so realistic. Nyrae Dawn's writing style, combined with the alternating POVs is so easy to read, I finished the book in nearly one sitting. I will read ANYTHING she writes. Sim: Delaney went in search to help someone, and maybe help herself, but found love instead. Completely unexpected, but maybe even better than what she set out for. Adrian was running from everything, but mostly himself. The love these two develop for one another is a deep one and the poetry that Adrian uses just intensifies it on so many levels. 'Haunt me, my little ghost, Possess me. Live inside me, And scare away my sins Until there's nothing left. But you.' Ana: This story felt so real. The characters were so real, so raw, yet so likeable. The pace was perfect. The heart stopping moments were intertwined with the bits of happiness, the confusion was linked to the past and present and the love was explored with kid gloves and trepidation in such a delicious way. The MCs: Celeste: Holy damaged goods. I don't know who had more of a haunted past, Adrian or Delaney. Both are totally hot, they know it, but are still full of self doubt which makes them so real. The story is told in alternating first person POVs, so we got to get in their heads and I can tell you...I adored both of them. They are down and devastated, but still keep going. Sim: Both have deep intense souls which makes me love them! Throughout all the bad stuff they had to deal with, they fight their own way back at life. You can't help but understand the decisions they made, even if they were not always the right ones and that's a great accomplishment of the writer. 'Her tears rival my rain,' Ana: I fell head over heels in love with both of these characters very early on. I rooted for them in their struggles and cheered them on in their attempts to save themselves and each other. Their relationship was so intense and their struggles so huge yet, somehow, I was able to connect with them. These two characters needed each other in order to find the strength that was deep down inside each of them. Their struggles were heart wrenching but their story was worth the ugly cry and the tissues. Romance /Chemistry: Celeste: Nyrae Dawn hit this one out of the park. The attraction was undeniable from the word go. It's not just the physical side of things (which was AMAZING), but the emotional connection was so strong. "I can't.... We shouldn't..." If you knew, you would want to. You'd throw me out. "I think we can and maybe it doesn't matter if we should." His voice is low, sexy. I shiver. Sim: From a seemingly no-ties hookup, to a deep deep connection that had the sparks flying; loved every second! There's no teasing or fooling around but an intense connection. And the poetry: omg I loved it!!! The intensity: just wow! She's the rapid pulse in my neck and the welcomed ache in my chest.... Celeste: Sim, omg. that quote *dies* Ana: Utter perfection. The chemistry was strong and deep. These two were meant for each other and the intensity of their connection left me breathless! "She knows my words, which are part of my soul, a part I've never willingly let anyone else see, yet I show them to her. I write them for her. She knows those part of me - the only parts of me that aren't a lie." Title/Cover: Celeste: Love them both! The title is seriously perfect, and the cover is just right. It's like they are about to kiss and connect but are still holding back a bit. I feel like I saw another cover of this somewhere and liked that one a bit better, but this is still good. Sim: This cover fits the book better. It could still use a bit more intensity IMO. Ana: Easy to see where the title came from since the word was used several times in the book. The title and the cover suit the story well. Twists and Turns: Celeste: There was definitely something that came up that I didn't' expect and it hurt my heart even more. It was painful, but added so much depth to the story. I loved it. Well done, Nyrae! But you might owe me a box of tissues. Sim: There was one point in the book that had me blown away and gasping for air. It hurt my heart even more but it explained a lot as well. Ana: Well, I didn't see that coming and let me tell you that, from that point on, there was no consoling me...tears, tissues and tweets about how my heart was breaking...yup, that's what happened! Ending: Celeste: The perfect ending was perfect. It was real. Adrian's note to Delaney...I don't even have any words....It's a fantastic stand alone book, but I hope I see some snippets of them in Maddox's story next. Sim: perfect! No butterflies and shiny sunsets but a real ending, fitting in perfectly with the characters. Ana: Great ending! The author must have known that I was all out of tears and it was time to bring it home...and she did a perfect job. Gripes/suggestions: Celeste: None. Well, maybe the fact that it's over and I wish there had been a longer epilogue. Sim: somehow the ending came too soon for me. Other then that: perfect. Ana: None that I can think of. This book captured my heart, exhausted my tear supply and made me a huge fan of Nyrae Dawn! I'm so looking forward to Maddox's story! Final Thoughts/Rec It? Celeste: A million trillion times YES. Sim: yup!!! And I can't wait to find out more about Maddox!!! (Masquerade: coming out January 2014) Ana: Absolutely no doubt...you must read this book!

(Book chosen for review by poll) This is, of course, one of the most discussed books of recent years, usually for either a) being rubbish or b) its supposed novelty value and taboo-breaking or shocking ideological angles. Like a lot of very popular, much-discussed books (cf. Twilight, Fifty Shades of Grey) it's actually not particularly radical or original. The "conspiracy theory" it expounds is largely fictional (which would be unremarkable if so much of the "buzz" around it didn't revolve around the teasing of the possibility that it was all true) and in fact so similar to the non-fiction book Holy Blood, Holy Grail that the authors of that book tried to sue Dan Brown. Similarly, fiction that portrays the Catholic Church in a negative or villainous light or that uses theology to spin a thriller plot is hardly revolutionary. The above paragraph was just to get all that out of the way, since I'm more interested in talking about The Da Vinci Code's merits as a novel (or lack thereof) separate from any brouhaha over its subject matter. I read it (via charity shop, like so many) sometime after it came out to see what all the fuss was about, and the two main impressions I gained from it were: 1) It was pretty dull and not at all worthy of so much controversy - I probably had a more exciting and memorable time scrambling around out-of-the-way bits of my Oxford college library looking for resources that might indicate whether there was any grain of truth in any of the Biblical conspiracy stuff. 2) In addition to generally dull/clunky writing, it committed a massive, blatant basic storytelling fail. It was largely this (combined with its undeserved fame) that caused me to put it on my "hall of shame" shelf. The big writing fail, to which most of the rest of this review will be devoted, is, put simply: the book has the wrong main character. Robert Langdon, our nominal hero, is thoroughly dull, seemingly existing solely to spout exposition and solve puzzles (I can't remember a single distinctive personal detail about him, not even some mundane Characterization 101 element like how he takes his coffee, what he wears, or even what he looks like). Worse, he's not only largely unengaged emotionally with the central plot, but he already knows much of the central "mystery" (with the only thing at stake being proof of this central conspiracy theory which he knows of but doesn't seem to care strongly about). This would be bad enough, were it not for the fact that the book has a much more suitable protagonist in Sophie Neveu. She has significantly more emotional investment in the plot (since it's her estranged grandfather who is murdered at the beginning) combined with the skills to actively assist in solving it (unlike a typical bereaved relative in a murder mystery), and all of the Biblical conspiracy theory flim-flam is new to her but not (to a great extent) to Langdon. All this means that our "hero" spends most of the book as something of a detached tag-along and exposition dispenser on the much more emotional and potentially much more interesting, but largely unexplored, journey of another character. The obvious reason for this, of course, is that this is the second book in a franchise revolving around Langdon, a sort of nerdy middle-aged James Bond (complete with "getting the girl" at the end, uuuurgh), and so he has to be the central character. (One could hypothesize that the other obvious reason is that Dan Brown prefers to write a middle-aged know-it-all male American protagonist, even in a novel set in France about religious attitudes to women, and if one were to go full gender politics on the subject, label this Mansplaining: The Novel.) This, to me, simply exposes the obvious problems with writing a franchise about a globe-trotting action-hero professor who solves mysteries others have more personal investment in, and isn't really a good excuse even if one accepts the franchise concept; it's perfectly possible to write a novel from one character's perspective that is more about another character's struggles and/or emotional journey; this article discusses the idea, using To Kill A Mockingbird and The Great Gatsby as examples. However, I suspect that Dan Brown isn't really too concerned with Novel-Writing 101 concepts like "who is this book about" or "what is the emotional journey", as opposed to lurid violence and grotesquerie (I didn't even mention the questionable "mad albino assassin monk" character), routine plot twists (WHAT A TWEEST!) or clever-sounding exposition about historical trivia, conspiracy theories etc. that keeps people reading and the columnists controversy-ing. So I guess my conclusion, like so many others, is that he's simply a writer of high-concept plot-driven airport thrillers who's managed through clever marketing and adherence to formula (apparently analysis has shown that his writing style is highly suited to keeping people turning the pages) to make it really, really big. (Not that there's any reason why high-concept thrillers have to insult people's intelligence or neglect interesting characterization - see for example Neal Stephenson's Reamde, which I've often described using the phrase "the best airport thriller in the world".)

3.5 Rockin' Stars! "Jet Keller was all kinds of temptation wrapped up in too-tight pants and with too many personal demons hidden in those dark, golden-rimmed eyes. He was every girl's rock-and-roll fantasy, with an edge that made him just sharp enough to be hard to handle." "Ayden Cross was a puzzle that, every time I thought I was close to solving, proved to have five extra pieces and no corners. For a long time, I thought she was Southern belle, complete with mile-long legs in cowboy boots, but then she would turn and do something that knocked me on my ass." Firstly, let me start by saying the guy on the cover does Jet absolutely no justice. Jet is hot! that guy..... not so much. After reading and loving Rule , I could not wait to start this book. I had loved both Ayden and Jet in the previous book and was really looking forward to their story. It pains me to say this but I'm afraid this book fell into what I like to refer to as second book slump, you know that second book in the series that never lives up to the standard set by the one before it?. I really think I could have loved this book if it had not been for the fact that for the vast majority of it I hated Ayden. She was completely self absorbed and utterly frustrating. She wallowed in self pity and made stupid decisions that really made no sense. Her continual inner monologues about what her future should be like and her determination that Jet is good enough to sleep with right now but has no place in her future was both frustrating and infuriating. She came across as shallow and insensitive in the way she treated both Jet and Adam for that matter. I understand she was trying to escape from a past she was ashamed of but the girl she thinks she should be was not that great either. I found her analytical approach to relationships tiring to the point that when she was expressing emotion I didn't really feel it. I am not going to lie, Jet was the saving grace for this book and the main reason I pushed through. He had a lot of emotional baggage thanks to his parents horrible relationship and has thus caused him to have some negative views and be fearful of love and relationships. But underneath that gorgeous rocker exterior was a vulnerable beautiful heart, full of passion who was loyal, protective and loving. I was so thankful that around the 75% Ayden finally transformed back into the sweet southern girl I had previously loved and got her head and heart straight. There was probably a lot of unnecessary drama in this book, but when they finally sorted all their issues out they were completely adorable together. Beneath their inner demons they both had good hearts and were totally and utterly in love with each other regardless of pasts or fears. "Ayden, I'm here. Of course I love you. I loved you before, I love you after, and I'll love you for everything in between." "You need it. The fire is your passion, it's your creative drive. You feel strongly about things, and care deeply about the people you love. I can handle the fire in you, Jet. It's just part of you." "Call me if you need me." "I'll always need you. I'll just call you because." Whilst I admit I did not love it as much as Rule I still enjoyed Jet and Ayden's (sometimes frustrating) journey and will be continuing with the series and hoping Crownover returns to delivering the same level of awesomeness she produced with her first book. ***These are just my personal opinions. Some people may agree with me, others may not and that's okay. I still appreciate and respect every ounce of work a writer puts in to creating their book and I enjoy reading them regardless of whether I loved them, liked them or loathed them.
