For some reason I didn't write a review for the first book, so I was a bit lost when I started The Eternity Cure. Allie has left Eden, leaving behind the humans she traveled with to reach their final destination. She knows Kanin is in some kind of trouble, his memories of being tortured haunt her nightmares. She can feel the faint pull of her sires blood, and is determined to rescue him for Sarren. Sarren is batshit crazy and has only just begun torturing Kanin for his betrayal sixty years ago. Kanin turned over his own kind, vampires, to the scientists who were seeking a cure. Sarren was one of those vampires, who was tested and experimented on for years. He recovered physically, but his mental state is downright psychotic. Allie can't stop thinking about Ezekial, (Zeek) the human she left behind in Eden, but she knows it's best for him. Fighting the urge of her very nature, trying not to bite him will only end in bloodshed. ***Spoilers*** While following the pull of her bloodline, it splits into two directions. She picks the strongest, which leads her to Jackal, her blood brother who killed some of her friends in book 1. He needs to find the cure, and she needs to find Kanin and Sarren. She reluctantly agrees to work with Jackal, knowing she can't best Sarren on her own. Their search leads them back to New Covington, Allies home. While trying to get into the vampire city, which is on lock-down because all the humans in the Fringe are crazy with a new strain of Red Lung disease, she runs into a group of the only humans left. Surprisingly Zeek is their leader, though he is not happy to see her with Jackal. He came here looking for Allie when she slipped out of Eden without saying goodbye. He joins the two of them, trying to get into the city, because without the Prince's help the humans he has been protecting will die. The three of them are met by the Prince's top pet, who is none other than Stick, the spineless punk Allie protected half of her life only to be stabbed in the back as soon as she's turned. As they are meeting with the prince, explaining that it was Sarren who released the virus on his city, Sarren steps out and attempts to kill them all, including the prince. Zeek gets a shot in on Sarren before he leaps out of the window. Prince Salazar agrees to release Kanin, as long as they all agree to return with the cure and/or Sarren. He poisons the blood given to Kanin with the infected blood of a human, guaranteeing they will search for Sarren instead of disappear. They have roughly 72 hours before the effects of the disease take over Kanins body. Fighting off a crowd of bleeders, Zeek is bitten, and infected with the Red Lung. They are forced to leave him behind while searching for Sarren. Jackal appears to have joined sides with Sarren when they find him, but releases Allie and attempts to fight him in the end. Sarren has the upper-hand against the two until Zeek surprises them, and shoots Sarren. He gets away from them but then they realize that Zeek is cured, b/c of the vaccines the doctors in Eden gave him. They give Kanin some of his blood and he gets better as well. They bring Salazar a vial of blood back, without telling him where it came from. The spiny bastard Stick, lures Zeek out to turn over to Sarren, but ends up stabbed for his effort. Kanin, Jackal, and Allie all return to the old hospital to find a video message from Sarren, showing him torturing Zeek until he reveals where Eden is located, then kills him. Allie is destroyed, but determined to get revenge as soon as she catches up to Sarren.

A book with a great start that unfortunately ends with a fallacious conclusion. At the end of the ninth chapter, the author asserts that there would be twice as many hockey players if we had two cut off dates. This is ridiculous. It would of course mitigate the bias of age (i.e. what month you are born would not have such a big impact on getting selected). At best we would have marginally better players (though it is quite possible that some other arbitrary cutoff would replace the old one). There can be only so many NHL teams and therefore so many professional players. He also asks, what if a million teenagers had access to the same advantages as Bill Gates, how many Microsoft would we have today? Well, it's quite obvious from his own argument that if so many had the same advantages, Bill would simply no longer be an outlier, and there would probably be no Microsoft. (This is not necessarily a bad thing, the combined contributions to society from these teenagers might be greater than those of Microsoft, a company with dubious achievements). Ultimately the biggest let down is that this book frustratingly refuses to address the subject of inequality. If outliers are, basically, those who got lucky among those who were capable, then what implication does this have for social policy? Is it reasonable that these outliers amass extraordinary amounts of wealth when fundamentally their contributions are the result of chance (not exclusively, of course. Outliers are all hard working individuals, my point here is about the difference in renumeration compared to other similar yet not as lucky individuals). Tyrants are outliers as well. And we could do without them.

Many months ago, I ordered some books online, and when the box arrived I discovered Peter Abrahams' Down the Rabbit Hole had mistakenly found its way into my box. Being the anarchic thief that I am, I decided to keep the book, tossing it on my tertiary to-read pile and promptly forgot about it. But last week I needed a book to read while doing the dishes, and noticed Down the Rabbit Hole sandwiched between A Game of Thrones and The Drawing of the Three, and since it fulfilled my doing-the-dishes requirements I decided to give it a go. My doing-the-dishes requirements are: 1. it has to be a book that can get wet, which means I can't care about it before reading; 2. it has to be something that doesn't require undivided attention (for instance, Gravity's Rainbow wouldn't qualify); & 3. it has to be a book I can toss aside without guilt (a complex internal system I can't explain here) if I'm not enjoying the experience. Down the Rabbit Hole fulfilled those three requirements, so I found myself reading this totally random book that's full of problems yet somehow manages to be a damn fine read. Problem 1. It is written in the third person, but just screams to be written in the first. Problem 2. Its reference to Alice in the title creates some reader expectations (at least in me) that were never fulfilled. Problem 3. The end made me feel like a lemming who suddenly realizes he's falling off the cliff. I was invested, I was excited, I was looking for more, and then it was over and the chapter to the next book was beginning. Not good. Problem 4. The Sherlock Holmes love fest was just too damn silly for me. Problem 5. Abrahams left too much hanging for future books, making me want to find out about Grampy's farm, how Joey and Ingrid develop as a couple, and all sorts of other things. Clever bastard! "Imagine if Bridget Jones fell into A million little pieces, flew over the cuckoo's nest and befriended Lindsey Lohan along the way." Okay I might have stolen that quote from the back of the book but it does describe Spin perfectly, so I couldn't help myself. This was a fantastic read and from a new Canadian author no less. Totally relatable, addictive and hilarious, I had trouble putting this one down. It's written along the lines of Sophia Kinsley's Confessions of a Shopaholic series or as I mentioned Bridget Jones's Diary, I also had flashes of Girl, Interrupted (if the loony bin were rehab) And yet despite all the comparisons Spin still manages to have a unique feel to it. Peppered with pop culture references from movies, TV and music there's even a chapter by chapter playlist included at the end. I also just love books that are written the way we girls actually think, you know with random disjointed thoughts and crazy insecurities. And how much fun is it to follow a heroine who isn't perfect? Kate, well she's a mess so it was an absolute blast stumbling along with her while she finds herself. Kate,(Katie, whatever) Sanford has just landed the job interview she's been dreaming about her entire adult life, (other than writing for Rolling Stone that is.) It's an interview with her favourite music magazine The Line. It's also Katie's 30th birthday which is all the more reason to celebrate, right? I mean what harm can meeting her friend Greer and having one little drink do? She'll still get home early enough to be clear headed and fresh for the big interview tomorrow. Well as most of us know there's no such thing as one drink (especially with friends like Greer.) Katie's botched interview is hilarious, she's late arriving, still a bit drunk and concludes the meeting by excusing herself to throw up and lie on the restroom floor. Needless to say she doesn't get the job. She is however just perfect for another assignment they have in mind; entering a 30 day stint in rehab to spy on the new "it" girl of the moment and writing a 5,000 word expose for their subsidiary gossip magazine. (Should she succeed the job she actually wants will also be waiting for her.) It's a no brainer really, at this point Katie has burned almost every bridge she can and has nothing left to loose, besides its only for 30 days. Kate's observations from rehab while somewhat heartbreaking still retain the comedy. Her experiments with jogging had me laughing out loud as did the descriptions of her dog obsessed counsellor. Of course there's a romance in bloom and hey what do you know she might just have a drinking issue after all. At the very least Katie needs to grow up and stop telling people she's still in college or at least partying with college kids. The rehab section of the story is predictable but that doesn't make it any less fun to watch the train wreck and cheer from the sidelines. The ending reads like a Hugh Grant movie and I loved it. Cheers 284jb5

Stuck in a tiny fortress situated between high mountains, a glacier, and a frozen fjord, Solveig, her brother Harald, and sister Asa, are surrounded by their father's warriors, a few servants, and a skald (storyteller). The king sent them to the far north for their protection during a war, but no one considered treachery from one of their own. Solveig has always been the overlooked on. She is not beautiful like her older sister, nor a male heir like her younger brother. She's just Solveig. Even her father rarely acknowledges her. But Solveig is important in a different way, as she finds out during the long winter. She is the one whose stories calm the restless warriors during the long nights and bring them comfort when they are struck down by a fatal poison. Thanks to the tutelage of Alric, her father's skald, she learns she has a voice and that gives her power. Forced to face harsh realities, she comes to understand that the fiercest warriors may have the gentlest hearts and the ones you trusted most may have dark secrets. She also learns that courage comes in many forms. Mr. Kirby has written a moving story full of action and adventure that will appeal to both boys and girls. It is the type of story that draws you in and doesn't let go until the last page. Though younger readers may not understand all the Viking references and terms, they'll figure it out through contextual clues, and even if they don't, it's still a great story. For a strong story set in distant Viking times with a touch of suspense, myths, action, and emotional ups and downs, definitely pick up Icefall when it comes out in October. Your tweens will enjoy it - and while you're at it, read it yourself. You'll be glad you did. It's definitely a story worth reading.

Reviewer: Diane Genre: M/M Contemporary 5 Hearts Review: Jake and Nate are the same age, they have been friends since birth since their mothers were best friends and the two boys became best friends as well. Jake was the athlete, Nate was the "scary smart" one! Nate came out in 8th grade, first to Jake, who supported him - and if the smart did not make him a bully target, add gay to that and if not for Jake, school would have been a lot more challenging! The story is told from the alternating points of view of Jake and Nate. These two men were first introduced in the first Home story, He Completes Me, so that could be a bit of a spoiler for the ending, however, that book does not explain how they came to be a couple or what challenges they had to deal with to get there. Boy, does this book do that in spades! Okay, this is two in a row where the author had me crying early on in the book! And for anyone who reads my reviews, you know if a book can make me cry, I usually love it! That was the case here, especially with Jake who sees so much and makes some very tough choices before he even finishes high school! Then to put himself on the line to the man he loves, his bestfriend, who then does not believe him! As the story progresses, they each go back to memories of key events with each other growing up. Nate realized he was gay because of Jake, he always wanted him but felt his feelings were not returned, which is likely why he has such a tough time believing him. Sadly, he also manages to hurt him a few times as well because people make assumptions about Jake and who he is, and Nate had done it as well. On the other side, Jake thought he'd offered himself, but since it was very clear in his head but not in his actions, Nate has believed Jake is straight all this time - and the number of times he had sex with women while in their teen years only added to Nate's belief, understandably so! I don't want to say too much, but if you have read He Completes Me, you know Jake has a perceived intimidating presence, what I loved about this book is that not only to learn why, but the vulnerability of Jake just under that surface, made this book a favorite in the series. If you like strong men with soft insides and romance that is full of heart along with misunderstanding, I would highly recommend this book! The entire time I was reading Eden's Root, one thought kept resonating: this wasn't just sci-fi - this was realistic science fiction. And for me, that is usually the most terrifying kind...the sort that isn't out of the real of possibility. This suspenseful novel forced me to think about possibilities that, although they scared me, also made me appreciate the Fi and her family live in, and the choices she makes to keep them safe. Ultimately, Eden's Root had a few issues that detracted from my enjoyment of it, but I still found it to be a wild ride I won't soon forget! While reading Rachel Fisher's novel, I struggled a bit with some of the characters. I've waited awhile after finishing to write my review, and I think there was something off in the character's voices for me. I liked the actual characters themselves well enough - Fi was brave and loyal, Sean was protective and strong, Asher was devoted and swoon-worthy, and the other members of the Family all had important roles to play. But in retrospect, even though I understand she was forced to grow up fast, Fi never felt like a teenager, nor did Sean or Asher, really. The only way I can describe it is that maybe Rachel struggled to really find their identities as teens - even teens who had grown up before they should have had to, due to their circumstances. Also there was a bit of a distance between the writing and their voices, almost as if she was afraid to get to close to the characters. However, I did find a lot to like about Eden's Root. I really loved the scenes with Fi and her father - to me, that's where part of the heart of the story lies, in Fi's devotion to her father, and in his wish to prepare her for the harsh realities she'd face after he was gone, another victim of the Sickness, a cancer-like disease transmitted through the very food they're eating. I also liked the unexpected romance between Fi and Asher! At first I thought Rachel Fisher was going in a different direction with the romance, but I'm happy with the way it all played out - it felt natural. Despite the fact that the pacing when it came to large passages of time felt choppy, Asher and Fi ARE given time to grow as friends and as a couple, so that their pairing felt more natural than rushed. Overall, I liked Eden's Root, and read it in one sitting, so that says something about the story being told and about the writing! I think Rachel Fisher has a lot of promise, because while there are a few aspects to this book that felt under-developed, there was also a great deal of potential for a brilliant sci-fi trilogy!

For a book with a premise so fitting my interests, I was surprised how ill-suited it was to my taste. All the voices seemed so similar: given to metaphor, a bit melodramatic, prone to over-explaining their choices about what they have and haven't included in their story... There were superficial habits to distinguish them, like a penchant for postscripts or a tendency abbreviate sentences by dropping the pronoun "I." But for such a diverse cast of characters, they all seemed remarkably literary in their descriptions. I began to wonder if the similarity of voices was intentional, given that they all come together in Eva, the babybot who introduces and closes the book. And you could trace a line of influence from Mary to Ruth, who edited Mary's diaries, from Mary and Ruth to Stephen Chinn, who pulled from both voices to develop Mary3, and from there to Eva, a version of Mary3, and Gaby, who grew up talking to Eva. But there's no reason for Mary and Alan Turing to have such similar voices or for Carl Dettman for that matter. In theory, Ruth and Carl, particularly Ruth, learned English in young adulthood, and yet they both manage it with the skill of highly literate native speakers -- not impossible, but still unlikely. Throughout the book, women wield silence as a weapon. Ruth and Dolores stop speaking to their husbands. Gaby cuts off conversations with Mary3. Mary refuses to speak to her new husband and her parents at various points. The author seems to want to beat you over the head with this theme, and yet... to what end? Similarly, the fibonacci connection of past and future in present is brought up in countless ways by each and every major character. I felt like the book was grasping at depth but failing. And my god. I could not stand Mary's silly reveries over her dog Ralph. Apart from repetitive and annoying, anachronistic methinks.

Their names are:- Quin Shinobu John. This book is very hard to review, in the sense that if i go into too much detail, I'll give a lot of things away and if i don't give enough detail, it'll be one confusing review! Quin, Shinobu and John have studied the art of becoming a seeker since they were young. To them becoming a seeker is to be a hero. It's all they ever wanted, all they've ever yearned and when time comes for the ultimate test, Quin and Shinobu passes but John fails. Quin and Shinoby realise quickly that being a seeker is not what they were told, they have been lied to since infancy and the scars they bear are too deep to contemplate. John after being kicked out and shamed strikes out and places their lives in danger. In her heart break Quin realises that the boy she's always loved- John is not exactly who she thought he was and with his bullet in her chest she is rescued by the boy who has silently loved her all along. Quin wakes up with no memorises of what happened and who did what. Shinobu loses himself in Hong Kong, running away from everything, including the girl he's always loved and who will never love him back...maybe. Sworn to never go back, fate has another plan. John is looking for them, because they stole something he wants and he will do anything to get it back and if need be, remove anyone who is in his way. The question is who is right and who is wrong? Are Quin and Shinobu the heros or villain? Or was John right all along and he is the one who is right? That is what this book is about and it's awesome in terms of the complexities of world-building. My one main complaint is that there was so many POVs and scenes from the past and then into the present that it confused me a bit. So why I rated it a 2- I didn't feel any connection to the characters, and the way the story went, I didn't have a moment where I had to guess at what would happen next. At times, the characters annoyed me too. I didn't feel that internal struggle in wishing I was there to help them during their plight. So maybe this book just wasn't for me per se, it may be more your thing! :) try it, seriously. Have a nice read :) -The Book Herald Find me on twitter- @thebookherald

This book is probably the best action-adventure fantasy I've ever read. The author's world-building is breathtaking. He even uses dialogue from several fictive languages (at least I didn't recognize them). A young boy (Kvothe) travels with his parents in a caravan of actors/musicians from town-to-town. This is their heritage and their talent. He learns about the use of sympathy - a form of magic - from an arcanist who travels with the troupe for a time and decides he wants to go to University to learn how to be an arcanist himself. Then things take a turn for the worse in his life. The story does not really slow down at any point. Although there are sections that seem a little slower than others, the pace is really perfect. There is an overarching plot, which I suppose is the glue that will hold this series together, in addition to many subplots. One of the most interesting things about the way this story is told is that it is in the first person because Kvothe is telling the story of his past to a Chronicler (in the present). That part of the story is told in third person perspective. A hard trick to pull off, but it felt seamless to me. In the present, there are several other points-of-view. But when Kvothe is telling his story, it is all in first-person limited - that is, only from his perspective. It works, believe me. Highly recommended - run out and buy it now.

The only reason why I bought this book was because of the gorgeous cover. My excitement over this book only grew more once I read the synopsis. I absolutely love stories where the characters escape to virtual worlds. I was not a big fan of this book. It was an uphill battle to read. I didn't particularly enjoy the writing style, mainly due to the main character rephrasing what was implied in the previous sentence. I understand why Regan supported Patrick while simultaneously rifled through the lies with Josh, I just wished she realized who was in the wrong sooner. Yes, Elusion is her father's second child and she wants to protect the last thing she has of her father. But when the proof is staring her straight in the face, it drags out the story. Lies. Lies. And more lies. This book wasn't terrible, it just wasn't my cup of tea. I did enjoy the scattered plot twist and mind puzzles thrown in throughout the book. But I found it difficult to predict the outcome if the main character is caught up in her own problems. That leads me to another thing. I think the story could've done without Regan and Josh getting together. Only because she began to question everything soon after they met. Not that is not necessarily a bad thing, but when she doubted her trust in Josh numerous times it felt like useless fluff. Especially when she took one glance at this face and instantly trusted him again. Again, I this book has potential and could be really enjoyable to some. It just wasn't for me, which I hate to say because I already bought the second book.
God, I read this such a long time ago. I don't even remember enough to give it a rating....

Smiley retells the story of King Lear through a small farming family. I am not familiar with King Lear, and I may have appreciated this book more if I was. Instead the drama and characters often seems unconnected, out of the blue and out of touch with reality. I believe a retelling should still be able to stand fully and solidly on its own, and I'm not sure this book does. However Smiley's writing and overall dark sense of relationships keep this novel interesting and pull the reader into a story that would otherwise lack coherence.
This book was read sometime during my Goodreads hiatus in June 2015 - September 2016

Unwind is a book that will honestly stay with me forever. It has forever changed my view of life, and quite frankly it scared me. After a certain part I literally had to stop and my only action was just to stare at the wall and just think "Wow." That's all I could muster up. This book was a strong hit, and it kept me guessing for more. The world and the characters were so vivid, I just ate the book up through 2 sittings. Although an easy read, it really has people thinking. I felt each emotion that the characters went through, and the Unwind part was just too much for me to bear. It was emotional, and I had the urge to stop reading it. Why? I just had that strong feeling after that part that some part of my mind wanted me to stop. But I got through it, and I was glad I did. The rest was smooth sailing. The only thing was the ending. I was hoping for a more conclusive like ending, but I heard of a sequel, so I'm anxiously awaiting for that to be published. Overall I enjoyed this book, and I would give it more than a 5 if that was possible on here, but I will read it again. Probably the best dystopian novel I've read since 1984.

I gave up, something I do rarely, but I just couldn't be bothered. The edition I read is plastered with rave reviews so it was a real disappointment after about 300 pages to realise that the writing wasn't going to improve. The plot was all over the place. It wasn't gripping. The leaps in deductive logic that the protagonist made were often ludicrous. What limited description there was of female characters was at best surface - more often simply sexist - and all the attempts to give a female viewpoint (e.g. the Saracen's mother) were simply unconvincing. I'm surprised at the high average score (currently 4.21). Maybe I'm missing something, or maybe it's just another book with a hefty marketing budget and an author who is too big to fail.

I'M FINALLY DONE WITH THIS BOOK. This took me ages. I can see why people would like this book, but it just doesn't work for me. I thought it was extremely slow and it used unneccesarily rich language. But the most annoying thing was how literary it was. I know that sounds weird and please understand: I like a book that knows how to be literary. I like solving the puzzles of the symbolism. But apparentely Salman Rushdie doesn't think I can handle a bit of symbolism, so he takes you be the hand and explains everything! I even came across a fragment where he continues to explain the title of the chapter for three paragraphs long! Stop it, that's my puzzle. It just made the book boring for me because it prevented me from having to work to get to the deeper meaning. I guess this does make this book very suitable for high schools: I know of a lot of people who had trouble recognising that kind of literaryness in high school and this book may be a solution for them. But to me, it just took all the fun out of it.

This series is well on the way on becoming one of my favorite series of all time, but I'm gonna hold my judgment until I've read all books. After all, its the ending that matters the most. This book was more than a fantasy, it was a political science book. I learned so much on how a person grows to become a leader and how he must not think of himself higher than the law, even if he is the one who made them. "I will not be an exception to my own law". I was so overwhelmed by this statement. Standing firm on your beliefs even when you have an entire army under your command is a bloody difficult thing to accomplish. but the way Elend kept his word regarding his laws and never once tried to force his will on the Assembly and the people was SO HEARTWARMING! He proved to be such a good man that sometimes I thought he can't be that good, he'll turn evil eventually. "Oh, now he's gonna kill them for taking his throne". "Oh, now he'll ditch Vin for killing Cett's army". But no, this guy actually loves and trusts those around him by all his heart. But I don't aspire him, because I know I can never be like him. But one thing is for sure, Elend has become a man that Kelsier never could, but I still love Kelsier more. I don't know why, I just do. Speaking of, oh how I wished that Watcher was Kelsier in the start of the book, but it turned out to be that evil Zane. I was so mad when he blatantly kept lying to Vin and misleading her away from his friends and Elend. I was mad at Vin for trusting him so much but I can't blame her. She had too much power, and too many people who relied on her. And when she found someone like her, it was natural for her to feel understood. If this were a YA book, Vin would've definitely ditched Elend and made out with Zane before realizing she made the wrong choice. But because this is an adult book, Vin was smart and finally saw she should be with the man who loved and trusted her. I knew Elend would snap sooner or later. I knew he would become a mistborn and I'm so glad he finally became one, albeit in unfavorable circumstances. I also thought he would be the one who became the Hero of Ages, but oh well. For such a long book, I was disappointed when it ended. It was just that good. I can't wait to find how Hero of Ages turns out. I hope it will be as good as its predecessors.

WHAT IS LIFE? THIS BOOK HAS KILLED ME. I'm just going to get right to the point. I loved this book. I can't think of any real negative things to say. Right from the start, I loved the writing and concept. Sarah J. Mass is such an amazing storyteller. She's such an amazing author. Everything about this book is so fantastical and glorious. Even though I loved the writing and concept from the start, it took me to about page 180 to really get invested in the characters. I really like Feyre. I didn't think she was annoying or stupid and she could really hold her own. She was so well written and awesome. I did want to slap her up the head a couple of times though. Tamlin was also a really cool character. He was really interesting and right away I wanted a back story. However, as the story progressed, he got less and less interesting compared to two other characters. Rhysand and Lucien completely stole the book for me. Both are such interesting, complex characters and I couldn't wait to read more about them. Towards the end of the book, Rhysand had completely hooked. I just wanted to know more about him as a character. I loved the pace of this book. It was fast but not rushed and kept me entertained the whole time. So much happens in this book but it all unfolded at a natural pace. This book could easily have been a standalone (though I'm glad it's not) so I'm insanely curious to know what happens in the next book. Overall, A Court of Thorns and Roses is definitely one of the best books I've read this year and one of my new all time favorites. I loved everything about this book and the last quarter had me half dead (in the best way). I couldn't put it down and I was completely hooked. I highly recommend this book to everyone.

2014 is going to be known as my year of disappointment with dust jackets. Either they leave out crucial trigger-warnings (Passion Play) or because they completely lie about what direction the story is going (A Darkling Sea) or in the case of The Godless, THEY TELL THE WHOLE DAMN PLOT! No, literally, the dust jacket says, "Split between three points of view, this masterful narrative reaches it's conclusion during an epic siege, during which all sides must fight for their lives. As the siege of Mireea is laid, the loyalties of Ayae, Zaifyr, and Bueralan will be tested, as from beneath the city and its bloodstained caverns, secrets emerge, enemies are revealed, and their world hangs in the balance." I actually flipped to the conclusion to double-check. WTF St. Martin's Press??? I was so excited reading this book's first five "chapters" on Tor.com that I immediately requested its purchase at my local library (buy 5 copies!) and eagerly awaited the weeks before it arrived. Then I sat down to read and I got this horrible sinking feeling like when some jerk sees you watching the penultimate episode of a super-popular series and shouts out, "Character X dies at the end!" Really? I got spoilered by the DUST JACKET??? But it is true. The worst part is that the spoiler destroys the whole narrative purpose for one of the three viewpoint characters. Knowing that he failed at the outset was disappointing because I was quite interested to see if he would succeed in his assignment. I have a theory about why the blurb writer did it, which I'll return to at the end. Anyway, there is a lot to like about this book, and that is why I gave it three stars despite that pushes it above a lot of other books I have liked better. First of all, its magic system is so unique and awesome. A world built on the backs of buried gods? Their rotting bodies the source of the magic infecting people in the world? Very awesome! Zaifyr's power is especially interesting to me. A half-crazed immortal who is cursed with seeing, and sometimes granting the evil wishes of, the spirits of everything that has died since the God of Death was killed. I could have had an entire book from his perspective alone. I was actually hoping for a romance between him and Ayae just so I could have more book-time with him. He was fascinating. Second, the gender disparity in this book. It was amazingly equal! Women rulers, women soldiers, women mercenaries, women priestesses, women immortals, women gods. I enjoyed it and it felt natural. I will probably pick up the second book just to see how it goes. After all of the other crap fantasy I've read this year, a book where violence against women wasn't a plot point or where there was more than one female fighter in a sea of testosterone makes The Godless stand out like a rare, valuable jewel. I was also quite interested in the Chinese-influence names (though I had a little trouble pronouncing some them in my head), the sweeping scope of history, and the wonderful inclusion of fables. This feels like a complete world. I could almost see the fractured sun. I definitely want to know what happens next. But what I didn't like was... ...this entire book feels like a prologue. What, you say? A city fell and all of the inhabitants had to flee, the heroine learned to embrace her curse-powers, two bad guys got killed which will restart a war of the immortals, and uber-bad the "Child of the Gods" was introduced, and you feel like nothing important happened? Answer: Yes. And it kind of gets back to the dust jacket, weirdly. It's like this whole book is the prologue for something much more interesting to come. So, the dust jacket is supposed to tell all of the interesting stuff in the beginning. But if the whole book is the prologue, then it hasn't really spoiled anything, has it? I sort of wonder where the rest of the series is going to go. A lot of people died in Book 1, and that was just to get all of the set pieces onto the table. By the end of it, we finally know the actual stakes of the series: a God is returning to the world, and no one will have a good afterlife until something has been done about it. That's opening-chapter stuff right there. I think that this series will not wrap up in a neat trilogy. It will be one of those series that goes on and on and on. I'm not really into those kinds of books. I prefer a neat, tidy novel that I can sit down with and finish a storyline. I loved the Kushiel's Dart series because each book was interconnected to a larger whole and the whole series made an arc, but in each book, you felt like the challenge was met and the resolution was satisfying. I'm really not interested in the Wheel of Time phenomenon where you read 600 pages and two weeks pass in the storylines of eight characters. No thanks. If that is your bag, then this probably won't bother you. But that's usually a two-star or lower rating for me. The other thing that I at first enjoyed, then grew to dislike, was the practice of interweaving a bunch of flashbacks. It is constant, especially at the end. One character is running across a bedroom, then thinking of a conversation that happened half an hour earlier in a hospital, then returning to the bedroom, then flashing back to the important outcome where someone died half an hour ago, and then you know why they're running across a bedroom now. It's like having a conversation with someone who keeps interrupting themselves to say, "Oh wait, I thought of one more thing that happened before." After multiple chapters like this in a row, I just wanted to shake the book and say, "Tell me the damned story! Start over at the beginning, and just lay it out one at a time." It didn't bother me at the beginning, and even interweaving chapters in ancient time & modern time didn't bother me, but at the end it started to grate. It's possible that it's an echo of how the gods experience time differently than people. Which, okay. But I would have preferred a straight up adventure epic, so it didn't entirely work for me. Hmm, speaking of epic, I think this is my most epic review on Goodreads to date. Conclusion: I didn't love this book as much as I was hoping to based on the first five chapters on Tor.com. I love the magic and the world, and I think the story might actually get interesting from Book 2 onward once the set pieces introduced in Book 1 start their big moves. We'll see.

Former rich-girl Audrey never really knew what to do with her life. She tried college, twice. Didn't work out. After that, her Boston-royalty mom cut her off from the family money. And Audrey found her passion on her own...she went to culinary school and became a chef. Only she's not really working as a chef yet. She's interning at this huge Restaurant-group, BPG, as the girl for everything. Everything she's not really talented for. They send her off to Vermont to talk farmers into selling their fine products to Boston restaurants. That's where she runs into Griffin. Again. They had a little - and verrry hot - two-week-affair five years ago. And the attraction is still there. So between fighting about cider prices and Audrey cooking in Griff's mom's kitchen, there will be some very sexy moments. But can a farmer from Vermont and an up-and-coming cooking legend from Boston ever get their Happy Ending with each other? What will happen to Audrey & Griff? Will there be a Happily Ever After? Or will there be a huge Cliffy? I'm not spoiling anything!! Oooohh - the cover! Such a hot cover-guy. Even though he kinda had me thinking of some kind of shapeshifter-vampire-werewolves book at first I think the cover - even though it's really hot - is a tiny bit too dark for this happy-sunny-apple-cider story. And I LoOoOoOoVED the story! I can't even find enough words to say how much I loved this book!!! Griff and Audrey are sooo adorable! Griffin, the brooding, grouchy, quiet farmer. Who's had to worry about the family farm ever since his dad died and he had to give up his football future. But who is now so very adorably proud of his cider and everything he achieved. And this cute former rich sorority girl, who finally knows what she wants to do with her life. It's just too cute to watch them argue and make up. And I loved how Audrey felt right at home with Griff's family. She only ever had her not very loving, single mom and cooks and maids growing up. She was never allowed in the kitchen. But Griff's mom lets her do whatever she wants in the kitchen. You just want Griffin and Audrey to hurry the eff up and get married, so that she can move in there and cook for the farm. But of course it's not as simple as that. She's dreaming of owning her own restaurant ... in Boston. This book had everything a great romance needs. VERRY funny and adorable and even some very moving scenes and of course .... lots of SEXY times!!! I'm not really good with words and writing, so I can't really express how much I adored this book. But I did. You should go and read it asap. Or not - because I wouldn't mind keeping Griff and his cider all for myself And I loved all the supporting characters - Griff's family and the farm-helperlings... perfect cast! I wouldn't mind seeing this series on HBO one day Can't wait to see what Jude will tell us in the next book! BITTERSWEET was an amazingly funny & adorable & sexy & moving Romance! What's not to love about a hot & adorable bearded apple farmer? I'm planning of moving there asap, get rid of Audrey and move in with Griff to 'make cider' for the rest of our lives!!! Sorry Audrey

It was like being punched in the face with rainbows and puppies. P.S. Henry Cheng, tho P.P.S. Gansey is a precious little cinnamon roll, and I love him dearly.

Miles was completely obsessed with Mallory. Like, in a weird scary way (in my opinion). But she found it hot so ... *shrugs* At least she realized he was an obsessed stalker. She just happened to like that about him. She needed that. So I guess I can't judge. This book was like a tame version of 50 Shades. I didn't love it, but it was fun to read because of the running commentary in my head and all the mental eye rolling that happened whenever Mallory would admit she should probably be afraid of Miles but was turned on by his stalkerish actions. Plus, it actually has me interested in the next part in the series to see what happens with Paige and Ryan.

"This is something I know: no matter how far you have run, no matter how long you have been lost, it is never too late to be found...Remember, those who are loved are never lost." Naomi is a child finder -- she searches for missing children. Her past is lost to her, but she feels that one day she may become whole again -- if only. Madison Culver, 5 years old, disappeared when her family went up into the Skookum National Forest to look for a Christmas tree. The parents hire Naomi to find their daughter who would now be 8 years old -- if she survived. Well. This book has been praised in so many circles and was recommended to me by a friend (thanks, Kim) and I can definitely see why it's getting so many accolades. This atomospheric drama is rife with beautiful prose and a sad but lovely narrative. One can feel the bite of the cold and the beauty of the snowy wilderness and isolation of the high mountains. One can agonize over the fate of one little girl while also lamenting the horrors that created the one who terrorized her. Naomi is an enigma even to herself -- she has no memories beyond the time when she came as a foster child to live with Mrs. Cottle and another foster, Jerome. She almost knows love, but she's afraid and she cannot stop running -- she's "a wind traveling over the field, always searching, never stopping, and never knowing that true peace is when you curl around one little piece of something." This is a story that will stay with me for a long time. I can't recommend it highly enough but don't want to give more detail or spoilers. Thank you to Edelweiss and Harper Publishing for this e-book ARC to read and review.

Ho hum. I tried reading this book last year or the year before. Ever since reading The Left Hand of Darkness in college for a science fiction class (super cutting edge to have one of those at the time in the late 1970s, by the way), I avoided her work because it seemed so message-heavy (just hit me with a hammer, why don't you? and yes I know it won a zillion awards ...) It was my daughter Hannah who told me this book was more of a wizardry type book than a message-driven work. I knew it was famous so I gave it a shot. If I'd read it when I was much younger I think I'd have loved it. Or if I'd read it before being exposed to all the other books which this one undoubtedly influenced, I might have enjoyed it more. As it is, I knew quite well where it was going ... or close enough ... and got bored about halfway through. That part isn't Le Guin's fault I feel, but probably is due to the fact that her influence put others on the track to pushing the "coming of age, wizardry" genre past the ground this book covered. In essence, it suffers from its own worth. And, of course, there is the fact that I've been reading sf/fantasy since the 1960s (oh the dating of myself, how it hurts! ha!) so I've seen this story done a lot. A lot. And better. Hence the two stars. It was ok.
